file: An Empire Run Amid Rice Paddies.txt
text:
ï»¿
Retailers in bankruptcy?
A crumbling real estate market?
A global recession?
The problems might as well be happening on Mars, as far as Zhang Guoxi is concerned.
While gnarled old peasants slog barefoot behind water buffaloes in the rice paddies here, Mr. Zhang, apparently China's richest private businessman, has found a better way to make a living.
A balding 39-year-old who dropped out of school after the sixth grade, Mr. Zhang runs an international business empire based on furniture exports, property development and stock trading from his 10-story corporate headquarters, which juts above the paddies. 
From this remote country town he has emerged as an entrepreneur with assets worth tens of millions of dollars.
Â 
Defining the Limits
Mr. Zhang (whose full name is pronounced JAHNG gwaw-shee) is one of the best measures of how much capitalism the Communist authorities are prepared to tolerate in their drive for national prosperity. 
For 15 years, he has more or less defined the frontier of what can be tolerated, and despite the hardline oratory from Beijing in the last few years, he continues to thrive.
"Sure, I live very well," he said, grinning, when he was asked how many homes he owns. 
"Very well!"
After a pause, he added with a mischievous gleam in his eye: "So I should say, 'Long live Comrade Xiaoping!'
" The reference was to Deng Xiaoping, the 87-year-old paramount Chinese leader, who since January has led a new drive to carry out further capitalist-style changes in the economy.
In a society where peasants earn cash incomes of about $150 a year, Mr. Zhang is rich in a way that can scarcely be fathomed, rich in a way that the Rockefellers are rich. 
He sips Remy Martin cognac, and he has a chauffeur-driven car waiting for him in each city where he has an office. 
The state even provides him with his own police station of a dozen officers solely to protect his company and serve as his bodyguards.
Mr. Zhang may be leading the pack, but there are many other business tycoons emerging across China, capturing the spirit of the times. 
In the 1970's, many Chinese wanted to be revolutionary; today, they want to be rich. 
Most private businesses are only about a dozen years old, but they are expanding rapidly and branching across the nation and even the world. 
By the end of the century, China's private industrialists may be far more numerous and powerful than they are today.
"Deng Xiaoping has always said that China should let some people get rich first and let these people pull the economy along," said Christine Wong, an associate professor of economics at the University of California at Santa Cruz. 
"Now that Deng Xiaoping has reasserted his dominance in trying to formulate economic policy, I expect that things will look up for people like that."
Already the wealth and power that Mr. Zhang has gathered are jarring, partly because his base is not Beijing or Shanghai, but this small county seat of Yujiang in Jiangxi Province. 
Jiangxi is a poor, landlocked area that early in the century was a Communist guerrilla base. 
Most of the buildings around Yujiang are dilapidated brick homes with propaganda slogans proclaiming "Socialism is Good!" or calling on people to have just one child.
Â 
Touches of Modernity
Mr. Zhang's corporate headquarters rises abruptly from these surroundings, 10 stories of gleaming modernity with international direct dialing and fax service, in a sprawling compound that also includes a goldfish pond and two marble arches -- "I'm an artist, after all," he explained. 
His buildings have their own slogans, but they are not political: "Guard against fires!" the banners warn.
Financial success carries political risks in China, and for that reason Mr. Zhang prefers to refer to his enterprise not as "privately run" but as "people run."
But he does not dispute that his company is privately owned -- after all it is called the Guoxi Group, named after him -- and Government ministries have publicly referred to it as a private company.
Mr. Zhang is also discreet enough to dodge questions about his personal spending habits and about his net worth, but he finally acknowledges that $30 million or more might be a good estimate.
"More or less, more or less," he repeats, each time accenting the word "more."
Â 
Some Special Skills
Entrepreneurs in China often run into trouble with grasping officials, who arbitrarily impose huge taxes or who force the owner to sell to the Government. 
Mr. Zhang has had few such problems, and his methods offer a window into the skills that business tycoons need to succeed in China.
One of the most crucial skills is cultivation of Government and Communist Party officials, a task that the gregarious Mr. Zhang assumes with ease. 
He is a good friend of the provincial governor and of county officials, and he has contributed more than $1.5 million in recent years to local charities and public causes.
"He is a good party member and an excellent businessman," Gov. Wu Guanzheng said of Mr. Zhang at a recent public meeting. 
"For many years he has loved the party and the people, and done many good deeds."
The latest good deed -- and the purpose of the meeting -- was Mr. Zhang's contribution of $200,000 to endow a new Zhang Guoxi Education Foundation. 
Everything he contributes to seems to bear his name: the Zhang Guoxi Big Bridge is being completed to link Yujiang with the other side of a broad river.
"Boss, three cars can pass at a time on the bridge, no problem!"
Luo Genshen, the head of the construction team, says obsequiously as Mr. Zhang stands in the middle of the bridge and inspects the work. 
After asking a few questions, Mr. Zhang returns to his Nissan Cedrick to be chauffeured to his next spot on a round of inspections.
Â 
Providing Services
Mr. Zhang also helped pay to bring running water and international telephone service to Yujiang. 
In addition, he contributed the only other structures in Yujiang that rival his headquarters in height: a television relay tower to improve local reception and a seven-story science tower at the local school.
Perhaps because of the philanthropy, local officials regard Mr. Zhang as a great hero rather than an evil capitalist. 
"We hope that more Zhang Guoxis will emerge!"
The Jiangxi Daily News declared in a front-page headline. 
And local Communist Party officials have formally called on the entire community to "learn from Comrade Zhang Guoxi."
In some parts of China, including Beijing, Communist Party organizations have officially banned wealthy entrepreneurs from joining the party. 
But Mr. Zhang joined the party in 1972, long before he struck it rich, and he not only remains in the party but serves as party boss of his enterprise group, while also holding down the posts of chairman and general manager.
Zhang Guoxi's name means fruit of happiness, because at birth he was only a bit more than four pounds, the size of a small fruit. 
His mother died when he was 2, and after finishing elementary school he dropped out and began work as a carpenter. 
A few years later, in 1973, he sold his family home for $250 and used the money to start his company.
Initially, the company made carved wooden chests, when it was not fighting off criticisms and investigations by Communist Party ideologues who denounced it as the "tail of capitalism."
Â 
Recalling Rough Times
"I'm fine now, and people see me going abroad and praised in the papers, and so on," Mr. Zhang said soberly. 
"But back in 1973 to 1977, it was really rough and I was often hungry. 
If I told you about those years, you'd be in tears."
After Mr. Deng came to power in 1978, the company prospered and began to export the wooden chests and other carved furniture to Japan. 
Then it branched into the manufacture of gold-plated Buddhist altars, which in Japan sell for about $10,000 each.
As business grew, Mr. Zhang opened offices in three Chinese cities, as well as Japan, Hong Kong, Canada and Germany. 
The Guoxi Group became a general international trading company, with interests ranging from stock trading in Hong Kong to Chinese restaurants in Germany. 
The company is about to open a new trading office in Thailand and is building a nine-story hotel in the southern Chinese resort of Sanya.

file: As China_s Economy Thrives, The Public Sector Flounders.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Avenue of Eternal Peace, the main road through the capital, ends at the gate to one of the country's gargantuan state enterprises, a steel factory that employs 186,000 workers and sprawls from the edge of the city into the mountains and plains beyond.
It takes half an hour by train to go from one end to the other of the central factory of the Capital Iron and Steel Mill, where giant blast furnaces run 24 hours a day. 
Along the way, the main path splinters into the different parts of this mini-society: a park, a flower garden with a small zoo, a hospital, two colleges, a nursery, a kindergarten, and a farm that grows fish, poultry and vegetables for the factory workers.
In its conception, Capital Steel was the Communist antidote to a class society; it was an integrated community where people work for the state and the state supplies them with their every need, where men and women would be entitled to a job, a house, free health care and a few bowls of subsidized rice each day.
After 40 years of Communist Party rule, however, that dream has collapsed and the system has decayed into a giant labyrinth of mismanagement, an underclass in an emerging dual economy that pits the market mechanism against central planning.
Â 
A Two-Tier Economy
The import of capitalistic attitudes by private businesses and collectives has brought economic expansion and prosperity to southeast China's provinces, such as Guangdong, Fujian and Zhejiang. 
But China seems compelled to cling to the lagging state sector, and the growing economic inequalities between the two tiers of the economy are leading to political headaches for China's Communist leaders.
With orthodox ideology discredited throughout the country, China's state sector, still the largest part of the country's economy, is one of the most important Communist symbols left and it is slowly withering: some 40 percent of the state enterprises are losing money, stockpiles of unsold goods are mounting, and losses are growing daily.
Government-owned businesses continue to benefit from all sorts of preferential policies and the Government has agreed to lighten their tax burden, but even so, these enterprises are being pummeled by competition from private and collective enterprises, and these days many no longer pay their bills or their debts.
"They are the state's main source of income and the backbone of the socialist economy," Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader, said recently. 
"So whether we can revive them affects not only the stabilityI of the national economy, but also the status of the public ownership economy and the solidity of the entire socialist system."
Â 
The System's Pride Becomes Albatross
Because these enterprises are seen as the bulwark of Chinese Communism, the Chinese leadership is devoting enormous efforts to reviving them. 
Perhaps no issue is now attracting so much attention of top Government leaders, and they likely face no greater frustration than the chronic losses and inefficiencies of the state sector.
With a growing number of factories refusing to pay their debts, doing business in China requires a measure of imagination. 
One factory recently resorted to sending a team of elderly, sick and disabled workers to plead, snivel and cry for repayment of loans from another enterprise.
That did not work, so the factory then dispatched a group of women employees with their babies crying piteously for food, according to an account in an official Shanghai newspaper. 
The hope was that the enterprise that owed the money would fear that the wails of babies would bring bad luck and would promptly repay. 
But that did not work either. 
These days, nothing seems to work.
"There is no hope for the state enterprises, no way out," said a Chinese economist who has worked for the Government on these problems. 
The best hope, she said, is that the state sector will expire quietly.
But many Chinese believe that is unlikely, and the leaders themselves apparently are afraid to allow the enterprises to collapse. 
A few years ago, when economic reformers were in control, there was an effort to introduce Western-style bankruptcy and force out of business those enterprises that were inefficient.
But the architect of the bankruptcy program was imprisoned after the 1989 crackdown, and the Chinese leadership now seems caught in a painful dilemma: it cannot afford the mounting losses of the state sector, but it dares not close the factories for fear of unrest from laid-off workers.
State-owned companies have dominated Chinese industry and manufacturing for four decades, but their share of the economy dropped sharply after Deng Xiaoping began the economic restructuring of the 1980's. 
The state sector accounts for only about 53 percent of industrial production, and the figure is dropping steadily.
Â 
Private Sector To Outstrip Public
This year or next will be a milestone: for the first time in more than four decades of Communist Party rule, less than half of industrial output will come from state enterprises. 
The leaders are aghast, but they seem to have no alternative but to accept economic growth, whatever its source. 
If the private sector will provide revenue and jobs, they will apparently accept it.
When Prime Minister Li Peng was examining the problems at a state-run enterprise in Guangdong recently, he reportedly said, in a fit of exasperation, "Share-ownership is the only way out."
Mr. Li's offhand remarks were never published, and so they are unlikely to reflect a policy shift. 
Nevertheless, as passed around in economic circles, they suggest the despair and disillusionment with the state sector at the highest level of Government. 
State-owned banks are forced to lend more and more money to keep state enterprises afloat, but for many enterprises there is little prospect that the debts will be repaid.
"It's a cancer to the economy," said Han Qiaowen, chief editor of a journal in Shanghai on debt problems. 
"The system of credit is breaking down. 
People no longer respect the need for credit, and there is no way to control this. 
If you owe money, there is no punishment."
Nationally, unpaid debts among enterprises totaled some $56 billion at the end of June. 
The Government said in October that about $19 billion in debts had been repaid, but did not say whether the total amount had fallen or risen.
In fact, many enterprises may actually have the funds to repay their debts to suppliers or other creditors, but they simply choose not to. 
Instead, they spread their funds among various accounts at several banks so that authorities would have difficulty proving that could repay.
"Just because we don't repay our loans doesn't mean our enterprise is going broke," said Zhang Guangde, deputy director of the China Textile Machinery Manufacturing Works in Shanghai. 
His enterprise owes nearly $2 million to suppliers, but he said it is also owed about the same amount by customers.
Â 
Borrowers Win, Creditors Lose
Because there is no legal framework to enforce loan repayment, collecting loans has become one of the biggest headaches among factory managers. 
A popular saying these days among businessmen goes: "Lending money is like spilling water on the floor."
Another goes: "Those who owe money are bold and self-assured; those who want repayment must crawl on their knees and beg."
To be sure, not all state enterprises are in such bad shape. 
The state is still immensely proud of Capital Steel and a few other factories that are still held up as examples of the best of Communism. 
By official count, one third of state enterprises are making money, nearly 40 percent are losing money and the rest are approximately breaking even.
Most of China's Government is financed by the one-third of companies that are still turning a profit. 
Anywhere from 55 percent to 75 percent of an enterprise's profits currently go to the Government in the form of various kinds of taxes.
The profitable companies also have to subsidize the money-losing ones. 
Subsidies to unprofitable companies rose from $8.4 billion in 1988 to $10.9 billion in 1990, and may be even higher this year. 
One third of the Government's revenues, far more than is spent on either the military or education, goes to bail out these money-losing enterprises.
One reason why the enterprises perform so poorly is that their main role has been not so much insuring profits as insuring political stabilityII by looking out for workers. 
Enterprises almost never dismiss workers, wages move up with seniority no matter how slovenly or unproductive people are, and so work places often resemble nothing so much as tea parties. 
Meanwhile, the companies still are responsible for the cradle-to-grave services for each tea-drinker.
At the Shanghai No. 2 Cotton Mill, for instance, there is a payroll of 10,600 people -- of whom only 4,000 are engaged in production. 
About 2,500 more are engaged in non-production work, ranging from preparing Communist Party slogans for meetings to fixing the plumbing in worker housing. 
In addition, the factory must pay pensions and provide housing for 4,100 retired workers.
The factories are also facing new commercial pressures. 
Two years ago, the Government determined everything: the amount that the factory would produce, the sale price, and the price of the raw materials. 
But this year, the state said it would buy only half the factory output and supply only half of the raw materials.
The result is that the mill was forced to buy raw cotton at a high free- market price for the other half of its production. 
But there is an oversupply of cotton yarn, and the factory says it cannot get a reasonable price for the yarn that the state no longer buys. 
For a factory that never had to make its own decisions or worry about profits, this is a rude awakening.
Last year profits were $2.5 million on revenues of $27 million, which is considered strong by Chinese standards. 
But not all of these profits can go into renovating machinery. 
The factory pays $566 per year per worker and then on top of that, it must dig into its profits to pay for all sorts of subsidies and to purchase or build housing for its workers.
Â 
Diverting Profits To Worker Benefits
Managers at many state-owned factories aim not to maximize profits but to maximize incomes and benefits for their workers, the constituency that is perhaps most important to them. 
Regulators scrutinize corporate accounts to insure that they are reinvesting enough in equipment and not diverting funds to buy eggs or vacation trips or housing for workers, but the No. 2 Cotton Mill admits glumly that it is not able to provide much for employees these days.
"Most of the workers have to find their own housing," said Zheng Fangyou, a deputy director at the factory. 
"I can't say that we provide most of our workers housing."
Understanding the problems of money-losing enterprises is complicated by the fact that everyone is trying to conceal problems from everyone else. 
Factory managers hide problems from Government officials, and the officials hide difficulties from foreigners. 
Every request in various parts of China to interview officials of unprofitable or barely profitable state enterprises was turned down.
But Chinese newspapers have revealed some aspects of the problem. 
Recent reports suggest that many enterprises may have "hidden losses," either because they under-report losses or siphon off a portion of the earnings.
An investigation into the fiscal accounts of 257 enterprises in nine provinces and cities discovered that 202 of them had accumulated over the last four years hidden losses of $257 million, nearly twice the amount of losses they officially reported. 
The report, published earlier this month in the People's Daily, said the companies had overstated earnings, partly because costs, such as amortization, were not included and partly because of theft.
In the case of a shoe factory in Hebei Province, accountants discovered 5,000 pairs of shoes were missing, at a loss of $19,000. 
A cigarette factory in Jilin Province found 13,872 cartons had vanished.
Perhaps the best solution to the problems of the state enterprises, says a Western economist in Beijing, is for private and collective enterprises to continue to take over their role and share of production gradually. 
He explains, "Then these dinosaurs will simply fade away."

file: At Bush_s Beijing Villa, Marxists Pursue Profit.txt
text:
ï»¿
As President Bush visits here this weekend, his lodgings will be testimony to China's growing interest in market economics.
China is waiving the $20,000-a-night charge for the elegant 24-bedroom villa where Mr. Bush will stay. 
But these days the historic Diaoyutai Guest House, a one-time imperial park where visiting dignitaries are housed in any one of 15 villas, is renting out its accommodations to tourists, business people and anyone else with hard currency.
Indeed, while Mr. Bush and about 35 other top officials will be given free lodging as state guests, the United States will have to pay for the scores of other guests in the official delegation who will stay here.
Protocol officers are still working out the lodging arrangements, including the bill, but even the least expensive rooms cost $140 a night. 
Many Chinese workers do not earn that much money in a month. 
#800 Years of Intrigue Diaoyutai Guest House, in short, has taken seriously the Communist Party's advice that business is honorable and that to get rich is glorious.
Throughout China, state institutions are searching for new ways to make money. 
The army is manufacturing televisions, schools are operating shoe factories on the side, and the Public Security Bureau is managing hotels.
In the last few years, Diaoyutai has proved that it can keep up with anyone in finding new sources of revenue. 
Indeed, the legendary guest house, with 800 years of history and intrigue, even turns a small profit these days in spite of the large number of official guests for whom it is obliged to provide free accommodation.
If Mr. Bush decides to swim in the Diaoyutai pool, for instance, he may find that a few other people have already paid for the privilege. 
A little more than a year ago, the Diaoyutai management began to offer corporate club memberships - $40,000 each - that allow two top corporate officers to use the accommodations indefinitely.
Â 
A Place to Relax
So far, 60 companies have signed up, including Occidental Petroleum Corporation, Johnson & Johnson, and AT&T, according to Sun Guotong, the deputy director general of Diaoyutai. 
The honorary members, who do not have to pay, include President Yang Shangkun and Prime Minister Li Peng.
''It's a place where leading businessmen and leading officials can relax together,'' said Mr. Sun, explaining the club's marketing strategy.
Since the early 1980's, the compound also has rented rooms out to what it reckons are high-class visitors. 
A potential guest cannot simply show up at the front door, because the armed guards at the gate turn away all cars whose license plates have not been cleared in advance. 
But bookings can be made in advance.
''High-level tourists can come here to stay,'' Mr. Sun said. 
''Just high-level people, and only on recommendations.''
But he acknowledged that anyone could book a room through a few select travel agencies.
The famous Yang Yuan restaurant, where Deng Xiaoping sometimes entertains visitors, is also open to bookings. 
It is not cheap. 
A banquet starts at $200 a person, and goes up to $400.
Diaoyutai, which means fishing terrace, is a former park with a history dating to the days in the 12th century when the emperor Zhang Zhong built an angling platform on a lake here.
Subsequent emperors also enjoyed the park, and the 200-year-old calligraphy of Emperor Qian Long is still preserved on one of the buildings.
In 1959, the Government built 15 villas on the 104-acre site to accommodate visiting dignitaries. 
In the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976, Chairman Mao's wife, Jiang Qing, lived here and watched American movies while chaos raged outside.
In 1972, President Richard M. Nixon met Prime Minister Zhou Enlai in another of the villas.
Â 
Gorbachev Due in May
Mr. Bush will be staying at the best of the villas, refurbished only three years ago. 
Queen Elizabeth was the first guest after the refurbishment, and this year the villa is expected to accommodate not only the President but also the Soviet leader, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, who visits in May, and Prince Charles and Princess Diana, who are due in November.
A few people have rented out the villa, even at $20,000 a night, which comes with 40 attendants.
In its bid to serve the state by making money, Diaoyutai is even engaged in a joint venture with Hong Kong interests to build an outside hotel that will be called the Diaoyutai Hotel, to capitalize on the guest house's name.
The guest house has been frantically busy preparing for Mr. Bush.
''We hear he likes to swim,'' Mr. Sun said early this week. 
''We have the pool here, but we don't know what temperature he likes the water. 
We have asked them what temperature we should set the thermostat.''

file: Banks Follow Immigrants to Flushing.txt
text:
ï»¿
On a street where hardware, electronics and shoe stores competed for space 10 years ago, a gleaming new glass obelisk juts above the squat buildings. 
Each block, it seems, has a new type of tenant -- with sleek gray steel, polished brass and tinted windows suggesting an international financial center.
Seven banks crowd into just two blocks in the din and traffic of Main Street in downtown Flushing, Queens, and the incongruous glass obelisk will make eight. 
Wander down the side streets or nearby Roosevelt Avenue and Northern Boulevard and the number of banks multiplies to at least 35 -- American, Chinese, Korean, British, Indian, Pakistani and Colombian.
As thousands of immigrants, particularly Chinese and Koreans, have settled in Flushing in the last decade, the banks have followed, tailoring their strategies to serve the savings-minded workers and flourishing small businesses.
Many are branches of the big American banks, which continue to dominate business in Flushing. 
But small AsianAmerican banks, with headquarters in Flushing or Chinatown, also compete fiercely for customers, and the latest arrival is a branch of a large Taiwan-based bank.
The China Trust Bank -- the largest private bank in Taiwan, which has its American headquarters in lower Manhattan -- opened its doors four weeks ago in a temporary office that was once a vegetable stand at 40-36 Main Street. 
Just a few steps away are the Hong Kong-Shanghai Banking Corporation, Amerasia Bank and Golden City Bank, which will open soon in the new glass obelisk on Main Street. 
Across the street is Manufacturers Hanover, and a block away are Green Point Savings and Citibank. 
Around the corner is Asia Bank, the oldest Chinese-American bank in Flushing, which opened in 1984.
In its first two weeks, the China Trust branch took in $6 million from 400 depositors, said the manager, Frank Lin. 
"It's fantastic," Mr. Lin said of the new business, and a state banking official described the total as "pretty darn good."
China Trust officials say they expect business in Flushing to keep growing, and they are spending $13 million to build a new three-story office just down the street.
The banks have in part been lured by the booming businesses in the area, where scores of restaurants and flashy boutiques have helped transform Flushing into the fourth-largest retail center in New York City. 
Pauline Chu, a Community School Board member who is running for City Council, said there are 200 stores in a three-block area and 800 restaurants in the neighborhood. 
A new 175-room Sheraton hotel will open in November.
But business executives and state banking officials say another big reason for the influx of banks and capital is fear over the Chinese takeover of Hong Kong in 1997. 
Uncertainty over the future of the British colony has prompted a flight of people and money from Hong Kong and Taiwan into the area since the early 1980's.
"The scare over 1997 is definitely one of the factors," said Clare E. Sykes, a spokeswoman for the State Banking Department. 
"Flushing is a fast-growth, healthy area, a good bankable area. 
It is faster growing than Chinatown."
Â 
Separate From Chinatown
Ms. Chu said about 140,000 Chinese and Korean immigrants now live in the Flushing area, which had few Asian residents 10 years ago.
Many residents and business owners envision Flushing as a flourishing international community, separate from Chinatown in Manhattan and uniquely positioned between New York City, Long Island, New Jersey and Connecticut, said Ho Pei Lee, a developer and builder.
A study comparing banks in Chinatown and Flushing convinced China Trust Bank to open its new Main Street branch, Mr. Lin said. 
The 1990 study showed that deposits in 28 Chinatown banks totaled $3.24 billion, while deposits in 34 Flushing banks totaled $3.13 billion.
"We are going to surpass the money deposited in Chinatown," Mr. Lee said. 
"Flushing has a lot of potential for the future."
Â 
A Mix of Strategies
The study found that American banks still have the greatest share of deposits in the area, and many have tailored their banking strategies to the community. 
Automatic teller machines offer transactions in three languages, and Citibank has a special Asian Banking Center where Korean, Mandarin and Cantonese are spoken.
The much smaller Chinese-American banks, including Asia Bank, Amerasia, Great Eastern and others, held only 12 percent of the deposits in the 1990 study. 
But they have managed to survive and thrive in Flushing, where banking strategies are a mix of old world and new.
The Chinese and Korean immigrants, traditionally great savers, are often wary of outsiders. 
Many prefer to speak their native language with tellers and say they find a more personal touch -- and shorter lines -- at the Chinese-American and Korean banks.
"We have a lot of new blood here -- immigrants, money and investments," said Thomas Tai, president of the Flushing Chinese Business Association. 
"Chinese banks thrive because of their personal relationships. 
They pay attention to past records, reputations of friends and family from the original country."
Mr. Lin, the manager of the new China Trust branch, said his bank expected to attract many Taiwanese as well as immigrants from Hong Kong and mainland China familiar with the bank's reputation. 
It has a capital base 10 times that of local Chinese-American banks and therefore can compete directly with the American giants, Mr. Lin said. 
"Chinese people have a lot of savings," he said. 
"They will come to us because we are Chinese. 
Chinese people are traditionally shy. 
They won't talk to strangers."
Â 
Service and Interest Rates
China Bank also hopes to lure non-Asian customers, Mr. Lin said, with automatic teller machines and high rates on certificates of deposit. 
"We are here to compete against Citibank and Chase, not with the local Chinese community banks," he said.
Many market-wise depositors in Flushing keep accounts in both Asian and American banks, and shop around for the best deposit yields. 
Competition centers on the rates on certificates of deposit, with the Chinese banks generally offering higher rates than the American banks. 
Many of the banks have weekend hours, and some even offer free parking, a premium in traffic-jammed Flushing.
Joy Xu, 25 years old, arrived in the United States two years ago and banks at Asia Bank. 
"My uncle introduced me, and they speak Chinese," Ms. Xu said. 
"It's quick here, while in Citibank you have to wait a long time and they're always out to lunch."
Yeming Wang, 40, a Shanghai native, uses an American bank but has also kept an account at Asia Bank because, she said, the interest and the service is good and "they always give you a gift for Chinese New Year."
Some residents choose a bank because they know its reputation. 
"I feel better in two banks," said Alex Lee, 22, a construction worker. 
"One is Hong-Kong Shanghai, because I had it before in Hong Kong and I feel familiar with it."

file: Big Board Contends Company Is Hong Kong, Not Chinese.txt
text:
ï»¿
If the International Monetary Fund and its equally staid sister, the World Bank, can embrace former Soviet republics, what is to prevent the New York Stock Exchange from drawing a Chinese company to its capitalist bosom?
Nothing, apparently, except that Big Board officials say Brilliance China Automotive Holdings Ltd., a Bermuda-based holding company whose sole business is the manufacture and sale of mini-vans in China, is really based in Hong Kong.
The boundary dispute came to light yesterday after Brilliance China, the 37th-largest industrial enterprise in China, announced that it had filed a registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission covering the proposed sale of five million common shares at an anticipated initial offering price of $14 to $16 a share.
The Big Board, which already makes markets for 115 foreign companies from 22 countries, was eager to add China to its list. 
Unfortunately, it now acknowledges that this one does not quite qualify as Chinese.
Â 
Â 
Offices in Hong Kong
Company perquisites prevent it. 
It seems that the Shenyang Jinbei Passenger Vehicle Manufacturing Company, Brilliance China's sole holding, has its principal executive offices on the 65th floor of the sleek Bank of China Tower in downtown Hong Kong.
The fact that the bulk of the company's 51.375 employees and all of the manufacturing operations are in Shenyang, the capital of Liaoning Province in northeastern China, did not sway the Big Board.
"Domicile is established by where the company has its executive headquarters," said Ray Pellechia, a spokesman for the New York Stock Exchange.
Nevertheless, investors considering the purchase of Brilliance China shares should be well versed in movements in the value of Renminbis, the "people's currency," and not Hong Kong dollars. 
And they should know that Shenyang Jinbei, which has the Toyota Motor Company and the General Motors Corporation as joint-venture partners in some of its operations, now imports more than 95 percent of the components that make up its Deluxe Mini-bus, and that those imports are subject to a tariff of 120 percent.
In the share offering prospectus, the company says it intends to increase domestic component content to more than 60 percent by the end of 1994, thereby lowering import levies to 80 percent.
Even though Shenyang Jinbei was converted from a state-owned enterprise into a share-owned company in 1988, the first large-scale state-owned business to do so, the market the company caters to still qualifies as captive.
More than 75 percent of Brilliance China is owned by the Bank of China and the Chinese Financial Education Development Foundation, and Shenyang Jinbei sells almost 90 percent of its mini-buses to Government agencies or state-owned enterprises.
Last year Shenyang Jinbei produced more than 11,500 mini-buses, about 40 percent of all the 11-seat to 15-seat vehicles produced in China, and had net income of $8.4 million on sales of $114.4 million.
Shenyang Jinbei's Deluxe Mini-buses have a list price of $49,490, while its Standard Mini-buses sell for $7,802.

text:

The hottest cassettes in China these days are underground copies of a speech on agriculture by a Politburo member addressing the Central Communist Party School for senior officials.
Bootleg videos and cassettes of the speech are in demand because of a tongue-in-cheek proposal by Tian Jiyun, a reform-minded Deputy Prime Minister, that the Government set up special zones in which hard-line officials could live according to their orthodox Marxist principles.
"Couldn't you establish a special economic zone for leftists?" he suggests in his Shandong Province accent. 
"Salaries would be low, prices of goods would be low, you would rely on coupons, you would have to stand on line to buy everything and suffer everything else that goes along with leftism."
Mr. Tian then describes how the zone could compete with southern China's current special economic zones that have adopted capitalist-style management techniques. 
Those zones, like Shenzhen, are the most prosperous parts of the country, and millions of Chinese try to get permission to move there. 
In contrast, the "leftist" zone would be open to anyone.
"If we actually set up a place to do this, would anybody want to go?"
Mr. Tian asks. 
There are peals of laughter in the audience.
Â 
Deng Rival May Be Target
Mr. Tian does not name any leftist, but many of those listening to the tapes volunteer names of people like Chun Yun, a conservative central planner who is the rival of Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader. 
Another person whom Mr. Tian persumably had in mind is Deng Liqun, a hard-liner active in ideology and propaganda decisions.
The speech was never publicized in the official Chinese press, but it was apparently given about a month ago. 
A video recording was made officially, and that was apparently then copied unofficially -- perhaps with the backing of senior officials trying to discredit the hard-liners.
Mr. Tian's address is the first time recently that any Politburo member has made a humorous speech, at least intentionally, and it suggests that reformers may be taking a new tack in the political struggles within the leadership. 
While Mr. Tian's comments are viewed as daring attacks on the hard-liners, they fit in with a campaign that Mr. Deng began in January to accelerate economic change.
Mr. Deng declared that China must be wary of rightists but that the main danger comes from leftists.
In Communist parlance, "rightism" means sympathies for democracy and Western-style capitalism. 
"Leftism" means a Maoist-style preference for waging class struggle and maintaining a centrally-planned economy.
Â 
Reports Are Exaggerated
Word about the tapes is spreading even faster than the copies themselves, and accounts of Mr. Tian's speech are becoming exaggerated with various ideas that he never mentioned.
Some people, for instance, say Mr. Tian called for a prohibition on residents of the leftist zones from being allowed to send their children abroad. 
That strikes an immediate chord with many Chinese, for it is common for some of the most anti-Western Chinese leaders to send their children to the United States for graduate study.
While Mr. Tian never said these things, he certainly makes a mockery of Communism as it existed in the 1960's and 1970's, when life was full of shortages and it was difficult to find a restaurant open after dark.
"We would all talk beforehand about what we needed to buy with our meat coupons," Mr. Tian, who interspersed his comments with a few earthy phrases, recalled. 
"Then the next day, we'd all run to the stores to get in line, no matter what line, only to find out that there wasn't anything there that we wanted. 
We'd just back away and run up to get into another line."
Some say that such a strong message would certainly have been backed in advance by a top leader, possibly Mr. Deng himself and at least by Qiao Shi, the Politburo member in charge of security and the president of the Central Party School.
"Someone certainly is putting him up to it," said a Chinese who circulates among top officials. 
"He wouldn't have the courage to say all that otherwise."

file: Calls for Economic Changes Rise Among Chinese Officials.txt
text:
ï»¿
After a two-year freeze on the process of opening China's state-controlled economy to market forces, a growing number of Chinese economic officials are openly calling for a wave of changes, arguing that without further liberalization China's march toward development may reverse.
For several months, China's leaders have acknowledged a need to ease the austerity measures imposed in the fall of 1988 to battle soaring inflation. 
Now, momentum is building for more basic changes, like those of the early 1980's, when China was a leader among Communist countries in experimenting with market-oriented policies to revitalize its state-run economy.
''In China, without real reform, the economic situation will become hopeless,'' Ren Junyin, deputy director of planning at the nation's central bank, the People's Bank of China, said in an interview in Beijing. 
''It is only a matter of time and the conditions before we undertake serious reform.''
No Changes in Policy
Chinese officials and some Western experts say the tolerance being shown for opening the market of economic ideas suggests some easing of the tense political climate that has existed since tanks were sent into Tiananmen Square in Beijing last June to crush the democracy movement. 
They add that it also shows some acknowledgement of the depth of the current problems on the part of the leadership.
Finance Minister Wang Bingqian has described the economic situation as fairly grim, and Prime Minister Li Peng recently acknowledged that the economy was fragile. 
Still, the leadership has produced no changes in policy in response to the calls for change.
Dwight H. Perkins, a China expert at Harvard University who recently con-ducted research with the State Planning Commission in Beijing, said: ''I don't think there's any real commitment for reform now. 
What I see is lots of ad hoc thinking about administrative intervention in the economy, but no real plan. 
Most of the people at the top have no real understanding or confidence in how markets work.''
Yet the calls for change have grown louder.
Zheng Hongqing, head of an important Government research center, was quoted on the front page of The China Daily newspaper last week, saying the Government has too much control over bloated state enterprises. 
He proposed a shareholding system for companies and the introduction of competition among banks.
In fact, China's first organized stock exchange is scheduled to open near here in Shenzhen within a few months. 
It will be closely watched as a sign of how tolerant the authorities will be.
Other proposals being floated are the creation of a national stock market, an easing of price controls and an opening of banks that make loans based on the prospect of getting repaid rather than on Government policy. 
Even with such ideas being widely circulated, China's current leadership is still expressing its suspicions about market-oriented changes, making the prospects for fundamental change uncertain.
Li Guixian, president of the People's Bank, recently told a financial conference in Shenyong, in northeast China, that banks ''are supposed to provide lending mainly in light of the state policies rather than for profit.''
Â 
Alert to Conspiracy
And a broadside was recently issued by Communist Party officials insisting that China would maintain its vigilance against ''peaceful evolution,'' code words here for what is believed to be an American conspiracy to transform the Communist planned system into a capitalist system.
The mood was expressed well by Rong Yiren, one of Chinese Communism's best-known capitalists. 
Mr. Rong is chairman of the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, known as Citic, a multifaceted Government-owned merchant bank in Beijing born of the open-door policies a decade ago. 
Citic has survived by deftly sensing and conforming to the prevailing winds.
''My view is that we should adopt a very gradual, stable reform policy that does not proceed hastily,'' Mr. Rong said, seated in his modern office under a picture of himself with Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader.
Â 
Expression of Disapproval
Nonetheless, it does not appear that the debate or the pressure for change will be halted. 
''China's economy is too large to be run efficiently on the basis of commands from the center,'' the World Bank said in a recent report. 
In blunt language the report stated the case for pushing ahead with liberalization, saying disapprovingly that China's leadership seemed to believe that ''problems encountered in the course of reform,'' like inflation, could be fixed by resorting to the same inflexible mechanism ''responsible for the distortions the reform was designed to correct.''
Nicholas R. Lardy, an expert on the Chinese economy at the University of Washington, observed: ''They are at a critical point. 
The underlying economy is much softer than most of the figures suggest.''
The profits of state-owned enterprises plummeted 60 percent in the first half of the year, cutting even further into state revenues already depleted by heavy Government price subsidies. 
Industry is suffering from nagging shortages of basic commodities like energy and water because state-fixed prices are too low and promote inefficiency, economists say. 
And there could be an even more severe slowdown in foreign investment, which has tumbled 22 percent this year.
Â 
Enormous Changes
Before the economic liberalization ground to a halt two years ago, enormous changes had been wrought. 
Farmers were freed to grow more of what they wanted and to sell in more open markets; some central Government functions were taken on by the provinces; the economy was opened to a limited amount of foreign investment and trade, and the seeds of a real banking system were sown.
The changes put China far ahead of most Communist countries in liberalizing its economy, and they brought a large measure of prosperity to the countryside.
The region around Canton was a major beneficiary of the reforms. 
Farmers' incomes rose, and a flood of investment from Hong Kong caused a boom in factory and hotel construction. 
The region then suffered as the austerity measures and renewed emphasis on state control forced thousands of newly formed small businesses to close.
Â 
Some Positive Economic Signs
''This is like rowing a boat upstream,'' said Gao Xiqing, a graduate of the Duke University School of Law who is the general counsel of a new body trying to establish China's first formal stock exchange in Beijing. 
''You can't stand still. 
You have to go ahead or you go backwards.''
There are some positive economic signs, like vibrant exports this year. 
Inflation has fallen to about 3 percent. 
After a recession last year and earlier in 1990, industrial activity perked up modestly in the last two months. 
Urban store shelves are filled, and streets are lined with merchants sitting atop hillocks of watermelons, as city dwellers enjoy a bumper harvest.
After negative growth in the first months of this year, the Government has reported that the economy had an annual growth rate of 1.6 percent in the first half, compared with the first half of 1989. 
In the crucial area of industrial production, growth at state-owned enterprises rose 2.7 percent, less than half the 5.6 percent growth rate at more freely operated collectively run enterprises and a fraction of the 54.3 percent growth rate of foreign-financed ventures in China.
Â 
Experts' Recommendations
To put the whole economy on a more stable growth path, the experts advocate a number of changes:
* Creating broader markets for determining prices. 
To avoid jolting consumers too harshly, the World Bank and others have proposed phasing in market-determined prices.
* Permitting a greater element of private ownership. 
To many, this step is the most important and the one that seems to be the slowest in moving ahead.
* Freeing the financial system so that banks make their lending decisions on the basis of their likelihood of getting repaid.
''It boils down to a political question of what you can sell the people,'' said Mr. Lardy of the University of Washington.''There has to be some pain before they can really move ahead.''

file: Capitalist-Style Layoffs Ignite Sabotage and Strikes in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Worried by layoffs and rising prices, many Chinese workers seem increasingly disenchanted by the capitalist-style changes taking hold in shops and factory floors around the country.
As a result, for the first time since China began liberalizing its economy more than a dozen years ago, many ordinary citizens seem to be no longer agents of change but obstacles to it. 
Workers in several cities have attacked factory directors who have tried to introduce market-oriented changes, and there are growing reports of strikes and acts of sabotage.
Those incidents suggest that opposition to fundamental change is increasingly coming not only from octogenarian Communist hard-liners but also from many ordinary blue-collar workers.
Â 
Fear and Fury?
Similar tensions have erupted throughout the former Communist bloc. 
While China has been able to avoid deep social upheavals associated with "shock therapy" in other countries, the experience here suggests that even a gradual weaning away from central planning can lead to widespread fear and sometimes fury.
"There's enormous frustration out there with the reforms," a Chinese economic official said. 
"The leaders are running scared."
What alarms the leadership is cases like that of Huang Chuanying, a bank director whom the official Chinese press hailed as "a daring reformer."
Mr. Huang tried to curb the Maoist-style labor practices that have crippled state-owned enterprises all over China, and he began dismissing bank employees considered incompetent and unproductive.
One dismissed staff member, Cao Weihua, responded by firebombing Mr. Huang's house, severely wounding Mr. Huang, his wife and their two children. 
Mr. Cao was sentenced to death recently, but the incident seemed to reflect a broad concern among many Chinese that while a market economy may be more prosperous and efficient than a Communist one, it may also be less cozy.
The contrast is profound with the mood in most of the last dozen years, when ordinary Chinese were ardent backers of change. 
In those years, they often took the initiative and pushed liberalization more quickly than the Politburo intended.
"Reform used to be very easy and rewarding," a Chinese journalist said. 
"In the 1980's, it meant dividing up the land, and starting up free markets, and opening new businesses, and everybody loved it."
But in the 1990's, the agenda is different. 
While virtually all Chinese endorse "reform" as a general slogan, many workers worry about what it will mean: higher rents, rising rice prices, and destroying the "iron rice bowl" system that guarantees workers stable employment and steady incomes.
Â 
The Changing Rice Bowl
According to a folk ditty now making the rounds among workers: Before liberation, we had a clay rice bowl. 
Then Chairman Mao gave us an iron rice bowl. 
Deng Xiaoping poked a hole in it. 
Since reform, we've had a porcelain rice bowl.
"A porcelain rice bowl looks rather elegant," a manual laborer in her 40's explained dryly. 
"But it's no more sturdy than one made of clay."
A 26-year-old woman who works in a factory said that when she was in the university, she believed that most Chinese wanted more economic liberalization. 
But now she figures that aside from intellectuals, many people are against fundamental changes.
"We need housing reform and price reform, but nobody wants them," she said. 
"Who wants to pay more?
I figure that in my factory, 80 percent of the workers believe in the iron rice bowl system."
That may well be exaggeration, for most workers interviewed seem to be not so much hostile to change as worried by it. 
And while some are openly opposed, there also is a significant proportion that favors dog-eat-dog capitalism and believes that economic liberalization should be speeded up.
Â 
Weaning From Subsidies
Many of the problems arose because China's leaders have finally taken Western advice and moved to impose a market discipline on state-owned enterprises, one-third of which lose money. 
Exasperated by continuing inefficiency in those enterprises, China's leadership has waged a campaign since last year to wean factories from subsidies and expose them to market pressures.
As a result, a few factories began to dismiss workers considered unproductive, a practice that almost never occurred in the past. 
There is also talk of layoffs to trim the 26 percent overstaffing that the Government admits exists in state enterprises.
While many Chinese, particularly the university educated, say that such changes are essential, blue-collar workers are less enthusiastic. 
For the first time, a significant sector of the population, though probably not a majority, seems to be siding with Communist hard-liners in discouraging rapid market-style changes.
Early this year, a laid-off driver at a toothpaste factory drove his truck over his boss, a pioneering manager who had shaken up his factory by adopting Western-style management practices. 
The central Government suggested that the factory manager be hailed as a "martyr" for reform, but the factory workers refused to nominate the manager for the honor, said the official who related the incident.
In another case, reported in the official press, a 27-year-old factory worker was sentenced several weeks ago to 15 years in prison for shooting at his boss at a factory in Shanxi Province. 
The worker, who failed to wound the manager, had been dismissed last year.
Â 
Machinery Smashed
Factories in Xian, Tianjin and Dalian were reportedly also disrupted by angry workers, and in some cases machinery was smashed. 
After a watch factory in Tianjin temporarily laid off 2,400 workers early this year, rumors of suicides, sabotage and military intervention rapidly spread throughout Beijing. 
The official Economic Daily recently denied the allegations, and said the factory had retooled and reopened, providing jobs for all but 300 of the previous workers.
"The Government's talking about smashing our iron rice bowls, and making us pay for our own medical care," said a 29-year-old worker in Beijing. 
"Companies are even beginning to lay off workers!
Of course folks are angry."
To be sure, apprehension of market-style changes is common around the world, from Russians who fear rising bread prices to New Yorkers who worry about lifting controls on rent.
"We're very different from the former Soviet Union," said a Chinese Government economist who has studied former Communist economies. 
"We already have a foundation of a market, and people can get jobs on their own if they have to. 
The changes may not be pleasant, but we can take it. 
But in Russia, there's no real market to speak of, the economy is shrinking, and all the changes have been introduced very abruptly."
Han Dongfang, an independent labor organizer who was released a year ago after serving two years in prison, argues that the Government is caught in a dilemma.
"To raise living standards, the Government needs to go ahead with economic reform," Mr. Han said. 
"But reform will involve trampling on the rights of workers, and a lot of people won't be very happy about it. 
These contradictions will grow in the next few years."

file: Changes in China Offer Lessons for East Europe.txt
text:
ï»¿
When China specialists think about how Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union can reorganize their economies, they tend to agree on one point: transforming socialist countries into market competitors will be a far more complex and painful task than is often acknowledged.
The Chinese experience is relevant, diplomats and academics say, because China generally has a richer and more successful experience in economic liberalization than its socialist brethren. 
While political changes, symbolized by the Russian word glasnost, lag here, few experts dispute that China has the upper hand in the economic restructuring known as perestroika.
''If Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union do as well in the next 10 years as China has in the last 10 years, they will have done extremely well,'' said Gregory Chow, an economist at Princeton University.
Even after a dozen years of economic change, China is still grappling with some Herculean problems. 
But its achievements are also Herculean: until 1989, China's real growth rates averaged nearly 10 percent a year, among the highest in the world; shops and free markets are as bountiful as the Soviet Union's are bare; lavish joint-venture hotels and international direct-dial telephones are found in major cities; agriculture has been de-collectivized, and the state sector's share of industry has fallen to about 60 percent.
Â 
Successes and Mistakes
Thomas M. H. Chan, an economist at the Hong Kong Baptist College, observed, ''China may not be a solution for Eastern Europe, because it still has to find a solution for its own problems, but its examples of successes and its mistakes may be useful for the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.''
Mr. Chan noted that one of the main engines of China's economic growth in the last decade has been the township and village enterprises that have sprouted in coastal areas. 
More flexible and tuned to the markets rather than state-run behemoths, these small factories produce goods ranging from sweaters to plastic flowers. 
Mr. Chan suggested that Eastern Europe might study such enterprises to see if they could increase production there as well.
One area in which China has been most successful is in cultivating exports and integrating itself into the world economy. 
Nicholas Lardy, a China scholar at the University of Washington, said the Soviet Union should note China's relatively realistic valuation of the yuan and its use of currency swap markets to allocate $8 billion in foreign exchange last year.
For some economists, there is another lesson in the Chinese experience: national leaders should resist advice to free prices immediately. 
While these experts agree that irrational prices are a major burden for the economy, they suggest that decontrolling prices overnight will hurt the public and turn them against the entire liberalization program.
Â 
A Crucial Lesson
''The most important lesson of the Chinese experience is that price reform is not essential to reform,'' a Government economist said. 
''The most essential reform is that of the fundamental economic system, of ownership and management.''
Hua Sheng, a Chinese economist now studying at Oxford University, put it more strongly, ''It seems to me that to start with price reform is a very stupid idea, because the Government will become very unpopular.''
Mr. Hua noted that the Soviet Union had to back off earlier this year from a radical proposal to free prices, just as China had to retreat in the summer of 1988 from a plan to decontrol prices.
That 1988 proposal in China was followed by waves of panic buying and a steep rise in inflation. 
It also marked a watershed, for since then some urban residents have been soured on the whole idea of economic restructuring, and the Chinese leadership has been reluctant to push much further with any major initiative for economic change.
Delaying price decontrols is not a universal prescription, and there is still a camp of Chinese and foreign economists who believe that price liberalization is an essential starting point. 
They say that the chaos that began in the summer of 1988 in China was a result not of price decontrols but of an easy monetary policy. 
Without a prompt if painful adjustment to rational prices, they say, there is no way out of the economic quagmire.
Â 
An Impossible Task
Mr. Hua, who left China for Oxford early last year, said that the task that he and other economists faced in socialist countries, to combine public ownership with a market mechanism, was virtually impossible to complete satisfactorily.
''For the Soviet Union, the most important lesson is that public ownership doesn't work,'' Mr. Hua said. 
''If you want to carry out reform seriously, you have to carry out ownership reform, and denationalize industry on a large scale.''
Mr. Hua urged governments to sell off state factories and other assets to reduce their budget deficits and raise funds. 
He said those funds could then be used to sweeten the process and soothe the pain when prices were freed.

file: Chengdu Journal_China_s 50 Million Migrants Slip the Short Leash.txt
text:
ï»¿
The streets of this provincial capital are paved not with gold but with a layer of asphalt topped with dust, mud and decaying cabbage leaves, but still the peasants troop here in search of jobs and a new life.
''You can make a lot more money in the city,'' said Gao Jingru, a lithe 53-year-old in a Mao suit. 
Mr. Gao brings odd-shaped stones and fossils from his village 50 miles away to sell to the residents of Chengdu, and in a good month he can earn the equivalent of more than $32 - 10 times as much as he would earn in his village.
The market street in Chengdu and many other Chinese cities is full of migrant laborers like Mr. Gao, and they pose a growing challenge to the Government. 
About 50 million people in China, nearly 5 percent of the nation's population, are migrants, and increasingly they are beyond the tight control of the Government.
The economic slowdown, particularly the closing of millions of rural enterprises, could add to the number of migrants. 
Official figures indicate that China's countryside has about 80 million surplus laborers, including 10 million here in Sichuan Province. 
Many seem to be remaining in their villages rather than swarming to the cities, where jobs are also tough to find, but their movements are difficult to predict.
Â 
Ignoring Restrictions
Unlike most developing countries, where peasants have always rushed to the cities and put up shantytowns on the outskirts, China has tried to control people's movements through a complex household registration system. 
Chinese citizens are not supposed to move without getting their registration changed, but these days many people simply ignore the requirements and move anyway.
''If the city needs my things, then I'll be here selling,'' said Chen Kailie, 47 years old, who moved to Chengdu from a village 20 miles away to sell flower pots. 
''If I can't make ends meet, then I'll go back to my hometown.''
The swelling tide of migrant laborers is one of the clearest signs that China's old command structure is wearing down. 
In major cities like Chengdu, Beijing and Shanghai, more than 10 percent of the inhabitants are migrants who come and go largely as they please. 
China has a complex web of ''street committees'' to watch over urban residents and make sure they do not cause political problems or have unauthorized children, but this system of scrutiny does not succeed in controlling those who do not belong in the first place.
The existence of this large ''floating population,'' as the Chinese call it, helps explain how student leaders of last year's crushed democracy movement have been able to elude the security apparatus for months. 
Five or ten years ago, most Chinese say confidently, the student leaders would have been arrested promptly; these days, they can simply blend in with the flow of other wanderers.
Â 
Enlivening the Economy
The migrants also present a more direct challenge: Like Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping and other Chinese revolutionaries, they are peasants who go to the cities and risk picking up dangerous political ideas. 
In last year's rioting in cities like Beijing, Changsha and Chengdu, migrants played a significant role, perhaps partly because they were less likely to be identified and caught than permanent residents.
Government officials, like Yan Cheng, the deputy secretary general of the Chengdu municipality, acknowledge that the floating population creates some difficulties for family planning and for public security, but he adds that on the whole it is a good thing because it enlivens the economy.
''This is an economic phenomenon, not a political problem,'' said Mr. Yan, who noted that the peasant migrants fill an important niche by selling farm products and filling jobs in service industries in the city. 
In Beijing, always the most security-conscious of Chinese cities, the police have made periodic efforts to round up migrants and send them home, but in other cities officials point to the services they provide and seem to regard them as a blessing.
''It's reality beating ideology,'' said Aprodicio Laquian, who recently completed a term as country director in China for the United Nations Fund for Population Activities. 
''The migrants will really be the salvation of China, because they solve needs that central planning can't.''
That also seems to be the view of most urban residents, who are sometimes contemptuous of the migrants' unkempt appearance and uncouth manners but appreciate being able to find a business where the service is attentive and the hours are long -even if it consists only of cabbages in a cart or old magazines spread on a blanket on a sidewalk.
''We think the floating population is terrific,'' said the owner of a small business in Chengdu. 
''Why?
Because we can exploit them. 
They're willing to work hard in exchange for just enough money to buy some food. 
We need them and they need us. 
It's a great partnership.''

file: China Called Top Copyright Pirate.txt
text:
ï»¿
Companies producing books, records, films, computer software and other so-called intellectual property contended today that 12 countries, headed by China, are depriving the United States of more than $1.3 billion a year of foreign earnings through piracy of copyrighted material.
The International Intellectual Property Alliance, representing 1,600 companies that generated $270 billion in revenues in 1988, placed losses in China, with a population of a billion people and no copyright law, at $418 million, or about a third of the total of the 12 countries.
In a report to Carla A. Hills, the United States trade representative, the group said the problem was particularly acute in textbooks.
Â 
Collier Macmillan Loss in China
One example the report cited was English 900, a Collier Macmillan basic textbook used extensively around the world. 
It has had print runs in China of more than one million copies, yielding no income for Collier Macmillan, the report said.
American book publishers put their losses in China ''conservatively'' at $100 million a year, the report said.
In Saudi Arabia, the report said, 16 companies specialize solely in the distribution of pirate copies of Michael Jackson's music.
The alliance, which makes periodic assessments of piracy losses for the trade representative, named these other countries as the leading offenders: South Korea, India, the Philippines, Taiwan, Indonesia, Brazil, Egypt, Thailand, Nigeria and Malaysia.
Although the group has been providing data since 1984 on its members' losses, this year's report is getting unusual attention because of a requirement in the new United States trade law that the worst violators of intellectual property rights be identified for special Government action that could result in trade sanctions.
Trade officials noted that most of the countries named by the alliance are in some form of negotiation with the trade office to try to prevent their designation as a ''priority'' country under the Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988.
Mrs. Hills is required to inform Congress by May 30 of what countries she has designated. 
After the designation, her office must enter intensified talks with those countries. 
If the situation has not improved in a period of 18 months, the President may curb imports from those countries.
The United States has already taken action against one of the countries for intellectual property violations. 
On Jan. 
19, the last day of the Reagan Administration, President Reagan denied duty-free entry to $165 million of Thai imports because of what he said was Thailand's failure to protect copyrighted works.
Most of the 12 governments have agreed to try to correct abuses. 
''The question is how quickly or how resolutely,'' said Eric H. Smith, general counsel of the alliance.
China, for example, is working on the 19th draft of a copyright law, American officials said, and hopes to have one completed by year-end. 
Saudi Arabia is also drafting a law.
Â 
Statement by Chinese Embassy
''China is now actively accelerating legislation for the protection of intellectual property,'' a spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said. 
He noted that not long ago in the port city of Sheng Chen, a company that was found to have infringed on trademarks of the International Business Machines Corporation had been required to pay the highest such fine ever in China.
South Korea's Minister of Trade, Sung Soo Han, said at a news briefing here that his country had ''drastically overhauled and strengthened'' its intellectual property laws and had engaged 900 additional prosecutors and police officers to enforce them.
A report by the alliance in 1984 called Singapore ''the world's capital of piracy,'' but in the current survey Singapore is described as a ''success story.''
The 1984 losses from Singapore were put at $358 million, but they had been whittled to $10 million last year, the report said.
Â 
SOVIET COPYRIGHT PLAN
LONDON, April 19 (Reuters) -The Soviet Union will soon officially subscribe to the Bern Convention on literary copyrights and royalties, a Soviet official said today.
''I can inform you that our country is finalizing the necessary preparatory work which will soon enable us to accede to the Bern Copyright Convention,'' the Soviet Deputy Foreign Minister, Vladimir F. Petrovsky, told the London Information Forum of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe.
The Bern Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works has existed for more than a century.Last month the United States became the 78th nation to join.

text:

China has extended a commodity loan valued at $730 million to the Soviet Union, to buy Chinese grain, meat, peanuts, tea and other products, an official newspaper said today.

file: China Loosens Free-Enterprise Rules.txt
text:
ï»¿
In an unexpected departure from their harsh line against private enterprises, the authorities announced new regulations today that would encourage unemployed people to establish private and collective enterprises in the capital.
The new rules, which include substantial tax breaks, were described as a pragmatic measure to lower unemployment in the capital. 
But the move was a surprise because of the sharp criticisms in recent months of private enterprises in China.
The Communist Party lately has complained that private enterprises evade taxes, violate various laws, waste raw materials and widen disparities in incomes. 
This was the first sign that some private enterprises would be actively encouraged.
The measure came as a surprise also because the new regulations were adopted by the Beijing government, which has led the nation in taking a hard line on a number of political and economic issues. 
The rules were reported late tonight by the official New China News Agency.
In recent years, private and collective enterprises have absorbed enormous numbers of unemployed and underemployed workers. 
While the authorities have been highly critical of some practices at such enterprises, the leadership knows that such companies also ease unemployment problems and thereby reduce social tensions.
The report from the New China News Agency said Beijing had 130,000 young job seekers this year, 30,000 more than last year. 
Nationally, the unemployment rate is often said to be 2 percent, but many economists have said the true figure is higher.
The dispatch also said that 200,000 to 250,000 temporary workers, who lack permission to live in Beijing, would be forced out of the city. 
Beijing has periodically tried to control the number of unregistered workers, and evicted many of them just a month ago, in preparation for the Oct. 
1 National Day holiday.
Â 
Tax Holiday for Some
The new regulations encourage only those private enterprises involved in ''trades needed by the city,'' like those related to food, garments and repair services.
Newly established collective enterprises that employ otherwise jobless young people would receive a tax holiday for two to three years.
The Beijing authorities have recently stepped up their campaign to ''clean up'' the free markets by making vendors pay taxes and adhere to other regulations. 
The city has also attacked ''profiteers'' and said that ''exploiters'' would not be allowed to join the Communist Party.

file: China Plans Big Layoffs Of Coal Mine Workers.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has laid off 100,000 coal workers and will lay off hundreds of thousands more in the coming years, as part of a broad effort to modernize its energy industry, an official report said today.
The layoffs suggest that the Communist Party is finally grappling directly with the enormously complex and painful problems of industrial revamping.
Until now, the Government has resisted such layoffs for fear of provoking worker unrest -- the same kind of anxieties and outrage that erupted in Britain in October when the Government there proposed laying off 30,000 coal miners.
The Communist Party here sees the problem the same way that the Conservative Party perceives it in Britain: some mines cannot be operated economically at current prices. 
But the British Prime Minister, John Major, was forced to scale down his program in response to the public outrage, while the self-professed leaders of the Chinese working class seem determined to expose the miners to the discipline of the market.
The official China Daily said the China National Coal Corporation, a huge state-owned conglomerate that employs three million people, would close 30 inefficient mines in 1993 alone and lay off 30,000 miners and 70,000 workers in related jobs.
The newspaper said the company planned to reduce the number of its coal workers by 400,000 by the time the current five-year plan ended in 1995. 
The report added that another major state-run coal company, which it did not identify, also planned "massive layoffs to increase efficiency."
The China Daily also said that 100,000 coal workers had already been laid off, although it did not say when that had happened. 
It said that most had found other kinds of jobs, and the Government apparently also will help employees laid off in the future to find jobs in new companies in the service sector.
The Energy Ministry refused to comment today. 
The coal corporation directed phone calls to Tan Enli, its director of policy research, and he declined to discuss specifics. 
But he did say that the article in China Daily was premature and should not have been allowed to be published.
"We'd like to do these things," Mr. Tan said, referring to the prospective layoffs for 1993 and subsequent years. 
"But first we need approval. 
In January the company will hold a conference to decide whether to go ahead with these plans."
In China, if a conference is called to debate a topic, that usually means that the aim is to build a consensus and legitimacy for a decision that has already been made.
Â 
Â 
A Big Headache
State-owned corporations like the coal company have been a big headache for China's leaders. 
While the overall economy is booming at a 12 percent growth rate this year, the main beneficiaries are private and collective enterprises.
Among state companies, which account for about half of industrial output, only a third are earning profits, with another third showing losses and the rest breaking even. 
Coal mines have particularly suffered, because their costs have gone up while the price of the coal they sell is fixed at artificially low prices by the state.
The solution is twofold: to raise coal prices and to lay off surplus workers. 
But the Government has worried that consumers might protest rising prices for coal, which is used for both heating and cooking, and that miners might protest the layoffs.
Now the authorities appear to be moving on both fronts, not only in the coal industry, but throughout the economy.
Â 
Price of Coal to Be Raised
In addition to laying off surplus coal workers, China has said it is raising coal prices gradually so that they will reach market levels within the next few years. 
This year, for example, the National Coal Corporation is allowed to sell 20 percent of its output at market prices, and in 1993 the figure will rise sharply.
Elsewhere in the economy, state-owned companies are also revamping and laying off workers.
In the central Chinese city of Chongqing, for example, the local Foreign Affairs Office says a state-owned knitting mill was declared bankrupt in September, costing 3,000 workers their jobs. 
At the time, it was the biggest single bankruptcy ever allowed in China, the local officials say.
Until recently, the state normally bailed out such money-losing factories indefinitely, because of the fear of worker unrest. 
In the spring of this year, the Government was deeply worried by a series of wildcat strikes and attacks on change-minded factory managers.
As a result of those incidents, the leadership cooled down the talk about how beneficial layoffs were for economic efficiency. 
And now, while going ahead with the restructuring, it appears to have decided to provide as many sweeteners to the workers as possible.
Each laid-off coal worker will be eligible for a no-interest loan of up to $1,720 to help start a business or find work elsewhere. 
The Government will also give the coal corporation a $340 million loan to allow it to start service companies that can absorb some of the laid-off employees.
