file: China Revives Its Test of Capitalism.txt
text:
ï»¿
After the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown, China's bold experiment in fusing socialism and capitalism in this South China city stalled. 
By last summer, Shenzhen's mayor lost his position, economic reforms were halted, and the city's 10th anniversary celebration was postponed.
But now Shenzhen has talked its way back into Beijing's favor, and many leaders again point to it as a model for the nation's development.
Shenzhen officials, though wary of the power struggles in Beijing, are seeking a nearly open border with Hong Kong. 
A primitive stock market that has operated, literally, over the counters in small buildings around the city is about to expand into a modern, computerized exchange.
In a single decade, Shenzhen has developed from a barren patch of grassland into one of China's most modern metropolises. 
But the transformation has been marked by a battle between China's ardent central planners and those who envision a national economy far more open and free.
Shenzhen, a special economic zone in Guangdong province, is a product of China's effort to prove that a capitalist economy can thrive under a socialist government. 
Many central officials still fear that Shenzhen is becoming too capitalist and too unwieldy for the Government to control.
Local leaders say they have strong reasons for continuing to support the Beijing Government, which has allowed Shenzhen and other special economic zones to prosper. 
While some of Shenzhen's students protested in May 1989, the demonstrations were much smaller than in other big cities, as many citizens saw that protests would only stand in the way of making money.
Some say Shenzhen is turning into a mini-Hong Kong. 
Already, the Hong Kong dollar is Shenzhen's semiofficial currency, accepted by hotels, taxis and restaurants, which refuse the foreign currency exchange certificates required of foreigners everywhere else in China.
Â 
Rapid Industrial Growth
Industrial growth over the last decade averaged 69 percent annually, among the fastest of any city in the world. 
For a while, Shenzhen's tiny, nascent stock market was more free-wheeling -- and scandal-ridden -- than Hong Kong's.
While some Shenzhen officials agree about the increasing resemblance to Hong Kong, they insist that there is one major distinction: Shenzhen is still socialist, with most businesses run by the state.
"It is not impossible for Shenzhen to become a Chinese Hong Kong," said Wang Xinkuo, a senior manager at the Catic Shenzhen Enterprise Group, whose member companies include a maker of simple electronic components. 
"The biggest difference is that Hong Kong is a capitalist system, while in Shenzhen, public ownership is the main path."
Besides Shenzhen, with nearly 1.9 million people, there are four other special economic zones -- Zhuhai, Shantou, Xiamen and Hainan Island, all also in southern China. 
While officials still describe these zones as socialist, not everyone agrees that socialist planning will dominate these export-oriented cities.
Â 
Prices Set by Market
Almost all their prices, including those for raw materials, are set by the market. 
The rest of China buys many materials, including coal and oil, at subsidized prices.
"Only postage and bus fares are set by the Government, and that's because they are uniform for the whole nation," said Liang Wensen, a professor of economics at Shenzhen University.
"There is even a market in people's labor," Mr. Lian said, with most of Shenzhen's wages also determined primarily by market forces.
Partly because of its location next to Hong Kong, Shenzhen has attracted major foreign investments. 
Some 3,000 of Shenzhen's 7,000 companies have some foreign capital. 
Total foreign investment in Shenzhen amounts to about one-seventh the foreign investment in all of China, according to official statistics.
Â 
A Bumpy Ascent
But Shenzhen's ascent has not been smooth. 
When China's economic liberals had the upper hand in the late 1980's, Shenzhen was developing into a virtually free market. 
But when hard-liners took over two years ago during the Tiananmen crackdown, it seemed that Shenzhen's best years had ended.
Beijing refused to allow Shenzhen's modernized stock exchange to open; Li Hao, a reformer, was relieved as mayor, although he remained party secretary, and the city's 10th anniversary celebration, scheduled for last summer, was put off for nearly four months.
But now, Shenzhen seems to be back on the reform track. 
Once more, national leaders tout Shenzhen as a model, and again provincial officials from throughout China are visiting to learn how to help their own economies. 
Shenzhen has adopted an aggressive, 10-year growth plan, and a new airport is scheduled to open in the fall.
Shenzhen's leaders are sufficiently confident of their futures to press for more dramatic changes. 
Shenzhen is said to have sought Beijing's permission to establish its own currency and relax border restrictions with Hong Kong while tightening them with the rest of China. 
Already, other Chinese need special permission to cross the "second border" into Shenzhen.
Â 
Beijing's Concerns
Shenzhen's leaders apparently want to merge their economy into Hong Kong's, but it is unclear how far the hard-liners in Beijing will go along.
The central Government worries that Shenzhen will become too self-sufficient or closely integrated with Hong Kong, widening its economic lead over the rest of China.
"By the year 2000, Shenzhen's per capita G.N.P. should reach or almost reach the present level of typically developed countries," said Zheng Liangyu, Shenzhen's new Mayor, in a recent report. 
"The more profoundly we reform, the more contradictions and problems we shall face. 
This thus requires us to explore and experiment more bravely than we did 10 years ago, so as to really act as the pioneer and testing ground."
The saga of Shenzhen's stock market exemplifies the perils of economic revamping. 
For nearly a year after the stock market opened at the end of 1989, workers, clerks, taxi drivers and other residents viewed buying stocks as a sure way to riches because the market only went up.
Â 
Began With 5 Stocks
The stock market started with only five stocks, and the Government limited daily price changes to 5 percent. 
A lively black market developed where investors traded stocks at large premiums over official prices.
With no comprehensive securities law, there were no restrictions on Shenzhen officials owning stock. 
Many had bought stocks both to promote the new market and to make profits.
But in October, rumors circulated that to avoid conflicts of interest, Chinese officials would soon be banned from owning stock, and stock prices would be frozen. 
Many officials apparently tried to dump their stocks, and the black market crashed. 
Shenzhen had its first stock market scandal.
Â 
City Is Rebuked
The scandal soon came to Beijing's attention. 
In late November, the Government cracked down on the black market and reduced the limits on daily price changes to five-tenths of 1 percent.
Officials said privately that Vice President Wang Zhen, a hard-liner, circulated a memo among top leaders that criticized the chaotic Shenzhen market.
In response, Prime Minister Li Peng dispatched a team from Beijing to investigate. 
In a rebuke to Shenzhen, the central Government decided to allow Shanghai to become the first Chinese city to open a modern, computerized securities exchange.
The Shanghai market opened in December, and officials say that Beijing has now also approved the opening of a unified Shenzhen exchange, which is preparing to list an additional 10 stocks. 
Shenzhen, it seems, is supposed to develop and prosper, but in an orderly manner that does not alarm the central planners.
Local officials have learned to be more tactful in discussing stock markets and other initiatives.
"For some time we considered stock exchanges as something capitalist, but that is not right," said Lei Yu, the deputy mayor of Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong province, as he commented on Shenzhen's market. 
"It's just a good way to raise funds."

file: China Rushes From Mao to Markets.txt
text:
ï»¿
Perhaps the best-performing financial instrument in the world in 1992 has been a slip of white paper entitling the bearer to buy newly issued stocks on the Shanghai stock exchange. 
Sold early in the year for $5.50, by the summer these forms fetched nearly $300.
The soaring prices reflect the growing enthusiasm, bordering on desperation, of ordinary Chinese to become shareholders -- preferably rich ones.
After six years of on-and-off experimentation with shares, China is accelerating the development of a modern stock market. 
New companies are being listed each week, the number of investors is surging and hard-line critics have been muzzled.
Â 
Making a Transition
"The ideological problems are basically resolved," Wei Wenyuan, the executive director of the stock exchange, said in an interview in an alcove above the trading floor.
A local stockbroker put it more bluntly. 
"We're in a transition to capitalism, conducted under the leadership of the Communist Party," he said.
That is hyperbole, for the number of stock companies make up only an infinitesimal proportion of the economy. 
But the stock market is emerging as a central element of the nation's economic reorganization, and popular support seems boundless.
In early August, more than a million would-be investors waited in line -- some for days -- to buy applications for stocks being issued in the southern city of Shenzhen. 
The applications cost $20 and had only a random 10 percent chance of being approved to buy shares. 
Even so, the potential investors rioted when the applications ran out.
Some 50,000 people rampaged through the streets, attacking police cars and shouting anti-Government slogans. 
The police fired tear gas and some gunshots, and there were unconfirmed reports that two people were killed.
Â 
Leadership Meets
The clamor of a riot was not the kind of boom that reformers had hoped for. 
The Cabinet is said to have been worried as it met in the Zhongnanhai leadership compound in Beijing to watch secret police videotapes of the rioting, but so far there is no sign of a big slowdown in the move toward stocks.
"The Shenzhen incident was a problem arising at a technical level," said Wang Poming, the American-educated vice president of the Stock Exchange Executive Council of China. 
"It doesn't have anything to do with policy, or with the market itself. 
I don't see any major retreat from the shareholding system."
Mr. Wang said the rioting would probably lead to the establishment of a type of Securities and Exchange Commission to provide improved oversight.
China began to get excited about stocks late in 1986, and Shanghai and several other cities quickly set up rudimentary trading systems. 
A prominent economist, Li Yining, urged then that most of the nation's state-owned factories be turned into shareholder-owned companies.
Â 
A Popular Trend
Progress was slow, however, partly because of the rise of the hard-liners at the time of the Tiananmen crackdown in June 1989. 
Shanghai opened a much more credible stock exchange in December 1990, and Shenzhen formally opened its own a few weeks later. 
Now other cities are frantically trying to get Beijing's approval to open exchanges, but the authorities are refusing on the basis that Shanghai and Shenzhen should be national markets.
Foreigners have also been invited to buy Chinese stocks through special "B shares" listed on both the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges. 
Early this year, B shares were all the rage as investors dreamed of getting in on the ground floor of one of the most vibrant economies in the world.
Since then, the B share market has stalled, in part because the shares are relatively expensive and thinly traded.
"These are the ups and downs you get at the beginning of any emerging market," said Timothy Beardson, chairman of Crosby Securities Ltd. in Hong Kong. 
"China is going to have a very large stock market, one of the largest in the world, in our view. 
As the market gets bigger it'll get broader, and I think it's here to stay."
Â 
Foreigners Show Interest
About 20 stock funds have been set up by Crosby and other foreign brokerage firms to buy Chinese equities, and Chinese companies are also trying to list directly on exchanges in the United States, Hong Kong and Australia.
The Shanghai market now lists 17 A share issues, for Chinese investors, along with 8 B shares. 
Mr. Wei, the exchange's head, says that by the end of the year there will be 50 A shares and 10 B shares.
Likewise, the number of seats on the exchange has risen to 212 from 46. 
Soon, there will be 600 seats.
Mr. Wei estimates that 1.2 million people -- a bit more than two-thirds from Shanghai and the rest scattered around the country -- have bought shares through the exchange. 
Among them are 10,000 to 20,000 professional investors, known as the dahu, who have $100,000 or more in their brokerage accounts.
Â 
Some Fortunes Made
Some dahu -- the most famous is a Shanghai resident who goes by the name Millions Yang -- have made fortunes. 
For while B shares have been stagnating, the A shares traded by Chinese have been soaring.
"A fellow in my office put 5,000 yuan into Gold Cup Company shares a few years ago, and now it's worth 80,000 yuan," an envious official in Beijing said. 
Eighty thousand yuan is a bit less than $15,000.
These success stories have enticed more people into the market and created what is known here as "stock fever."
Books about stocks are selling wildly, night schools on how to trade stocks have been set up in major cities, and newspapers are running columns on how to invest.
Â 
Ignoring the Fundamentals
The only tactic that has not been tried has been analysis of fundamentals. 
Partly because of the unreliability of Chinese accounting, and partly because fundamentals do not matter as long as no one else looks at them either, trading often seems a bit divorced from reality. 
Price-earnings ratios exceed 100 for most Shanghai A shares, compared with a bit more than 10 for stocks in the less risky Hong Kong market.
Chinese investors seem to have a much clearer concept of upside potential than downside risk, even after a speculator lost $730 and committed suicide by electrocuting himself.
"What a numbskull," a Shanghai journalist said. 
"If he'd just waited, the market would have gone up again and he would have got his money back."
Restrictions on upward and downward movement of Shanghai stocks were lifted in May, and prices now generally follow the market. 
The first collapse came in Shanghai in August, with stocks abruptly plunging by nearly half. 
Some experts said the sharp selloff was a good thing, because it burned a few fingertips and chastened investors.
Â 
Talk of Intervention
Officials insist that the authorities did not intervene in the market collapse, but the word among Chinese brokers and journalists is quite different. 
They say the Communist Party General Secretary, Jiang Zemin, telephoned the Shanghai party leader and asked for smooth trading in advance of a party Congress this fall.
When stock prices continued to slump, the exchange apparently halted trading for 20 minutes -- under the guise of a computer breakdown -- and ordered brokers to buy and support the market. 
The intervention worked, and prices have returned to their earlier range.
"Privatization" is still a taboo word in China, sending shivers down the spines of Communist hard-liners. 
But some younger officials use the term "going public" to suggest that share issues are just another form of public ownership.
Â 
Pace of Change Is Disputed
"The key thing is that the Chinese have done it right," said William H. Overholt, executive director of the Bankers Trust Company in Hong Kong. 
"They've taken the time to create the institutional mechanisms for privatization before doing the privatization."
Some economists are impatient with China's relatively plodding steps, compared with the rapid changes in some former Communist countries. 
But others, including Mr. Overholt, say that China has prudently established a suitable foundation for capital markets.
"The East Europeans have done it utterly wrong, which is to rush pell-mell into reallocating the whole ownership and management of national productivity without having the institutional mechanisms in place to manage it properly," he said. 
"China will come out looking good."

file: China Taking A Harsh Line With Vendors.txt
text:
ï»¿
In front of a stall filled with tiny clothes in baby blues, pinks and greens, a man sits on a stool inhaling a cigarette with the intimidating nonchalance that he acquired in prison.
He spent five years in prison for street fighting, but after his release, with few friends and no work prospects, he decided to start a small vendor business. 
Last year, after three years in the clothing trade, this salesman - embarrassed about his past so that he gives only his surname, Zhao -made the equivalent of $5,400, about 10 times the average income in China.
While foreigners tend to regard entrepreneurs as heroes of the Chinese restructuring, many are social outcasts, and they are frequently accused of acquiring their goods by bribing factory managers. 
Their immense wealth also breeds growing resentment among many ordinary Chinese.
Partly because of such resentment, and perhaps because of its suspicion of private enterprise, the Government has begun a program to control the nation's 14.5 million individually owned businesses and raise their taxes. 
The Communist Party recently announced that ''exploiters'' would not be allowed to become members, and many believe this was a reference to wealthy entrepreneurs.
Â 
Drive Against Steet Traders
The authorities in Beijing also concluded a 100-day campaign against ''illegal street traders,'' including cigarette and clothing vendors, hair salons and food and drink outlets. 
The official English-language China Daily said the campaign had exposed 110,000 unauthorized businesses and produced more than half a million dollars in unpaid taxes and fines.
Official newspapers have said that much of the money made by the entrepreneurs is never reported to the tax collectors and that the majority of vendors have been in prison. 
A prison background apparently is common because released inmates have difficulty finding new employers, so they are forced to strike out on their own. 
On the other hand, most Chinese are reluctant to forsake their jobs and plunge into business, with its economic and political risks.
As a result, some former felons have been among the greatest beneficiaries of the economic restructuring policy of the last decade. 
There are no statistics on average incomes among private vendors, but it is certain that they earn many times China's average monthly wage of about $40.
The income disparities are creating discomfort for the Government, which prides itself on socialist egalitarianism. 
Since the new leadership took office in June, there have been ''cleanups'' in some of the capital's free markets. 
Police have closed down stalls of those vendors who do not pay rent, who evade taxes, who sell pornography or who ignore other regulations.
The Government complains that wealthy entrepreneurs are inflating prices, aggravating shortages and ''dampening the enthusiasm'' of state employees and intellectuals. 
Many of these vendors also contributed vast sums of money to the students during the democracy movement.
Â 
The Fastest-Growing Sector
It is not clear how far the Government will pursue its harsh line, partly because it needs private enterprises to help absorb a growing number of unemployed people. 
The authorities recently announced a tax break for private businesses that employ jobless workers in certain trades.
While private enterprises in the cities and rural areas are a minuscule portion of the overall economy, employing fewer than 27 million people, they constitute the fastest-growing economic sector. 
Their wealth is highly visible, for they can afford such conveniences as washing machines and video recorders, and they also have money to spend at wine bars and discos. 
Mr. Zhao complains about not having a Mercedes-Benz and an apartment large enough for his possessions.
Younger vendors also tend to dress better than most Chinese. 
One of their biggest problems is where to keep their money. 
A man selling athletic wear says he has four different bank accounts in the names of his wife, child and parents. 
He also keeps a large amount of money at home.
Small entrepreneurs pay rental and management fees for their stalls, and the total expenses including taxes could run to more than $160 a month. 
Normally, profits cover the expenses many times over, but since the violent crackdown on June 4, some vendors say earnings have been down by more than one-half. 
This is partly because of the shortage of foreign tourists. 
Even now, however, the vendors still earn much more than factory workers.
For all the anticipation of greater state control, the concern does not seem to show in their attitude.
Â 
'It Won't Rattle Us'
''They will put more controls on us,'' said a vendor selling women's blouses. 
''But we have already been through the worst. 
We've survived the Cultural Revolution, so no matter how tight their policy is, it won't rattle us and it won't last long.''
The Cultural Revolution, started by Mao in 1966, was a period of rigid Communist orthodoxy lasting 10 years.
Li Binglu, a 25-year-old former public relations manager, opened a restaurant and bar this fall. 
She paid $8,100 in capital, borrowed from friends, and pays the same in annual rent along with $270 in monthly taxes.
''My friends warned me that society was not stable and that the Government is severely controlling private enterprise,'' she said. 
''But if I make $27 a month from the state, it's just not worth it. 
I'd rather use a year's savings and get the experience, even if the Government shuts me down.''

file: China, in Crackdown, Orders Many Companies to Close.txt
text:

Continuing a crackdown on private enterprise that began after the crushing of the democracy movement in June, China announced today that it would close a large number of privately owned companies.
The Government's lengthy announcement of the new policy on page 1 of The People's Daily said that ''too many companies have been set up'' and in many cases ''management was in great disorder.''
It also said that private salaries have soared out of control for some top company officials and charged that Government officials have taken stakes in the companies they were regulating, leading to ''embezzelement, theft, profiteering and bribery.''
The announcement appeared to focus on Chinese-owned businesses and there was no immediate indication that the Government expected or wanted it to have any effect on the foreign companies that have ventures here. 
But foreigners and Chinese alike have said the Government is adopting a more hostile attitude toward private enterprise here and is starting to reassert control over the sectors of the economy that slipped its grasp as capitalism took hold.
Private enterprises in Beijing in particular were deeply involved in the democracy movement that was crushed in June. 
There has been widespread speculation in the diplomatic community that Government officials are trying to punish shops and factories that gave student demonstrators food, money and equipment.
Some observers suggested that the move bore the stamp of Jiang Zemin, the new Communist Party leader, who is generally viewed as being more comfortable with a centrally planned economy.
The article in The People's Daily set no target for the number of private enterprises to be eliminated. 
But it suggested that some have already been ordered closed. 
It is estimated that there are about 14.5 million businesses here that each employ fewer than eight people, and 225,000 that employ more. 
They account for only 3.5 percent of China's economy, but they have been the fastest-growing sector.
Their growth has highlighted the weaknesses of many of the state enterprises. 
In July, Chinese officials said that about 20 percent of the state-owned businesses are now operating at a loss.
Earlier this month the Government said it was beginning an inspection of all individually owned businesses, because of suspicions that they are avoiding taxes. 
It was not clear whether today's announcement was related to the earlier move.
Â 
Process Will End in April
The People's Daily article today said that the ''screening and rectification'' of companies would be finished by next April. 
While its criteria for eliminating companies appeared vague, the Government said that the first to close would be those that were ''an unnecessary copy of another company'' or in violation of a rule prohibiting Government administrators and Communist Party officials from taking part in running the companies. 
In some cases administrators who also have a stake in the companies they oversee have been reported to be a major source of corruption in China's economy.
''Those who still hold responsibility in the companies should give up their Government and party posts,'' the article said. 
''Companies with business power and at the same time administrative power will not be approved.''
It also said that ''special privileges'' enjoyed by some companies would be revoked.
It is not at all clear that the closing of the companies will have any significant effect on foreign companies operating in China. 
In recent weeks officials here have gone out of their way to stress that foreign investment is still welcome, meeting with bankers and industrialists and stressing that the anarchy in the streets during the May and June rebellions is over.
''I think there is a consensus among the senior leadership that the policy of openness will continue,'' said A. Robert Abboud, the chairman of First City Bancorporation of Texas and the head of a joint venture with a Chinese bank. 
Speaking in Tokyo during the weekend, on his way home from a meeting with Prime Minister Li Peng, Mr. Abboud said that the Chinese were trying to make a basic realignment of their economy.

Debate Has Just Begun
But if the Chinese press is any indication, the debate over how to reorganize the economy has just begun.
For example, in a lengthy article in the English language China Daily today, an unidentified official wrote, ''The Government will not tolerate indiscriminate Westernization and bourgeois liberalization, but it will continue to absorb and assimilate advanced foreign technology and management techniques.''

file: China_s Credit Rating Downgraded by Moody_s.txt
text:

Signaling uncertainty about China's political stabilityII, Moody's Investors Service Inc. today downgraded the country's long-term credit rating.
While the move reflected the likely difficulty China will have in returning to the financial marketplace since suppressing the democracy movement in June, bankers say China will still be able to raise money - though at higher prices than it is used to paying.
The downgrading of the debt rating from A3 to Baa1 is unlikely to have an immediate impact on China's borrowing costs since China has raised only about $5 billion in foreign currency bonds, none of it in United States markets. 
Bonds rated A are considered ''favorable'' and are one step above those with a Baa rating, which are considered medium grade.
Moreover, foreign banks are more concerned about when the World Bank will resume lending to China than they are about ratings.
The lower rating reflects the general assessment that China will have to pay more for its conventional loans than its previous typical margin of one-quarter percent above the London interbank offered rate, or Libor, a standard benchmark.
Indeed, bankers here and in Hong Kong say that since June, rates for trade credits and occasional other loans have generally risen by half a percentage point, and sometimes even more.

The rating change could have been more severe and the fact that it was not is one indication that financial analysts and bankers are being careful not to overestimate the impact of the June crackdown on China's creditworthiness.

file: China_s Divided Economy.txt
text:
ï»¿
About 60 percent of China's labor force is engaged in agriculture, where farmers essentially grow and sell their produce on the principle of private enterprise.
In 1990, agriculture accounted for about 33.3 percent of national income. 
Farmers do not own the land but since the early 1980's they have been given the right to use individual plots. 
They must sell a certain part of their produce to the state, but then can sell the rest on a relatively free market.
About 17 percent of the work force is involved in industry, which produced 46.5 percent of 1990's national income. 
The state sector is the largest category in industry, producing about 53 percent of industrial output in 1990. 
But private and collective enterprises in the countryside -- which are often far more efficient than state enterprises -- are gradually producing a larger share of the nation's industrial output.
Collectively owned enterprises sometimes blur the distinction between state and private sectors because they sometimes are run partly by village or township governments. 
In any case, they tend to operate on market principles and are much more entrepreneurial than Government-run enterprises.
Other parts of the economy, such as construction and retailing, are split between the private and state sectors. 
For example, large department stores are largely Government-owned, but in recent years, there has been a proliferation of small free markets and private stores and stalls. 
A growing number of collectively-owned construction companies also are now competing with large state companies for contracts to build homes and small buildings.

file: China_s Frontier_ The Search for Development.txt
text:
ï»¿
This is the ''other China,'' a land of poor peasants and occasional smokestacks, where for some households upward mobility means nothing more grand than moving out of their cave and into a house.
As China develops, the caves are giving way to brick or mud homes, and most people in northwestern China have basic clothing and enough food to eat. 
But there is still none of the sense of economic vibrancy and rapid change that permeates the coastal areas of southeast China.
The peasants here in Gansu Province earn an average of just $100 a year, the lowest of any province in China. 
Their basic needs have mostly been met, but economists and other analysts say that the people of Gansu have probably benefited less than other Chinese from the restructuring of the last decade.
''In recent years, the country has had a policy of regional favoritism,'' said Chai Zhuqing, an official of the provincial planning commission. 
''The coastal areas developed very quickly, with the help of the state and foreign investors. 
But we're in the hinterland, with long distances to transport goods.''
A recent survey suggested that the gap between China's rich and poor areas is continuing to grow. 
In the first half of this year, the survey found, per capita incomes of peasants were $49 higher than a year earlier in southern Guangdong Province, the wealthiest part of the country. 
In the poorest parts, like Gansu and Tibet, incomes grew by just $5, compared with those of a year earlier.
''The gaps have increased and I can't see that trend changing anytime soon,'' Nicholas Lardy, a China scholar at the University of Washington, said in a telephone interview. 
Professor Lardy said that the central government is no longer redistributing resources among regions the way it once did, and that this will limit Gansu's ability to bridge the gap.
Under Mao, China's economic planners milked rich areas such as Shanghai for the benefit of other parts of the country. 
The planners also tried to build up the industrial capacity of the interior, partly for national security reasons, so that the country could continue to produce if it were attacked.
Even so, China's industry is geographically lopsided. 
Of the nation's 500 largest industrial enterprises, 111 are either in Shanghai or in northeastern Liaoning Province, while only 25 are in the six provinces and autonomous regions of China's west.
The Government in recent months has expressed increased concern about the plight of the hinterland, and there is no longer as much conviction as there used to be that some areas should get rich first and then spread the wealth to the interior. 
But there is still not much of an economic strategy for China's interior.
''Opening the door on the northwest frontier'' read the headline of a front-page editorial in the semi-official China Economic News last month, but the article contained few specific ideas for how to develop the frontier. 
While rich in mineral resources, the northwest lacks the entrepreneurial tradition of coastal areas, as well as their wealth of overseas relatives and other links.
The People's Daily and other official publications have recently called for developing overland trade with other Asian countries and even rebuilding a ''land bridge'' to Europe. 
This revived form of the old Silk Route will take shape around the end of next year when China completes a rail link across its northwestern border with the Soviet rail system.
Officials here in Gansu Province are optimistic that the rail link will allow them to export their products to European ports, so that Gansu too can participate in the opening to the outside world that has left the coastal region so flush with wealth.
Much of China is now alarmed at the prospect of recession, because of an economic retrenchment, but Gansu seems less worried. 
In September, industrial production in the province was 8 percent higher than a year earlier, while in cities such as Shanghai production actually fell. 
Officials note that the local economy was never particularly overheated, so the slowdown will not be very painful.

file: CHINA_S INDUSTRIES QUITTING THE HILLS.txt
text:
ï»¿
A postscript to the cold war is being written here: a missile factory has been converted to make refrigerators.
Just as important, the refrigerators are rolling off assembly lines not in the company's old location in the mountains of south-central China but in a new industrial zone here in the provincial capital. 
As the people here say, the tiger has come out of the mountains.
The tiger is China's so-called Third Line of industry, built mostly in the 1960's. 
Fearing attack by the United States or the Soviet Union, Mao Zedong ordered 2,000 companies representing a large share of China's industrial and military capacity removed from vulnerable coastal areas to remote hillside towns in the country's interior. 
Mao thought that the Communists could rely on that Third Line of industry even if an enemy attacked the coast.
It was an extraordinary scheme, the most daring and perhaps the most ill-considered industrial relocation plan that any country had ever attempted. 
From the mid-1960's to the mid-1970's, nearly half of China's budget went to Third Line construction, but the new factories tended to be inefficient because of poor infrastructure and supply lines.
Â 
Moving Back to Cities
In this post-Mao, post-cold-war era, the Third Line companies are now moving back to the cities, and in many cases retooling to make consumer goods instead of weapons. 
Across the nation, enterprises that once produced tanks and missiles and other military products are now making 650 kinds of civilian goods. 
Here in Guiyang, the capital of Guizhou province, two new industrial zones are filling up with Third Line factories making everything from transistors to automobile headlights.
"Intellectuals are very happy with the move, after being in the mountains for two decades," said Wang Quan, director of the Guiyang office of the Zhenhua Electronics Industry Corporation, one such enterprise. 
"Life is better here, there is entertainment and culture, and there's better education for the kids."
Of the 700,000 industrial workers in Guizhou Province who work in Third Line enterprises, about a third have already moved to the cities or are in the process of doing so, according to Hu Lun, chief economist of the Guizhou Province Planning Commission.
Â 
Efficiency and Location
"We plan to move all our workers to Guiyang," said Mr. Wang, of Zhenhua, which has 30,000 employees at 21 factories scattered across Guizhou. 
"But that will depend on economics and on how efficient the factories are here."
One of the factories that already has moved and started operations in Guiyang is the Jianxin Machine Factory, a unit of Zhenhua that makes stone cutters, drill presses and other industrial equipment. 
In the past it exported some goods to Eastern Europe and now the managers are hoping that the improved location will improve exports to the West.
"It's much more convenient here," said Feng Yisong, a senior engineer of the factory. 
"Transportation is much easier, and it's far simpler to make contacts and get a hold of people. 
So our efficiency is much better now."
The factory shop -- emblazoned with huge red characters across the wall declaring: "Socialism is Good. 
The Communist Party is Good" -- is spacious and is taking advantage of a tax break to install some brand-new equipment in addition to assembly lines brought in from its old location near the town of Duyun.
Â 
Creating a Society
The director of the nearby New Cloud Equipment Factory, Long Hanmin, said that though there is a hefty cost to moving the plant and all of its employees to Guiyang, the move will soon pay for itself in improved efficiency and reduced transportation costs.
"We used to be a company town and had to create our own society," said Mr. Long. "We had to provide schools, restaurants, a movie theater and a hospital. 
In Guiyang, we don't have to do any of that."
Mr. Long's factory used to make electronic components for the army, but it shifted a half-dozen years ago to manufacturing similar civilian products, like transistors and capacitors. 
These days, the transition from military production to civilian production is well underway, not just in Guizhou but throughout China.
For Guizhou Province, one of the poorest in China, that switch -- coupled with the emergence from the mountains of the Third Line "tiger" -- also offers an important opportunity to lure foreign investment.

file: China_s Open-Door Stock Policy.txt
text:
ï»¿
Nearly a year after China's two securities exchanges opened with fits and starts, demand for stocks is so strong that people line up on the streets to buy them. 
Now, the Government is planning to let foreigners in on the action.
China's two stock exchanges, in Shanghai and in Shenzhen, a special economic zone on the southern border, are working furiously to bring out special shares for foreigners in the next few weeks.
But the process of issuing these shares, called B shares, has caused clashes between authoritarian-minded Chinese officials and Western financiers, who are helping to underwrite the deal. 
Moreover, a headshake of disapproval from one of China's octogenarian leaders could mean another delay or even a cancellation of the deal.
Still, compared with other emerging exchanges, like Taipei and Seoul, which have loosened their rules for foreign investors slowly, China's socialist Government is racing ahead.
"China has actually proceeded quite fast compared to Eastern Europe, for example, or even compared to some other Asian countries," said Rolf Gerber, managing director at SBCI Finance Asia Ltd., a Swiss Bank Corporation subsidiary that is coordinating the foreign underwriters of the new shares. 
"In this way they are very progressive, although they understand very little about the habits of how such transactions are done internationally."
China's bid to sell stocks to foreigners, without first developing the domestic stock markets more fully, underscores its appetite for ways to raise foreign capital.
Shanghai's exchange is still in its infancy and currently trades only eight stocks, with a total market value equivalent to about $430 million. 
At the end of November, Shenzhen listed 11 new companies, in addition to the six already traded, that have a total market capitalization of about $100 million. 
All are state-run enterprises.
Stocks are so popular that price-to-earnings ratios go as high as 428, many times those of even the most promising American and Japanese companies. 
But the authorities seem ambivalent. 
The Government has restricted listings and tried to curtail speculation for fear of subverting socialism.
The Government had not allowed any other new companies to be listed on the Shanghai exchange during its first year of operation, until 10 more won approval earlier this month, according to the English-language China Daily. 
Companies must wait at least three months before they are formally listed.
"The central Government is being very cautious," said Zhang Ling, a spokeswoman at the Shanghai Securities Exchange. 
"They think that if the market develops too quickly, there will be harmful effects. 
If there are no clear results or if the results are poor, then they will be even more careful."
Â 
Conflict Among Aging Leaders
The slow development of the markets also appears to result from indecision or conflict among China's octogenarian leaders, like Deng Xiaoping and Chen Yun, who are nominally retired but still hold real power.
Earlier this year, when Chen Yun and Li Xiannian, two of these octogenarians, were traveling in Shanghai during the Chinese New Year holiday, they happened to notice that many people were poring over the stock market pages of a local newspaper that prints the results of the week's activity. 
Apparently believing that the market's rapid growth was contrary to socialism, the two complained to Zhu Rongji, then Mayor of Shanghai.
Subsequently, the exchange's original plan to issue foreign shares as early as April was delayed until now. 
Foreign participation will be controlled and limited.
Just as China has separate currencies for foreigners and for local Chinese, there will be two kinds of shares: A shares for Chinese and B shares for foreigners, both in local currency. 
Foreigners will have to pay in foreign exchange for their local currency shares but will earn dividends in foreign exchange. 
Asian investors, particularly in Hong Kong and Taiwan, are expected to be among the major buyers of the B shares.
In Shenzhen, the Governmentsigned underwriting agreements last Thursday with 10 Hong Kong-based brokerages to market about $34 million in B shares issued by 10 Shenzhen enterprises.
But Shanghai, where the process began earlier, is likely to sell the first equity issue directly to foreigners. 
The Shanghai Vacuum Electronic Device Corporation, a state-run television picture-tube maker, has signed agreements with foreign underwriters to place about a million B shares, raising about $74 million.
The company has already issued two million shares domestically to individual investors and other Chinese companies, although it is restricted as to how many shares over all can be sold to individuals. 
On Dec. 
12, the price for A shares was 863.40 yuan.
The deal has been an eye-opener for both the Western underwriters and the Chinese officials. 
China hemmed and hawed for nearly a year before it gave final approval to the issuance of B shares, but then it expected the deal to be done immediately. 
Early in November, China abruptly asked a syndicate of six foreign underwriters to fix the share price at 420 yuan -- about $72 at the essentially free-market rate that will be used instead of the official exchange rate.
Â 
Chinese in "an Enormous Hurry"
The Chinese proposal included a tight timetable and a demand that the foreign firms respond by the end of the day. 
In the West, underwriters carefully negotiate the timing of a deal, fixing the price of shares around the time of the placement. 
But in this case, the price was to be set months in advance.
The foreign firms had not even had a chance to examine the financial condition of Shanghai Vacuum Electric. 
Arthur Andersen & Company, the accounting firm, was not allowed to begin its review of the company until early November, and even then, Shanghai Vacuum Electric executives complained that the accounting firm was scrutinizing the books too thoroughly.
Four of the six original participating firms found the terms of the deal unacceptable and withdrew. 
The Chinese "were in an enormous hurry," said Ted Rule, director at Standard Chartered Asia Ltd., one of the underwriters that stepped down. 
"They wanted things to get done in a period of time which I thought was unrealistically short."
Â 
A Replacement Syndicate
Before he even knew what the company's earnings were, Mr. Rule said, he was asked to commit to a price at which the underwriters would buy the shares. 
Part of the reason for the hurry appears to be the company's desire to issue the B shares -- representing a 33 percent interest -- before the end of the year to qualify for lower tax rates as a joint venture.
After the other underwriters left, Sun Hung Kai & Company, a Hong Kong securities firm, and SBCI Finance Asia, the Swiss Bank unit, remained. 
Salomon Brothers (Hong Kong) Ltd. joined to form a new consortium that completed the deal. 
The new consortium signed an underwriting agreement on Nov. 
30, with the price fixed at 420 yuan. 
The foreign underwriters insisted on a safety clause that would allow them to pull out or renegotiate the price if they found something in the company's books that they did not like. 
Now, the shares will probably be marketed in the first quarter of next year, in January at the earliest.
Â 
Swiss Bank's Examination
Recently, Swiss Bank was allowed to examine the company closely for the first time, touring its factory and talking with the company's managers. 
Discovering how China's planned economy meshes with the free market was a bit of a revelation, Mr. Gerber of Swiss Bank admitted, but he remains committed to the deal.
"I haven't seen any shocking things that would prevent us from doing it," he said. 
"But we're all used to a free market, so we had to revise our understanding in terms of how the Chinese economy works."
The Shanghai company has also agreed to allow Swiss Bank to become the 16th and only foreign member of its board, so that the Chinese can gain advice on how to adjust to a free market economy. 
Foreign underwriters will place 80 percent of the issue, while three Chinese securities firms will place the rest.
Â 
Takeovers Highly Unlikely
So far, China's rules do not limit the shares a Chinese individual can buy, nor is it expected that the regulations will limit the B shares a foreigner can buy. 
Theoretically, a foreign and a Chinese investor could team up to purchase more than 50 percent of a listed company.
But the Government is unlikely to allow such a move. 
"Takeovers?" a Chinese official exclaimed, laughing at the idea. 
"They may not yet have any rules that prevent this, but they don't need them. 
They just won't let it happen, at least for now."

Â

Friday that at the end of June the country had 12.34 million private businesses employing 19.43 million people, a drop of 2.19 million and 3.57 million respectively from the end of last year.

file: China_s Private Businesses Face Inspection.txt
text:
ï»¿
China announced today that it was initiating an inspection of the nation's 14.5 million individually owned businesses, the great majority of which are accused of evading taxes, and concern is growing that the Government is adopting a more hostile attitude toward private enterprise.
The announcement appeared in an article on top of the front page of today's People's Daily. 
The article said 70 percent to 80 percent of individual enterprises were evading taxes, and indicated the inspection would last two months.
''Tax evasion not only causes losses to state revenue,'' the official New China News Agency quoted Jin Xing, director of the State Administration of Taxation, as saying, ''but also disturbs the normal economic order and aggravates social problems caused by the distribution gap.''
Over the last 10 days, there have repeatedly been articles in The People's Daily and other newspapers accusing private enterprises of evading taxes, engaging in illicit activities like selling pornography, and causing growing income disparities in China.
Few people seem to expect a campaign to uproot private enterprises, which employ more than 26 million people for whom the state would then have to find other employment. 
But some foreign economists worry that the leadership could make life much more difficult for private enterprises.
''It does seem to be another step away from the reform direction,'' a Western diplomat said today. 
''The central leadership may just want to clear up some of the abuses. 
But without a clear line of support from Beijing to private enterprises, there is the potential that low-level officials will see this as a chance to settle scores: to impose new taxes, to demand kickbacks and in general to make life more difficult for them.''
Â 
Backing for Democracy Effort
Private enterprises in Beijing were deeply involved in the democracy movement this spring, and a crackdown could be a way of reducing their influence. 
Such enterprises, ranging from clothing shops to restaurants to small factories, gave student demonstrators money, food and equipment, and those entrepreneurs with motorcycles raced around the city to alert citizens about troop movements.
Economists and diplomats say that any crackdown would be difficult to enforce. 
Most private enterprises are family owned, and with bookkeeping still something of a novelty, it is very difficult even for China's 500,000 tax inspectors to prove tax evasion. 
Many enterprises, like the watermelon vendors now found throughout Beijing, are not even registered.
Likewise, the fate of the private enterprises will depend at least as much on the attitude of local officials as on the policy in Beijing. 
Those enterprises that have worked out mutually beneficial arrangements with local authorities are unlikely to face difficulties.
Â 
A Growing Private Sector
The private sector is the fastest-growing part of China's economy, but it is also by far the smallest. 
Officially, private enterprises account for only 3.5 percent of industrial production, compared with 63 percent from state enterprises and 33.5 percent from collectives.
But those figures underestimate the size of the private sector, both because many private enterprises call themselves collectives in the belief that it is safer politically, and because many entrepreneurs are involved in retailing and other services that are not measured in the industrial production statistics.
Formally, China distinguishes between privately owned enterprises employing eight or more people, of which there are 225,000 employing 3.6 million, and ''self-employed'' or ''individual businesses'' that employ fewer than eight people. 
There are 14.5 million of these businesses, with a total employment of 23 million people. 
Informally, both categories are normally referred to as private enterprises, and although the new tax inspections are said to be directed at the self-employed category, most experts expect all private enterprises to be affected.
Â 
An Easy Target
A Western economist working in Beijing cautioned that if the Government is trying to appease public anger about widespread corruption, it could find private enterprises an easy target. 
They are a tiny constituency without political muscle, and everyone believes that they, like other enterprises, are often corrupt.
''For now, I don't think any serious policy decisions have been made,'' he said. 
''But I think it's worth watching this space very carefully.''
There is no indication that a crackdown on private enterprises would directly affect foreign interests. 
Those officials who have been promoted to top positions since the democracy movement was crushed in early June have long histories of supporting joint ventures and welcoming foreign investment.
These officials - particularly the new Communist Party leader, Jiang Zemin, and a new member of the Politburo standing committee, Li Ruihuan - are generally viewed as supporters of continued economic change and development. 
But their background suggests that they are most comfortable with growth that is centrally planned and subject to strict control and that they may have reservations about private businesses.
Â 
Warning by New Party Leader
''Self-employed traders and peddlers cheat, embezzle, bribe and evade taxation,'' Mr. Jiang wrote in an article published in today's China Daily newspaper. 
His article warned against rising disparities in income distribution because of the wealth in the private sector, although he also cautioned against rigid egalitarianism.
Businesses that employ eight or fewer people are supposed to pay 52 percent of their profits in taxes, to reinvest 30 percent of the profits, and to pay only 18 percent to the owner. 
Businesses that employ more than eight people have 10 different tax rates, and many of these enterprises are supposed to pay a majority of profits in taxes.
On Saturday, the New China News Agency warned that ''China will soon inspect and clean up all individual businesses and private enterprises in the country.''
The dispatch warned that the Government would crack down on private businesses that produced pornography or shoddy or dangerous merchandise, or that were engaged in speculative investments that drove up commodity prices.

file: Chinese Banks Plan to Lend $27 Billion to Aid Businesses.txt
text:
ï»¿
Banks in China will lend $27 billion to state-operated enterprises that need cash, a central bank official said on Wednesday, although the Government's tight credit policy will remain in effect.
The loans are to be extended in the last quarter of the year, Hong Yuncheng, a spokesman for the People's Bank of China, was quoted as saying by the official Xinhua News Agency.
''The loans are still within the original plan set for this year, and the fund shortages will be eased to a certain extent,'' Mr. Hong said. 
''The tight credit policy is still proceeding in accordance with the schedule, and the total number of loans has been brought under control.''
Economy Is 'Bad'
One Asian economic expert in Beijing, who asked not to be identified, said the Government appeared to be relaxing its credit restrictions ''because the economy is so bad.''
The large injection of money is unlikely to be a heavy burden on China's economy, one Western diplomat said.
''The Government has been saving up pennies all year to have a big wad of cash in the fourth quarter when the harvest comes in, when they really need cash,'' the diplomat said. 
''They don't need to issue i.o.u.'s and can stay within budget.''
Last year, the Government issued large numbers of i.o.u.'s to farmers in exchange for grain, causing widespread resentment and some protests. 
This year there have been isolated reports of i.o.u.'s being issued.
''In China, it's not unusual for a lot of money to move into the economy in the fourth quarter,'' the Western official added. 
''What is unusual is that the Chinese have shown such restraint in the first three quarters.''
Â 
Warning on Program
Xinhua quoted unidentified analysts as saying that China must stick to its austerity program and its tight monetary and credit policies for up to three years. 
Inflation remains troubling and money demand is strong.
The central bank is joining the Industrial and Commercial Bank, the Bank of China, the Agricultural Bank and others to raise money for the loans to finance important state projects, purchases of agricultural goods and exports, said Mr. Hong, the People's Bank of China spokesman.
Chinese banks have offered $108 million in loans to hundreds of foreign-financed enterprises that face money shortages because of China's austerity program.
The austerity measures, which began a year ago, cut Government spending and credits extended to industry and canceled thousands of construction projects. 
The measures have pushed many small private and collective companies into bankruptcy and have nearly forced some larger enterprises to collapse.
Last month, the value of industrial output declined for the first time in a decade, raising fears that the economy was nearing a recession.

file: Chongqing Journal_China_s Dismal Truth_ 100 Million Out of Work.txt
text:
ï»¿
A score of grubby, lanky men marched into the cavernous and crowded Big Sheep Gully market, hauling buckets of potatoes, bricks and cloth on poles across their shoulders.
These men, who earn 64 cents a day for winding through the tangle of carts and peddlers and pungent smells, are part of the human migration of millions of Chinese peasants.
For the sake of a livelihood, they stream from their rural villages to cities far and near, like Chongqing, a sprawling metropolis on the Yangtze River in Sichuan Province.
"There's no need for me to work in the fields so much, and you can't produce money anyway, just grain," said a bucket carrier who must support his wife and three children.
Â 
100 Million Jobless Peasants
Throughout China's countryside, where three-fourths of the nation's population lives, there are an estimated 100 million jobless peasants, looking for odd tasks, chatting among each other, or standing around watching their crops grow.
Peasant restlessness has not led to major unrest in China in recent years, but serious underemployment in the countryside, let alone the vast numbers of those underemployed in China's state-run enterprises, poses a significant threat to social stabilityII. 
China's history is full of peasant rebellions, including the Communist revolution of 1949.
Peasants have a number of legitimate complaints, for despite the revolution's rural origins the Chinese Government discriminates in a number of ways against villagers. 
Most fundamentally, the Government pays an artificially low price to farmers for their grain, and then gives it at a subsidized price to urban workers -- who already have a substantially higher standard of living than the villagers.
Moreover, peasants generally do not receive financial support from the Government, while city dwellers are given subsidized food, health care, housing and many other benefits.
More and more peasants seem to realize that their work is helping the city slickers enjoy a comfortable life, and they resent it.
"The city folk get so many subsidies, and so do the cadres in the countryside," said a peasant doctor from the eastern province of Shandong. 
"But we get nothing. 
We even lose money when we grow grain."
Costs for farming, school and medicine are rising in the countryside, and if there is a bad harvest, if the economy falters, or if the Government goes so broke that it cannot afford to pay farmers for their grain, then a huge army of peasants could descend upon the cities in demand of jobs.
Â 
Projection of 300 Million Idle
According to some accounts, by the end of this century China will have 300 million idle peasants scouring the towns and cities for work outside their farming tasks. 
Already, peasants from China's relatively poor areas who migrate in giant waves to the cities are creating numerous headaches for the authorities. 
More than three million peasants, for example, have already come from other areas to work in the Pearl River Delta in southern China, according to a Chinese press report.
"We are under a lot of pressure," said Xiao Yang, Communist Party Secretary of Chongqing, a city with 14.5 million people. 
Mr. Xiao said the workers put it this way: "You give me a job. 
If you don't, how can you call yourself the people's government?"
There is virtually no labor mobility in China, and the Government restricts unplanned migration by forbidding its citizens to live in a place unless they have residence permits or official consent. 
But peasants flout the rules, and young women who want to become maids, young men seeking construction work, or people simply seeking a better life trickle out of the countryside into the cities.
Sichuan, China's largest province, with 108 million people, is particularly sensitive to unemployment problems because about a third of its rural work force -- 14 million farmers -- are idle, "surplus" laborers.
Â 
Unemployment Officially at 4%
China officially says its nationwide unemployment is about 4 percent, but those statistics exclude underemployment both in the cities and among the more than 800 million people in the countryside.
While jobs are tough to find, peasants say it is still worthwhile to go to the cities to look for work. 
There they join the "floating" population of workers without permanent residence permits.
In Bao An Village, about 60 miles north of Chongqing, Fang Qiong, 28 years old, does the family farming and child rearing on her own because her husband has gone off to the remote, northwestern province of Xinjiang to look for a job.
"About a dozen of the men went together to Xinjiang," Ms. Fang said as she was weeding her field. 
"He wanted to go, and I let him. 
What can I do about it?"
At a neighbor's house, four of the family's five daughters have gone to Shenzhen to work, while the parents look after their grandson.
"My daughters send money," said Yang Shengui, the 48-year-old mother. 
"Otherwise, we couldn't survive."

Executives of several corporations expressed guarded optimism yesterday about the potential benefits of the accord signed by China and the United States to remove a broad range of trade barriers to American goods, including computers, chemicals and cameras.
"It sounds very encouraging to us," Paul Allen, a spokesman for the Eastman Kodak Company, said of the agreement, which was signed Saturday.
Kodak, based in Rochester, has three offices in China, where it has sold film for both consumer and professional uses for several years. 
Mr. Allen said he did not know the specifics of China's current restrictions on film and other Kodak products. 
Even so, he said, "it's welcome news."
His comments were echoed by other executives, who said that even though they were not sure precisely how the trade agreement would affect their operations, the agreement signaled an opening of the Chinese market that would more than likely represent added business.
"It gives A.T.& T. the opportunity to compete in the Chinese market," a spokeswoman for the American Telephone & Telegraph Company said. 
A.T.& T. is likely to benefit from an agreement by China to eliminate by next March 31 all restrictions on purchases of digital switching equipment made by American telecommunications manufacturers.
Many American businesses will be examining the complex agreement this week to learn exactly how their particular industries are affected. 
Many companies will probably be formulating strategies for the Chinese market from a standing start, Ira Wolf, the assistant United States trade representative for Japan and China, said yesterday.
"The Chinese market has been so closed and opaque for so long, nobody is going to sell something tomorrow because of this," he said.
Â 
Trying to Curb Huge Deficit
Under the agreement, China committed itself to eliminating a vast majority of the quotas, import-licensing restrictions and secret rules it has used to impede imports.
Michael H. Moskow, the deputy United States trade representative, said at a news briefing on Saturday that the accord would mean hundreds of millions of dollars in extra United States exports in the short term and billions more within several years.

file: COMPANY NEWS_G.M. Sets Venture in China To Assemble Pickup Trucks.txt
text:
ï»¿
The General Motors Overseas Corporation announced today that it had formed a $100 million joint venture with a Chinese vehicle manufacturer to assemble pickup trucks for sale in China.
The joint venture represents General Motors' effort to enter a vehicle market that is expected to be one of the fastest growing in the world. 
China's 1.1 billion people now get around mostly on bicycles, but very rapid industrial growth rates are likely to mean enormous growth in the numbers of cars, buses and trucks on the roads in the future.
Volkswagen, Peugot and Chrysler are already active in China, mostly assembling passenger cars from parts imported from abroad. 
While there are enormous problems with quality control, high tariffs make imported vehicles frequently uncompetitive in China.
"We've been trying to do business in China since 1978," David Bodkin, a company spokesman, said in Beijing today. 
"We finally got an agreement."
The venture agreement, in which General Motors will take a 30 percent equity stake, will produce 600 to 1,000 trucks by the end of this year after the production line starts up sometime around June, Mr. Bodkin said. 
By 1998, the joint venture is expected to produce 50,000 trucks a year.
General Motors will provide mainly capital, while the Gold Cup Automobile Company will provide the production plant and about 5,000 workers. 
The workers, in the northeastern city of Shenyang, will assemble partial knockdown kits imported from General Motors S-class truck plants in the United States. 
These kits will be paid for in hard currency, a G.M. spokesman in Detroit said. 
Over time, the venture is expected to increase the portion of locally made parts.
There is also a provision in the agreement for G.M. to take profits out of China in a variety of ways including hard currency and currency exchanges, the spokesman said.
The agreement comes amid a recovery in China for automobile makers, including joint ventures, with the top seven or eight companies now turning profits after an austerity policy seriously hurt business in 1989 and 1990. 
Gold Cup lost the equivalent of about $11 million in 1990, according to an Associated Press report from Shenyang last year.
Â 
Company's Financial Innovations
Gold Cup, which in Chinese is known as Jinbei, attracted national renown a few years ago for its effort to become the first company in China to issue Western-style shares to domestic and foreign investors. 
Its shares were even peddled in a central Government compound, provoking sharp criticism from hard-liners that this practice was unbecoming in a Communist country.
Still, Gold Cup was better known for its financial innovations than for the quality of its trucks and mini-vans. 
Like most Chinese manufacturers, it is far behind Western standards.
Gold Cup recently spent $35 million to purchase a production line from the Toyota Motor Corporation to assemble 15-seat vans, and the two companies had considered further cooperation, according to a recent report in the official China Daily. 
It is not clear whether this cooperation will deepen, as had been intended, now that Gold Cup has formed the venture with G.M.
Â 
No Passenger Cars
Mr. Bodkin said there were no immediate plans to produce passenger cars, which several other foreign-financed operations, including Chrysler's well-known Beijing Jeep joint venture, have focused on. 
He added that the proposal to produce pickup trucks had come mainly from Gold Cup, which currently specializes in minivans and trucks and produced 20,000 light trucks in 1990. 
The two companies began discussions in 1988.
General Motors will have "operating and management responsibility," Mr. Bodkin said, and the president of the new company will be a General Motors representative. 
The joint venture will not have full autonomy in setting the prices of its cars, but it will make price proposals for approval by the Chinese Government.
General Motors currently is also installing an engine-manufacturing line that it has sold to the Beijing Engine Factory. 
These engines will be used in the pickup trucks.

file: Daqiuzhuang Journal_A Chinese Village Discovers the Road to Riches.txt
text:
ï»¿
Yang Yanru, a middle-aged woman who keeps her 11-room house spotless, could have been standing on a typical street in an affluent American suburb, bidding her guests goodbye after a luncheon.
Except for her crooked teeth, and a collar that suggested her man-tailored shirt was made in the 1960's, there was little to suggest that Ms. Yang was once a peasant who got her eggs from the chicken coop in the backyard. 
Now she is one of China's new rich, a woman who says she doesn't have to hold down a job because her husband makes so much money. 
She can spend her afternoons entertaining visitors, she said, or playing mah-jongg with friends.
About 45 miles down a narrow, bumpy road from the heart of Tianjin city, Daqiuzhuang has earned a reputation as a village that got rich through a strange blend of Communism and capitalism.
Factories here operate 24 hours a day, seven days a week, paying salaries of $800 to $900 a year to most village residents. 
Most of the rest of the money is plowed back into businesses or is spent on communal projects or perks for bosses and model workers.
"Even in my dreams, I never thought life could be so good," said Ms. Yang, who knits when she is not watching one of her three color televisions or talking on one of her two telephones.
Â 
Scores 0f Luxury Cars
This village of 4,400 people has 13 Mercedes Benzes and nearly 140 other imported luxury cars. 
In 1990, Daqiuzhuang's per capita income was $3,400, 10 times China's national average; last year, officials say, it soared even higher, to an estimated $8,400.
The village runs the factories that make the money -- 226 enterprises in all. 
Factory managers receive a share of profits in addition to their salaries, and their incomes can be enormous. 
In 1990, the last year for which figures are fully calculated, Ms. Yang's husband, who manages a construction business, was entitled to $9,300, though she said he took only a part of that and returned the rest to the enterprise.
No Daqiuzhuang citizen pays a cent for housing, electricity, hot water, gas, medical care or the 11 years of education to which every child is entitled. 
The village also invests about $3.7 million a year in building houses and apartment buildings for its 1,300 families. 
If an employee is rewarded as a model worker, as Ms. Yang's husband was, he receives one of 300 furnished, nicely painted two-story brick houses.
"Here we have reached the perfect form of socialism: Communism," said Sun Guiqiu, a senior official in the village.
But capitalism seems to be the major factor in the village's business success. 
Factories keep careful track of costs, pay their employees by the piece rate and use complex systems of incentives to increase production.
Despite detailed questioning, officials never made clear just how their village had managed do so much better than others. 
Perhaps there are further secrets here, or special benefits conferred by higher authorities.
One factor that surely helped is that Daqiuzhuang started earlier than most. 
More than a dozen years ago, the village established its first enterprise, a mill that processed rolled steel, and began selling the steel across the country.
Unlike most villages, which have a Communist Party Secretary as well as a village leader, Daqiuzhuang combined the two positions into one. 
That official is also chief executive of the holding company owning all village enterprises, suggesting that the village is actually one giant company.
Â 
$5.5 Million in Savings
The chief of Daqiuzhuang, Yu Zuomin, a 62-year-old native of the village, lives more like a tycoon than a Communist official. 
When his son married recently, the wedding and gifts, which included a beautiful new house, reportedly cost about $275,000.
After visiting the United States last year, Mr. Yu remarked that Daqiuzhuang residents were "much better off than the middle-class" of America, Mr. Sun said.
The village bank holds about $5.5 million in savings, the official said. 
As economic expansion has created work beyond what Daqiuzhuang's residents can manage themselves, the village has by official count added at least 7,000 laborers from across the nation; there may be many more.
These laborers are paid by the piece for their work. 
While they are also given housing, they have fewer opportunities for advancement than local people.
At Wanquan Industrial Company, a steel processing enterprise that reported earnings of nearly $5.5 million last year, 10 percent of the 2,100 employees are from Daqiuzhuang, and most of them hold positions in senior management. 
Liu Yunzhang, a villager who studied mathematics at Tianjin University and returned to become a senior personnel officer, is only 27 years old.
Mr. Sun is only 22 years old. 
While his annual salary is only $890, he negotiates high-powered business deals over elaborate lunches and lives in a spacious four-bedroom apartment.
Salaries are perhaps kept low to avoid taxes. 
Last year, the village's profits from its enterprises came to nearly $15 million, with one-fourth of that amount going to the Government in business taxes. 
Yet only a small handful of the 4,400 villagers paid any personal income tax, for a total of about $55,500. 
Income is sometimes distributed in the form of special perks like free cars for executives.
Perhaps because "guanxi," or business connections and relationships with powerful officials, are so important in China, the village also made big donations to flood-stricken areas last year. 
Such contributions may also be intended to ease criticism that Daqiuzhuang is too capitalist or too rich.
