Italy and Belgium announced economic penalties against China on Friday, suggesting that sentiment exists in the European Community for broader, concerted action when the organization's 12 members meet next week in Madrid.
Italy, which does not often take the West European lead in such matters, announced that it had suspended grants and loans to China to protest the Beijing Government's ''unacceptable repression'' of its citizens.
It was not clear how much money was involved, but the amount probably was not large. 
The Italians had approved a $260 million program in grants and credits for the three years from 1987 to 1989, and presumably most of that has already been passed along.
Foreign Minister Giulio Andreotti noted in a statement that the European Community was about to examine its policies toward China, but said Italy on its own felt it had ''no choice'' but to suspend consideration of future aid ''as a sign of our grave dissent from current executions and unacceptable repression.''
Â 
Belgium Freezes Loans
Belgium said it had frozen Government loans to China and halted financing for new development projects. 
The action affected a $7.5 million loan that had already been agreed to, as well as any new loans under consideration.
In Brussels, Reuters quoted a Foreign Ministry spokesman as saying the Chinese Ambassador had been summoned to the ministry on Thursday and told that ''the armed suppression of the legitimate aspirations of the Chinese people was a flagrant violation of human rights.''
It remained unclear, however, how much of an appetite the entire European Community has for unified action against China. 
On Thursday, Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher of Britain said she opposed sanctions as being ''too precipitate,'' creating the risk of ''a situation which could cause great panic in Hong Kong.''

file: Economic Progress in China Has a Seedy Side.txt
text:
ï»¿
A petite Chinese woman, with a skimpy skirt and a blouse revealing more than it covered, walked daintily across the lobby of the best hotel in this city. 
A few yards away, several smartly clad women sipping tea in the coffee shop smiled alluringly at the male guests.
It is an open secret that here in Shenzhen, a special economic zone just across the border from Hong Kong, economic progress has brought with it the seedy side of the free market: prostitution, corruption, smuggling and even drug trafficking.
Shenzhen is China's best-known boomtown, and it is renowned throughout the country for its economic growth, high salaries, modern fashions and adherence to "bourgeois" morals, if any. 
To many people in the rest of China, Shenzhen is a lawless place.
The Government is reluctant to disclose information on activities that are not supposed to occur in a Communist country, and police officials declined to be interviewed. 
Still, the underside of Shenzhen has become an explosive factor in the debate over how fast China should develop and how much capitalism should be brought in.
The Government's hard-liners argue that the capitalist influence is responsible for the decline in morality and the growth in pornography, bribery and drug smuggling. 
Some elderly conservatives would prefer to see Shenzhen's development proceed with more careful monitoring. 
In Shenzhen, some disagree.
"Prostitution, drugs and smuggling, yes, all these have appeared here," said Zhong Yaohua, an official in the Shenzhen Economic Development Bureau. 
"But slowing down economic development won't solve these problems."
Other defenders of Shenzhen admit that the bribes may be higher than in the rest of China and there may be a buoyant black-market economy, but they say the city is not entirely lawless. 
One law prevails even here, they say: the law of the market.
Shenzhen, designated a special economic zone more than a decade ago, has only in the last few years matured into a vibrant business center. 
But as trade links expand between Hong Kong and China's southern coastal areas, the entry points become more difficult to patrol and many goods slip out of the reach of border guards.
Last year, Chinese customs authorities confiscated $125 million worth of goods in 11,600 incidents of smuggling, a significant rise over the previous year, China's official press reported.
Shenzhen officials insist that only a small portion of smuggling occurs across its closely monitored borders. 
Still, more than $19.8 million worth of goods were seized by Shenzhen's police in 1990, and in the first quarter of this year, more than $5.2 million in merchandise was confiscated.
All sorts of items -- from antiques to cigarettes to guns to computer parts -- are smuggled into China. 
More than 90 percent of an estimated 10 million videocassette recorders sold in China are brought in illegally, and about 40,000 boxes of cigarettes, worth $14.6 million, were seized by police in 1990, official Chinese press reports said. 
The aim is to evade high import duties.
Greater contact with Hong Kong and Taiwan businessmen has cultivated a booming prostitution industry. 
A prostitute can make anywhere from $25 to $250 a customer, amounting to several times more than the average worker makes in a month.
Of course, most Chinese women would be scandalized at the thought of selling their bodies. 
But many apparently are not, for there are about 20,000 prostitutes in this city of nearly 1.9 million, according to one police estimate.
Drugs are also sold here, although much more secretly than other smuggled goods. 
While these social ills virtually disappeared for the first few decades of Communist rule, they are hardly new to China. 
Prostitution and drug trafficking, in particular, were rampant before the 1949 revolution.
"The Communist Party got rid of these seedy professions, but the sickness was still there," said Wang Xinkuo, a senior manager at Catic Shenzhen Enterprise Group. 
"Some of the black-market practices came in with the open-door policy, but some are simply the vestiges of the old society."

file: Ex-Im Bank Resumes Aid to China.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Export-Import Bank, an agency of the Federal Government that provides credit to the customers of American exporters, has made its first loan to China since the military crackdown against pro-democracy demonstrators in June, bank officials said today.
The loan is believed to be the first to China by any Western lending agency since June.
The $9.75 million loan to the China National Offshore Oil Corporation was signed in Washington on Friday. 
Wary of criticism by those who believe its China policies have been too lenient, the Administration did not announce the action.
Last month, Beijing lifted martial law, and the Bush Administration responded by easing some sanctions against China, including ending its blanket opposition to World Bank loans to China.
Bank officials said the loan, which is for 10 years at an annual interest rate of 8.3 percent, had been approved after a determination by the bank's board that the American company would lose the contract without the Government financing. 
Administration proposals to reduce the operations of the bank have drawn criticism from business leaders who are concerned about the loss of such export sales. 
[Page D8.] The new loan will enable the Chinese oil company to finance engineering services for a gas processing plant that the Chinese state enterprise is buying from McDermott International Inc. 
The plant is near the Bohai Gulf.
McDermott, based in New Orleans, has annual revenues of $2.4 billion and employs 2,800 workers, selling, among other things, oil and gas equipment and services. 
Much of its business is overseas.
World Bank officials said their board will take up two China loans on Thursday, one for $60 million for agricultural projects in Jiangxi province in eastern China, and one for $30 million for earthquake reconstruction in Shanxi and Hubei provinces in north China.
The actions of both the Export-Import Bank and the World Bank come against a backdrop of sharp Congressional criticism of the Administration's policies on China. 
Congressional critics argue that the Administration has been too willing to ease sanctions in the absence of significant improvement of human rights policies by Beijing.
Some officials said today that the United States might approve only the earthquake reconstruction loan because this would have the least political repercussions.
The Export-Import Bank makes loans at subsidized interest rates to foreign customers of American companies. 
It also guarantees export loans that commercial banks may make. 
For most of its loans, the bank looks for a guarantor, in case the money is not repaid. 
The guarantor usually is the national bank of the country receiving the goods.
In this case, the guarantor is Mitsui & Company, a giant Japanese trading concern that has close commercial relations with the Chinese oil enterprise and with McDermott.
Bank officials said a guarantee by a commercial enterprise in a third country was unusual but not unprecedented. 
''Mitsui offered the guarantee, and it certainly has the money,'' one bank official said.

file: Free-Market _Dragon_ Gains In the Fight for China_s Soul.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the struggle for China's soul, the hard-line leadership in Beijing seems to be losing ground to this southern Chinese region of fish farms, toy factories and private bars whose knack for free-market Communism has made it one of the fastest growing economies in the world.
Guangdong Province is China's greatest success story, and already it is becoming an international manufacturing center that in some ways recalls the early years of the "four dragons": Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan. 
While Guangdong used to be politically suspect within China for its laissez-faire ways, Deng Xiaoping and other Chinese leaders have recently praised it as a national model and called upon the province to become Asia's fifth "dragon."
Â 
The Bribes Help
That suggests that Guangdong has defeated Beijing, at least for now, in the competition to chart China's future. 
This could have enormous repercussions, for Guangdong represents a fundamentally different vision of China than Beijing.
"You can get anything done here," said an entrepreneur who found that bribes of $2,000 helped win commercial licenses and official support for his thriving business here in Guangzhou, also called Canton, the provincial capital. 
The businessman works 16-hour days, rakes in the cash, and has even bought a forged American passport for $20,000. 
He wants a foreign passport for ease of travel and for protection in case Chinese policy changes, but for now he prefers to remain in Guangzhou.
"There's more money to be made here," he said.
Guangdong (pronounced gwahng doong) is a symbol of aggressive restructuring, a place where people go to Paula Abdul concerts instead of Marxist study sessions, where entrepreneurs outnumber ideologues, where more people are rich than red. 
It is China's economic frontier, a magnet that draws the ambitious and restless from all over the country, and it is becoming a more important force than Beijing in shaping the values, fashions, economic understanding and social problems of the entire country.
Â 
The Underside of Success
A 25-year-old woman described her elation when she came down to Guangdong from Beijing in January and found a job as a secretary for a factory manager. 
Her salary was $190 a month, five times her previous wage.
But there were two problems. 
She was regularly exhausted by the long hours and heavy workload. 
And her boss made advances toward her and arranged for her to live in a room that was near to his and that had just a curtain for a door.
"So I quit," the woman said. 
"I got my old job back, and my parents ordered me never to leave Beijing again. 
But the pay and the opportunities were better in the south. 
Much better!
So I'm going to take the job as secretary again. 
I'll find a way of dealing with the boss. 
And if worse comes to worst. 
. . ."
Her voice trailed off and she shrugged.
Such social problems as sexual harassment, drug addiction and prostitution are more common in Guangdong than in most of the rest of China. 
But most people now accept that they are the inevitable underside of the economic integration of the province with Hong Kong and its rise as one of the world's major manufacturing bases for products like Mickey Mouse toys, Wendy Walker dolls, Adidas sweat pants, Yashica cameras, Accord watches and a cornucopia of sweaters, brassieres, purses and shoes.
The economic boom in Guangdong and Hong Kong may be one of the most important transformations under way in Asia. 
The boom, which is focused on the Pearl River delta towns nearest to Hong Kong, has lasted more than a dozen years and in many ways parallels the rise of the four dragons -- except that Guangdong's population of 68 million is about equal to that of all four dragons combined.
The Tiananmen crackdown and nationwide economic slowdown in 1989 caused a pause in the typical double-digit growth rates, but by last year Guangdong had rebounded: in 1991, the equivalent of gross national product jumped 13.5 percent, and industrial output soared 27.2 percent.
For someone arriving from northern China, the towns around here feel like the free world. 
Guangdong still has political prisoners -- including Wang Xizhe, a thoughtful democrat and essayist who is serving a 14-year sentence in solitary confinement -- but many fewer than Beijing. 
There is also less surveillance here, less intimidation, less political indoctrination, and less of a state sector.
In Guangdong Province, 38 percent of industrial production comes from private or foreign-financed businesses, while only about 35 percent is manufactured by the state sector. 
The remainder is produced by collective enterprises, which are often owned by the local townships.
Even the state-owned companies, because they must operate in a market environment, are far more competitive than state-run companies elsewhere in China. 
Bei Zhaohan, the chairman of the Baiyunshan Group Corporation, a state-owned conglomerate based in Guangzhou, seems not so different from Western business tycoons.
Â 
The Lure of Property
"We want to get into property development," said Mr. Bei, a dynamic 52-year-old man with a well-tailored suit and boardroom manners, "because I see that the richest people everywhere -- in the U.S., in Japan, in Hong Kong -- are all property magnates."
Guangdong's township enterprises are even more freewheeling, and many do without any Communist Party secretary. 
One prosperous township brimming with such companies is Houjie, a frenetic community about half-way between Guangzhou and Hong Kong.
Houjie has an official population of 75,000, mostly peasants who used to wade through the surrounding rice paddies, but it also is a temporary home to more than 80,000 migrant laborers who work on assembly lines in the township's 900 factories.
"There was nothing to do at home," Yan Jimei, a 20-year-old woman with long, neatly combed hair, said of her village in nearby Guangxi Province. 
"So I came here to look for a job. 
Life's much better here."
In a slightly squalid dormitory room in which 12 young women bunk together, 16-year-old Wang Zhiyin recalled that a year ago she was living quietly in the Sichuan Province countryside. 
Then several women returned to her village from their jobs in Guangdong and told of the wages they were making. 
A few days later, Miss Wang accompanied them back to Houjie and found an assembly line job making pink stuffed turtles for $50 a month.
American labor organizations have charged that Guangdong factories are inhuman sweatshops that frequently employ children. 
While some teen-agers do work in the factories, most are in their late teens and their dormitory living conditions are often better than those they left behind in their villages.
Wages are low by American standards, but extravagant by Chinese terms: $50 to $60 a month, more than some university professors earn. 
Almost all of the workers are women, who are regarded by factory managers as more responsible and adroit with their hands then men, and they typically work six days a week for up to about 10 hours a day. 
The women say this is far preferable to sloshing around the rice paddies.
The Communist Party Secretary in Houjie, a short, exuberant man named Fang Shuhui, is enormously proud of the town's progress and points out the sights -- the gleaming new movie theater, the mansionlike public toilet -- as he cruises around Houjie in the back seat of his chauffeur-driven gray Mercedes Benz 300 SEL. 
The car is nicer than those assigned to Cabinet ministers in Beijing, and Mr. Fang also has a cellular telephone, a beeper and other paraphernalia of a tycoon.
Communist Party bosses like Mr. Fang have nurtured a quasi-market economy, with 85 percent to 90 percent of prices in Guangdong determined by supply and demand, but the province is still a planned economy in one very useful way: the Government has devoted enormous resources to building bridges, roads, electricity plants and the like. 
The result is that some analysts believe that growth in Guangdong may be more sustainable than in places like Bangkok, where the economic boom of recent years has strained the infrastructure and led to constant traffic jams.
Â 
The News From Hong Kong
The opening up of Guangdong has created some risks for the local Communist leaders, however. 
News from Hong Kong, where newspapers and television report constantly and unflatteringly about the Chinese leadership, filters across the border more and more easily.
In the city of Dongguan, the local government even operates a cable television service for $7 a year, offering Hong Kong channels.
A major lesson of the south -- and one that Deng Xiaoping appears to have drawn, encouraging him to make Guangdong a national model -- is that the strategy of the moderates in Guangzhou appears to have been far more successful than that of the hard-liners in the north. 
The Communist Party seems much more likely to be toppled in Beijing than in Guangdong, and it was striking that during the Tiananmen democracy movement in 1989 the protests were far milder in southern cities than in the north.
As in Singapore and Taiwan, the ruling party here in southern China has won a measure of popular support simply by raising living standards.
"Folks complain here, too, but the volume is much lower than in Beijing," said a woman who abandoned a promising career in one of the most prestigious ministries in the central Government to come to Guangzhou to do business.
The willingness of such intellectuals to come to Guangdong to work, joining the uneducated peasants who hold assembly line jobs, reflects the rising status of Guangdong around the country. 
Increasingly, it is seen as China's economic frontier.
"There are more opportunities here," said Zhang Yanan, a 31-year-old university graduate from the central Chinese city of Wuhan who has just found work in a township. 
"Maybe there's not so much culture, but there's more money -- and with money, you can do a lot of things."

Cotton futures prices surged yesterday on New York's Cotton Exchange after the United States agricultural attache in Beijing lowered his estimate of the size of China's cotton crop.
On other markets, energy futures were mixed, grains were lower and soybeans were higher.
The attache, in a report written last Thursday and released yesterday, put China's 1992-93 cotton output at 4.33 million metric tons, or 19.9 million 480-pound bales, down from an earlier forecast of 5.50 million metric tons, or 25.3 million bales. 
The attache attributed the decline to a boll weevil infestation and damage caused by drought.
Cotton for delivery in December settled 2 cents higher at 54.93 cents a pound.
Â 
Doubts on Accuracy
Some analysts doubted the accuracy of the attache's report. 
Ernest Simon of Prudential Securities Inc., for example, said that while there was little doubt that the size of the Chinese cotton crop would decline this season, the 21.3 percent drop estimated by the attache was exaggerated.
Energy futures were mixed on the New York Mercantile Exchange after a day of roller-coaster movement before the release of weekly oil inventory figures.
Data from the American Petroleum Institute were expected to show a rise in stocks of crude oil and distillates -- heating oil and diesel fuel -- and a drop in gasoline stocks for the week that ended last Friday.
December light sweet crude was 7 cents lower at $20.70 a barrel; December heating oil was 0.66 cent lower at 59.43 cents a gallon; December unleaded gasoline was 0.11 cent higher at 57.96 cents a gallon, and December natural gas was 2 cents higher at $2.441 for 1,000 cubic feet.
Grain futures were lower and soybeans higher on the Chicago Board of Trade. 
Wheat futures were pulled lower by profit taking and the rejection by the Agriculture Department of a bid by Russia for 500,000 metric tons of United States subsidized wheat.

file: FUTURES_OPTIONS_Cotton Surges on Reports Of Export Curb by Pakistan.txt
text:
ï»¿
Cotton futures prices surged yesterday at the New York Cotton Exchange, bolstered by reports that Pakistan was halting all new export sales and by rumors of purchases by China.
The news from Pakistan, a leading cotton producer and exporter after China, the United States, Soviet Union and India, was the major factor in the cotton pit, said Ed Whitten, an analyst with the Balfour Maclaine Corporation in New York.
''Pakistan has issued an edict to not allow any more exports,'' he said, adding that rumors of Chinese purchases of American cotton also supported prices.

file: Heirs to Mao See Markets Trickle Down.txt
text:
ï»¿
The dusty main street of this rural Chinese community is a flourishing free market, with peasants and townspeople jostling each other to sell everything from shoulder pads to pictures of Hong Kong actresses.
Now, in a tribute to the maneuverings of the leadership in Beijing, 600 miles north, local Communist Party officials are planning to put up a red banner over the street along the lines of "Struggle for a socialist market economy!"
More to the point, they are also planning to establish several more free markets and to devote more attention to the needs of local businesses.
A five-day journey through Anhui province, a relatively poor region of rice paddies and mud-walled villages in east-central China, suggests that even remote places like this one are digesting the call of the recent 14th Communist Party Congress for an economic revolution along market lines.
Â 
Getting the Message
Few rural party workers know much about the leaders in Beijing who were promoted or demoted, nor do they care much about the party's contortions that enable it to borrow from capitalism to advance Communism. 
But in rural areas, the congress's outcome is being read as a green light to push ahead with economic changes and not to worry about ideology.
"Our big impression of the party congress was that the leaders said that the reform policy won't change for 100 years," said Hong Congmin, the Deputy Mayor here in Sanhe, a township with a population of 20,000. 
"That lets us all breathe more easily. 
We can pay more attention to running businesses."
Dai Zhaoyin, the 45-year-old Mayor, looked a bit puzzled when he was asked if Sanhe was bothered by "leftists" -- the code word for hard-liners, against whom the country is now supposed to be on guard.
"Well, I'm not sure they're leftists," he said doubtingly, as if speaking of some rare species of wildlife. 
"But there used to be some old comrades who weren't so flexible in their thinking. 
Now things will go a bit more smoothly with them."
In many ways, townships like Sanhe have long been far ahead of the leadership in Beijing. 
Nobody knows quite what the party means when it calls for a socialist market economy, but it probably is something like Sanhe: a bustling free market, a sharply rising living standard, income distribution that by Chinese standards is egalitarian, a docile population and a Communist Party organization that is unquestionably in charge.
Indeed, in many ways China has been led in the last dozen years not so much by the old men in Beijing who appear to call the shots as by towns like Sanhe that speckle the countryside. 
It was the peasants in most places who took the initiative in breaking up the communes, and it was they and the townspeople who started building the quasi-market economies that the party congress finally got around to endorsing a couple of weeks ago.
Â 
And What After Deng?
Still, even after 14 years of economic restructuring, many ordinary Chinese continue to worry whether such policies might be reversed after Deng Xiaoping, the nation's 88-year-old senior leader, dies.
"What people here care about most is whether the policy will change," said Yang Chuanzao, Mayor of Maoqian, a village of rice farmers 100 miles north of Sanhe. 
"That's what people fear. 
So they thought it was great when the congress said that the policy won't change. 
Everybody felt relieved."
Emboldened by all the talk of change and of a market economy, many Chinese seem to have found an excuse to do all the things they already wanted to do. 
Mr. Yang, for example, is busy making plans for his village to start collectively run factories producing carpets, lamps and embroidered cloth.
In Bengbu, a city of 2.8 million in northern Anhui province, the local newspaper is full of lofty phrases borrowed from the party congress, and a group of city officials who had gathered over a banquet table the other day agreed that the talk of change would have practical effects on the city. 
But they had a bit of trouble identifying precisely what changes might occur, until one mentioned the increased financial opportunities.
"Officials can now go into business," said Wang Wei, director of the city's external-affairs office. 
"Of course, the business can't interfere with your official work, but cadres can be managers of enterprises now."
All the officials beamed at that thought, and the conversation drifted to the possibilities of going into business on the side and making pots of money.

file: Hong Kong Empire_s _Junk_ Tactic.txt
text:
ï»¿
Li Ka-shing has built a multibillion-dollar fortune and a business empire by trusting his instincts rather than the crowd's. 
But for all his contrarian savvy, his attempt to burst into the United States by purchasing the $3 billion ''junk bond'' portfolio of the Columbia Savings and Loan Association is raising more eyebrows here than cheers.
For the time being, the United States Government has halted the transaction because regulators did not approve of the loan Columbia Savings, based in Beverly Hills, Calif., would be making to Mr. Li's group. 
But negotiations are continuing, and Mr. Li seems determined to buy the bond package. 
Through a spokesman, Mr. Li refused to be interviewed.
His determination highlights a sensitive challenge facing Chinese executives in this nervous British colony. 
As they spirit some, if not most, of their billions of dollars in capital out of Hong Kong before China takes over in 1997, will they also be able to export their money-spinning wizardry to the United States?
Periscope on Corporate America
''The big factor in the deal is that it would give us a periscope into corporate America,'' said Simon Murray, a wiry Briton with a dry wit who is group managing director of Mr. Li's flagship conglomerate, the publicly traded Hutchison Whampoa Ltd.
The United States has a far more competitive market, where the informal networks that tie together and control Hong Kong's economy do not reach.
Mr. Murray emphasized, nonetheless, that Mr. Li could not afford not to look to the United States as a potential home for some of his assets.
''We'd like to have a position in the U.S., but there are different rules in that game,'' Mr. Murray said, acknowledging that wandering outside the cozy confines of Hong Kong was easier said than done. 
''It sounds immodest to say that Hong Kong is getting too small for us, but the walls are getting close. 
We don't have much choice.''
Â 
Delicacy of the Situation
Making the situation even more delicate is that confidence in Hong Kong may be shattered if it appears that business leaders like Mr. Li are pulling up stakes.
''His options are limited by his profile,'' said John Mulcahy, an analyst at Peregrine Brokerage Ltd., a firm in which Mr. Li has an investment. 
''The impact on market sentiment if people thought he was really pulling out would be devastating.''
Undaunted, Mr. Li, who is 62 years old, has placed himself at the vanguard of those determined to gain a foothold in the largest, one of the safest and one of the most open economies in the world. 
That determination could eventually have a big impact on both Hong Kong and the United States, because of the tens of billions of dollars his companies control.
Mr. Li and various public and private interests he controls are a 50 percent partner in the group that won the bidding for Columbia Savings' junk bonds. 
With the market for such bonds nearly comatose, describing Mr. Li's move as being against the grain would be an understatement.
Â 
Potentially Attractive Terms
The deal, nonetheless, had potentially attractive terms. 
Mr. Li and his partner, Gordon Investment, a Canadian investment concern, would have put down just 10 percent, or $300 million, in cash. 
The remainder would have come in the form of a 10-year loan from Columbia, which lost $430 million in the first half of the year.
The $3 billion price tag was $70 million over the estimated market value at the time of the bid. 
At its peak, Columbia's junk bond portfolio had a face value of about $4.5 billion.
''I worry that they're going into something that they don't understand,'' said Marc Faber, an investment adviser here who previously ran the Hong Kong office of Drexel Burnham Lambert Inc., which sold most of the junk bonds to Columbia Savings. 
''They are very good, but what do they know about managing a junk bond portfolio?''
''I would prefer they stay in Hong Kong, where they have the expertise,'' said Steven So, an analyst here with Jardine Fleming Securities.
Â 
Further Drop in Bonds' Value
Joe Bencivenga, head of high-yield research at Salomon Brothers in New York and a former junk bond analyst at Drexel, said the value of the bonds had dropped another $200 million since the bidding. 
''They need to have a 5-to-10-year horizon to make this work,'' he commented.
As Mr. Murray emphasized in his office overlooking the Hong Kong harbor, this move would be not an investment play but an essential part of the group's future as it seeks to escape the uncertainty of Hong Kong.
It is also, Mr. Murray added, part of the testing of the next generation of leadership at the company; a key figure in it was Richard Li, Mr. Li's 23-year-old, American-educated son.
''Some people have expressed their doubts about the sons,'' Mr. Mulcahy said, ''but K. S. still has the final say. 
He's exposing them to the front line.''
Â 
Loans to 300 Companies
The acquisition would instantly make this canny entrepreneur a big lender to more than 300 large American companies, people familiar with the portfolio's contents said .
The companies, they said, range from RJR Nabisco to McCaw Cellular Communications, Pacific Lumber and Wickes. 
The deal would give Mr. Li access to potentially large amounts of inside data - as well as the responsibility for helping keep the companies afloat in difficult times.
''It is a good opportunity, but it will require an immense amount of manpower,'' said one Wall Street expert who had studied the portfolio. 
''There are going to be numerous workouts, bankruptcies and other negotiations associated with these securities.''
Â 
Possible Acquisitions Studied
Mr. Murray said Hutchison Whampoa had already studied possible acquisitions like Pan Am, Hilton Hotels and CSX, the transportation concern.
Despite its reputation as a bastion of free markets, Hong Kong's economy is actually a series of semi-monopolies and cartels, analysts contend. 
Much of Mr. Li's fortune was created from and is invested in such situations.
Mr. Li's background is like that of many Hong Kong entrepreneurs; he is a refugee from China. 
He left his family's home in southern China in 1940, and 10 years later had opened a factory, riding the crest of the first wave of industrialization in Hong Kong - making plastic flowers. 
That business provided him the capital to make his move, eight years later, into property investment, where he built his fortune, now estimated at $2 billion to $3 billion.
Â 
Member of Informal Cartel
By the early 1980's his principal real estate concern, the publicly traded Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd., in which he owns about 40 percent, was an industry leader. 
It is now a member of what analysts here describe as a sort of informal cartel that orchestrates the supply of apartments to the market every year to insure that supply will not slacken.
When Mr. Li bought control of Hutchison Whampoa - one of the old British trading companies, or hongs - he gained control of one of two leading retailers here and a more-than-60-percent share in the business of loading and unloading containers at what is one of the largest ports in the world. 
Later, Mr. Li acquired a large stake in a Government-sanctioned monopoly, Hongkong Electric Holdings, a power company.
In recognition of his position as a pre-eminent business figure, Mr. Li holds the title of non-executive deputy chairman of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, which dominates finance here.
Â 
Steps Taken Into Canada
Mr. Li has also taken several big steps into Canada, acquiring 43 percent of Husky Oil Operations Ltd. and buying a 204-acre site in downtown Vancouver, British Columbia, where the 1986 World's Fair was held. 
He is building, in a project in which his other son, 26-year-old Victor, is heavily involved, a $1.7 billion development at the site that will include more than 7,000 housing units and two million square feet of office space.
Recently, Hutchison has invested heavily in telecommunications. 
It now dominates the paging and cellular phone businesses here and is a big investor in Asiasat I, a satellite sent into orbit aboard a Chinese rocket earlier this year. 
Its signal will reach from Karachi, Pakistan, to Tokyo -more than two billion people.
It is an impressive history and array of businesses, but it has still been difficult to get American investment experts to take the company seriously, Mr. Murray complained. 
One of Mr. Li's problems in moving to the United States, he added, is that Wall Street investment bankers still do not bring him their best deals.
''We're an afterthought for some of these people,'' Mr. Murray said. 
''They say, 'There's this guy in Hong Kong named K. S. Li who has got a lot of bread. 
He'll buy anything.'
We have to find a way in that allows us to do the negotiated deals. 
That's what we hope this deal will do for us.''
