file: In Canton, Investors See Hong Kong After 1997.txt
text:
ï»¿
Throughout the 1980's, China's hottest growth area, and its biggest experiment in capitalism, was in Hong Kong's backyard: Guangdong province, a hotbed of entrepreneurial activity, economic experimentation and hundreds of Hong Kong-financed factories.
But Guangdong's reform-minded politicians and its soaring economic growth - 15.9 percent in 1988 -made it a prime target for Beijing's conservatives in the economic crackdowns that followed the Government's violent crackdown on the democracy movement last June. 
And when entrepreneurs in Hong Kong look at Guangdong, an area that includes the rich Pearl River basin and the former European trading outpost of Canton, they often feel they are staring at their own post-1997 future.
What they see today is a confused picture. 
The region is not the disaster that many predicted a year ago, nor is it enjoying the booming growth of the past. 
A Chinese Government campaign that started last summer to eliminate ''inefficient'' rural and township enterprises - hundreds of thousands of small companies and production centers in Guangdong alone - greatly slowed the region's output. 
So did a sharp downturn in China's domestic demand for the products Guangdong has become famous for: bicycles and color televisions, small washing machines, smaller refrigerators and sewing machines.
In recent months, the economy has shown signs of reviving, while other regions have ground to a standstill, or worse. 
''The reason is mostly subterfuge,'' said one foreigner living in the area who keeps close watch on the factories and small enterprises. 
''Many of the enterprises that the Government closed quickly merged or formed again, often using 'retained earnings' that were retained in big glass jars under the flood. 
And today the political pressure is easing up.''
In fact, on the streets of Guangzhou, as Canton is now called, Hong Kong's influence seems to be overshadowing Beijing's. 
Night markets are alive with a variety of products that one would rarely find in the capital, from fruits to locally produced Hitachi television sets. 
The Chinese-language newspapers are once again beginning, if cautiously, to hail the productivity of privately run factories, and local businesses have little interest in selling their raw materials to Government-run factories that are unwilling to pay market prices.
Nonetheless, there is a broad sense that Guangdong cannot again get too far ahead of the rest of China. 
''It creates too much jealousy and too many political tensions,'' said a Chinese banker based in Hong Kong.
Some development is going elsewhere, especially as Taiwanese entrepreneurs develop the coastal area closest to Taiwan itself, around the port of Tianjin. 
Other projects that a year ago seemed bound to fuel development are delayed until the direction of the political wind becomes clear. 
On nearby Hainan Island, where the Kumagai Gumi Company, a Japanese construction concern, paid a reported $30 million early last year for 30 square kilometers of land, the governor was ousted and the project has stalled.
The best news Guangdong has received in a year came last week, not from Beijing but from Washington. 
President Bush's decision to continue most-favored-nation trading status for China marks a reprieve for Guangdong, which is more dependent than ever on its exports.

file: In China, Capitalism Inches On.txt
text:
ï»¿
With the hard-line rhetoric blaring from the central Government these days, it may seem from abroad that China has abandoned liberalization in any form. 
But while the pace of economic change certainly has slowed significantly since the mid-1980's, in the last two years necessity has prompted leaders at all levels to take small but important steps toward a market system.
"There is reform, but it's regionalized," said a Chinese business executive. 
"It's coming from the bottom up. 
It's the local governments that are implementing reform, and they'll do as much as they can get away with."
Many of the visible changes are in trade, already much more unfettered than other areas. 
Export and import subsidies have been reduced, for example. 
But, Chinese economists say, there also have been a few price adjustments, advances in the bond and stock markets and city-by-city, county-by-county attempts to tackle the complex problem of urban housing, welfare and enterprise ownership.
Â 
'Moves Ahead Slowly'
"I wouldn't say reform is on the front burner, and Li Peng does not have a big appetite for reform," Nicholas R. Lardy, an economist at the University of Washington, said, referring to the Prime Minister. 
"But when faced with the alternatives, he moves ahead slowly."
China allowed its first government bond underwriting earlier this year and already the city of Shanghai and Shenzhen, the special economic zone created next to Hong Kong, have started modernized stock exchanges; Canton is waiting for approval. 
Scores of enterprises are hoping to raise money by obtaining a listing soon on these exchanges.
Shanghai, Canton and counties in poorer provinces like Anhui in central China, also have begun their own experiments in revamping housing. 
So far, however, there has been no nationwide attempt to overhaul urban housing, which is provided by employers.
One proposal supported by some Westerners is a national housing corporation that would buy homes and apartments from the various enterprises and manage them. 
Workers would turn to the housing corporation, rather than their employers, for mortgages and living accommodations. 
But so far, there seems to be no consensus on the concept.
Because of their financial burdens, as well as their overall inefficiencies, up to 38 percent of China's industrial state-run enterprises were losing money by the middle of this year, according to materials presented privately at a recent economic planning session. 
But China has been loath to make significant changes to loosen up government-run industry.
For this reason, some Chinese economists say that the last two years have been largely wasted from the standpoint of reform. 
They say that since the military crackdown in June 1989, central planners have regained control over much of the economy and that there is no longer much chance of a big change in the ownership system.
Proposals a few years ago to transform state-owned companies to shareholder-owned ones have been dropped or starkly scaled back because of accusations that this was the same as privatization -- an ideological taboo.
These economists also say that Chinese leaders missed an attractive opportunity to retool their economy, to raise prices during a period of low inflation, to close down money-losing enterprises and to literally force those enterprises to improve, instead of bailing them out with government loans.
"Parts of the economy show signs of improvement, but there has been no fundamental change," said a Chinese economist. 
"I don't think that in the next one to two years there'll be any major reform."
Â 
A Solid Exchange Rate
One of the more noticeable changes in the direction of a market economy has been in the foreign exchange markets. 
Since the 1989 crackdown in Tiananmen Square, China has devalued the renminbi, the local currency, by 43 percent. 
The rate of 5.3 yuan, as the unit of currency is called, to the dollar is generally thought to be not too far off from what it would be in a free market. 
Economists say a realistic exchange rate is very important in pricing imports and exports appropriately, and in this respect China is well ahead of many other developing countries that enormously overvalue their exchange rates.
A year ago, Prime Minister Li agreed to a plan to allow the Government's Administration of Foreign Exchange Control to make tiny, daily adjustments to the exchange rate, according to a Chinese official. 
The purpose apparently was to save companies from having to accommodate large jumps in the exchange rate.
But it also meant that China's exchange rate began to operate almost as a managed floating exchange rate. 
In fact, the rate has gradually risen another 2 percent in the last 10 months.
These days, many companies trade their dollars legally on the swap markets, where last month, 5.8 yuan could be changed for one dollar, essentially a market rate. 
Last year, a total of $13.16 billion was traded in 100 such official exchange centers, compared with $8.57 billion in 1989. 
In the first half of this year, $8.75 billion passed through swap centers, according to an article last month in the English-language China Daily.
Companies still have to give a portion of their foreign exchange export earnings to the Government, but now, much of those earnings are converted into local currency at the swap market rate, which offers a greater incentive to export. 
In return for this benefit, however, the Government this year began slowly reducing export and import subsidies, in part because it could no longer afford the swelling payments.
Â 
Price Revisions
Some of the most important measures in the last two years involved raising fixed prices for food and raw materials, which had been sold well below market levels. 
Economists regarded it as crucial to rationalize these prices and the Government has now obliged. 
But the main reason apparently was not so much an enthusiasm for markets but that the Government could not afford the subsidies.
China this year, for example, raised the prices of steel and cement, and it took a big step in May by raising the average price of grain by 71 percent and the average price of edible oils by 168 percent. 
For years, the Government had purchased grain and oils from farmers at prices much higher than it charged urban residents for them.
Such subsidies amounted to the equivalent of $7.5 billion in 1990, but the new price hikes will shave the burden by nearly a third in the case of grain and by more than two-thirds in the case of edible oils.
"They have been raising some prices, but in many cases it's been more for budgetary reasons rather than to rationalize prices," said Christine Wong, a China economist at the University of California at Santa Cruz. 
"It's hard to say they aren't moving forward on reform because they've done little things here and there. 
What's lacking is a comprehensive vision of where they ought to be going and what they need to do to get there."
Still, China's state sector is shrinking as a share of the economy and by the end of the 1980's, it produced less than 40 percent of China's national income. 
That is not far off from government contributions in Italy and France, according to Professor Lardy.
One Chinese business executive said he remained optimistic even though he expected few big reform measures from the nation's current leadership.
"The leaders?" he asked rhetorically. 
"It is not in their interest to reform. 
Their interest lies in planning, which means control and power. 
Power means better treatment, better living conditions."
But he added that 60 percent of the labor force, most of which is in the countryside, is essentially working for itself, and that even if China took no steps toward reform, the state sector would continue to shrink.
With a smile, he added, "The private sector will just keep expanding, and as long as more people are working for themselves, things will get better."

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_China Feels The Cuts in Its Economy.txt
text:
ï»¿
Displaying the bravado and ambition that have fired China's economic growth in the last decade, this little village had originally expected to increase its industrial production by 50 percent this year.
But such high hopes are becoming dimmer here and in thousands of other villages along China's coast, where the nation's striking economic growth has been concentrated in the last decade. 
In the country's economic retrenchment, imposed after the political upheaval and bloodshed of May and June, the coastal regions stand to lose the most.
While not all will suffer real economic declines, these regions are sure to see their supercharged growth rates cool down.
Effects of Austerity Program
The nation is already feeling the effects of Beijing's general austerity program. 
In October, nationwide industrial production fell 2.1 percent, compared with October of 1988. 
That was the first such decline in a decade. 
Yet, the central Government has said the austerity program will last at least until 1991.
Officials in Beijing said they decided to re-impose stronger central economic controls to deal with inflation problems, supply-and-demand imbalances, economic inefficiencies, overinvestment in certain industries and deficiencies in others. 
The inflation rate has dropped to 8.7 percent in October from 27 percent in January. 
But some Chinese worry that the program will lower the growth rate but not necessarily raise economic efficiency.
''In theory it sounds very reasonable, but in practice it will be co-mingled with politics so that nothing will get done,'' a Chinese businessman said.
This village of 2,850 people still plans to raise its economic output, and so far the austerity program has hampered but not crippled most of the 14 factories here making everything from champagne to chemicals. 
But in the surrounding area of Qingdao, about two-thirds the way up the coast, officials expect economic growth to drop to 12 percent this year from 24 percent in 1988.
Â 
Businesses Are Closing
That pace may still seem remarkable compared with growth rates in Western countries. 
But the sudden slowdown is causing thousands of small factories and businesses to close and could lead to grave economic problems in the coastal areas.
It is difficult to gauge the economic discontent among local officials, who do not feel free to speak out, and reliable statistics are hard to come by. 
But the austerity measures are beginning to result in business closings and a reduced flow of money to support new ventures, and this is likely to increase resentment against the central Government.
Just a few years ago, growth in the coastal provinces was vigorously trumpeted as a means to infuse the rest of the economy with a new spirit.
The leaders in these areas harnessed the energy of peasants pent up over years of rigid control, and small collective enterprises cropped up throughout the countryside. 
Their work in making consumer and exportable products in thousands of small factories resulted in double-digit growth rates.
Â 
Plan of '39 Stipulations'
But since the military put down the student democracy movement last summer, and particularly after the Communist Party Central Committee met in November to discuss the economy, the Government has reinforced austerity with a blueprint of ''39 stipulations'' for the economy. 
The effect is to shore up socialist bastions in the economy: central control and state-run enterprises.
The Government announced in November that in the first nine months of this year, one million rural enterprises were shut down and several hundred thousand others halted production or were forced to switch product lines.
The casualties may even be higher. 
The official China Daily referred in passing recently to three million rural enterprises being closed. 
Part of the discrepancy may be that the larger number includes planned projects that have been canceled or postponed as well as those that have been shut down, merged or converted.
Instead of the nationwide annual growth of about 10 percent over the last decade, China's leaders want 5 to 6 percent a year.
Â 
Tight Credit Policy
They have tightened credit to bring down inflation and slow down the economy, leaving many small collective enterprises severely strapped for cash.
Recently, the Government eased credit slightly, but local officials and business managers say a prolonged lending squeeze without economic alternatives could cause the localities to stop listening to central directives. 
As they have with previous policies mandated from Beijing, local officials could prove adept at skirting obstacles.
In Liaoning Province in the northeast, about one-third of the state-run enterprises are losing money, said a Chinese businessman with access to high-level information.
Nationwide, that figure is about one-fifth. 
But Liaoning is part of China's industrial belt, with many steel plants and machinery factories, the kind the Government wants to shore up.
Â 
Payroll Problems
Some factories have even had trouble covering their monthly payroll. 
One Chinese executive said 80,000 employees in a large city in Liaoning were not being paid. 
The situation was so severe, he said, that one factory manager reportedly wept as he pleaded with a Government banker to provide a loan to pay thousands of employees.
In Shandong Province, there are clear signs that the situation is not yet as bleak as the national statistics would suggest, although the area is probably an anomaly. 
Two Party members said economic planners considered the province's economy to be among the most stable and orderly in the nation. 
They say that means the local authorities may be able to dance around the tough measures without much backlash from the central Government.
Indeed, officials in Qingdao, one of the province's two coastal regions, say that only about 165 companies -mostly medium-sized collectives -were shut down or merged, and most of them were product distributors, not manufacturers. 
Over all, Qingdao has tens of thousands of collective enterprises, which produce 70 percent of the area's output.
Â 
'Efficiency Is Important'
One of the few rural collectives closed was a brick maker in Xiaowang village, but the local officials insist the closing was based on their own economic decisions and not forced by the austerity program.
''No one told us to shut it down,'' said Sui Lishan, the village party secretary in Xiaowang. 
''Efficiency is important to us. 
The land is important to us. 
And this enterprise ate up a lot of energy and land.''
As in the past when faced with directives from Beijing, local officials here also seem adept at turning some austerity measures to their benefit.
Officials said that before the austerity program was implemented, they had planned several projects to produce energy because the supply of electricity and other energy was not enough to accommodate their plans for industrial growth. 
Now with the retrenchment, they found they could cancel some other ventures and channel money to the energy projects to insure their completion.
A result is that the growth rate in Qingdao crept up again in November, said Zhang Rui, a deputy secretary general in the municipal government.
''But we don't expect it to reach 30 percent again,'' Mr. Zhang said. 
''After all, 12 percent is not that bad.''
China's coastal areas, which enjoyed striking growth in the 1980's, may be the hardest hit by the Government's economic retrenchment. 
In the Shan dong Province, however, the the situation does not seem too bleak for some manufacturers like the Number Nine Rubber Factory in Qingdao. 
(NYT/Sheryl WuDunn); map of China showing location of Xiaowang (NYT)

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_China Opens Grain Market.txt
text:
ï»¿
In one of its few efforts this year to overhaul its economy, China opened a national wheat market last week to replace central allocation of the nation's 85-million-ton annual wheat harvest.
More than 200 grain trading companies started dealing at the Wholesale Grain Market in Zhengzhou, the provincial capital of Henan, China's wheat heartland, the official New China News Agency reported.
The market's opening was delayed for two years. 
But it was ultimately allowed to proceed because it may help the Government manage grain distribution, long a serious problem.
Although the Government buys most grain grown in China, it lacks a modern storage network, and in bumper years much grain is left to rot outdoors. 
Serious shortages have occurred in some regions while others have surpluses.
China still lacks wholesale markets for the 169 million metric tons of rice, its main crop, harvested annually.
A futures market allows buyers and sellers to negotiate a price for what they think a commodity will be worth at a future date.

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_China Problems That Slow Economy Are Reflected in Lag for Port Project.txt
text:
ï»¿
Perhaps the boldest single project envisioned during the last decade of China's economic restructuring was a plan to copy the success of Hong Kong, 300 miles to the northeast, here on southern China's Hainan Island.
The Yangpu Port project, as it is known, came to symbolize the vaulting aspirations of Hainan, where a chunk of land was to be leased to a foreign company for a transformation into a duty-free port and a modern city of several hundred thousand people. 
The project was the centerpiece of a broad program to promote a market economy on Hainan.
But Hainan's progress has been stalled, along with the Yangpu project. 
There are several reasons for the slowdown, but they seem to add up to the clearest example yet of how Beijing's political crackdown has spilled over into, and put a damper on, some areas of the nation's economy.
Trend to Recentralization
Foreign investment was supposed to make the difference here, but getting it depended on the central Government's willingness to allow Hainan unprecedented autonomy. 
Since the June crackdown, many foreigners say, Hainan's autonomy may be evaporating in the general trend toward a recentralization of authority.
The Yangpu project has not yet been approved by Beijing and some officials say Premier Li Peng has rejected the idea that it become a free port. 
And while some foreign investors have come to take a look, they have been reluctant to put their money down.
Worst of all for Hainan, three of the most widely known supporters of the province's bold plans - Communist Party General Secretary Zhao Ziyang; his son, Zhao Erjun, a businessman, and Hainan's Governor, Liang Xiang - have all fallen from power in the last six months.
The island still has an industrial growth rate of more than 10 percent while most of the mainland is suffering a drop in industrial output. 
But Hainan officials are coming to realize that it may be difficult to get the foreign investment the island province of 6.7 million people needs.
''The central Government gives us lots of policies, but it's short of money,'' said Jiang Wei, an economic planning official. 
''So we depend on foreign investors. 
We have lots of good projects, but we need investors to develop them.''
Hainan, an agricultural backwater, lacks the basic roads, water and communication structures to develop a modern base that will attract Western-financed export companies.
In the early 1980's, the central Government plowed enormous sums into other special economic zones, like the town of Shenzhen, next to Hong Kong, but these are times of austerity, and Beijing is giving Hainan much less money than it gave Shenzhen.
''There's been some impact since June, and development will be a bit slower,'' acknowledged Li Huiliang, a Canton native who is now running Haikou's Southyang Footwear Factory, a Taiwan- and Hong Kong-financed company that exports athletic shoes to the United States.
But Mr. Li and others here are reluctant to accept defeat. 
Mr. Li says Hainan can still prosper, given its advantages over parts of the mainland. 
There is no electricity shortage, he said, and land costs are lower here than in some other coastal areas. 
Mr. Li says his company makes a profit of 30 to 40 cents on a pair of shoes and the profit would be 20 to 30 cents a pair if they were made in Taiwan.
Â 
Headaches for Executives
Another manager of a foreign venture, Rennie Velasco, is less enthusiastic. 
Miss Velasco, who is from the Philippines and runs the Haikou Lone Star Cafe, an American-financed fast-food restaurant, said that while Hainan might prosper if it became more flexible, for now it gives foreign executives the same headaches as the rest of China. 
''It's so difficult to do business here,'' she added. 
''It's so frustrating.''
To many foreigners, still waiting to see what will happen here, the Yangpu project is a barometer of the conditions in Hainan, and these days it is not a reassuring one.
The initial plan was for Kumagai Gumi Ltd. of Hong Kong, a 35 percent-owned subsidiary of a Japanese construction company, to lease 12.5 square miles at Yangpu. 
There, on the northwest side of Hainan, the company was to develop a free port, like Hong Kong.
Kumagai Gumi was to pay for the construction of local roads, power plants, water systems and other infrastructure projects. 
Foreign companies would then be expected to swarm to the area to take advantage of the cheap labor force.
Kumagai Gumi has already paid the equivalent of $6.75 million as the first installment on its lease. 
And the province's party secretary, Xu Shijie, and other leaders all insist the Yangpu project will go through.
Â 
'Won't Be Like Hong Kong'
But local officials and foreign business executives note that the project has yet to be approved by the State Council in Beijing. 
''There must be some differences between Yangpu and the rest of Hainan, but Yangpu won't be duty-free,'' said Mr. Jiang, the economic planner. 
''It won't be like Hong Kong.''
A foreign executive close to the project said that if Beijing did not allow the area to be duty-free, it might no longer be worthwhile for foreign investors.
Despite the Yangpu uncertainty, Hainan is still trying to arrange other long-term land leases, including 21.1 square miles near Haikou. 
Ye Zhanghe, an official in the province's economic cooperation bureau, said the province wanted the area to become a recreational zone with hotels, golf courses and other resort facilities.
''Certainly there has been an influence from June 4, but it hasn't been so great,'' Mr. Ye said, referring to the day Chinese troops moved against protestors and crushed the democracy movement. 
He added that since that time more than 100 foreign companies had come to Hainan to establish businesses.
But others, Chinese officials and foreign analysts alike, have less optimistic views, noting the apparent reluctance of foreign investors to commit themselves.
In addition, some Chinese and foreigners, contending that Hainan's dreams were never realistic, note that it lacks the geographic and developmental advantages of boom economies like Guangdong Province, which adjoins Hong Kong.
One of Hainan's clear natural advantages is its southern shore, which boasts beautiful palm-lined beaches. 
If the southern coast could be developed into a winter resort, it might attract residents of Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan who now go to Thailand.
Â 
Six Hours From Beaches
But the island's only international airport is here at Haikou, six hours by car from the southern beaches, and it will probably be at least five years before an international airport is built and resorts are put along the sandy beaches.
The province acknowledges that it is relatively new to the tourism business, and there are signs that it does not perfectly understand how to promote itself to attract foreign tourists.
''The scent is not obvious, not stirring, but internal, harmonious and penetrating in the air,'' reads an account about a suggested local culinary specialty. 
''Dog meat is superb if black or brown dogs with smooth skin and short fur are used.''

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_Consumer Demand Drops in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Last year was a nightmare for the Wanbao Electric Company: 100,000 refrigerators sat for months in warehouses, it could not pay its debts, a potential American partner put off a deal and its general manager fled to Canada.
The Chinese company, the nation's largest refrigerator manufacturer, blames fickle consumers for the problems. 
Buying evaporated as a result of the program of economic retrenchment begun 18 months ago.
Across China, factories have been wrestling with a problem: what to do if no one buys their products?
It is a new challenge for many of China's makers of luxury consumer goods, like color televisions, washing machines, ovens and refrigerators. 
After years of selling to an eager market, manufacturers had begun to learn how to speed up production to meet soaring demand, which culminated in 1988 in an inflation-inspired buying spree that had consumers grabbing goods from the shelves.
Now, Wanbao has responded with fundamental changes, including lower prices, new models and a production cutback to meet the diminished demand.
''In the past, we would sell according to how much we produced,'' said Chen Canguang, a deputy manager at the company. 
''This is our lesson from last year. 
We won't produce in excessive quantities. 
We don't want stockpiles again.''
Â 
Stockpiles Dwindle
Stockpiles of refrigerators have dwindled, and the company has cut its production to 30 percent of operating capacity to match the consumer demand.
The company says it designed seven models last year, after sticking with the same basic types for about six years. 
It says it also slashed office and travel expenses by 60 percent and reduced its storage of raw materials. 
Previously, it had piled up a year's worth.
The company also acknowledges that a nationwide tightening of credit severely hampered the company, and that it was saved, in part, by an injection of loans from Government banks. 
Rumors about bankruptcy swirled for a while, but Wanbao says it ended the year with large profits.
Â 
Big Share of the Market
''We have one-sixth of China's refrigerator market,'' Mr. Chen said. 
''How can we go into bankruptcy?''
The state has never allowed so reputable a company as Wanbao, which has 30,000 workers and can make one million refrigerators a year, to go into bankruptcy.
It used to seem that there would always be enough of a market for consumer products. 
But now the effects of the austerity plan seem to have been more severe than leaders expected, leaving many large producers at a loss to pay their payroll and other bills.
To avoid stockpiling their products, many have stopped production and sent their workers home with as little as 50 percent of their salaries. 
Some factories have even resorted to paying employees with products, leaving it to the workers to sell the products if they need cash.
Â 
Government Loans
In turn, the factories have turned to the Government for loans. 
The Government provided credit late last year and again earlier this year, when it made about $2.2 billion in loans.
But the hue and cry from factory managers and local leaders has been so vociferous that Prime Minister Li Peng is already believed to be searching for policies to ease the economic problems.
The austerity policy may be having a positive effect on a small number of companies, especially ones like Wanbao that are trying to gain worldwide attention. 
These companies may be learning how to overhaul themselves to compete on price and quality. 
At least for the moment, it appears that some of them are picking up the ways of the market, even if that means starting with the basics.
The China Refrigeration Industry Company, a Wanbao competitor that is one-quarter owned by a Hong Kong company, began formulating a design to better compete in the high end of the market in 1989, its first year.
Â 
Storing 'Half a Pig'
The company, based in a suburb of Canton, says it did extensive market research and came up with a refrigerator that has a middle section, which is adjustable so that it can be turned into either a freezer or a simple cooler.
''In the northeast, they don't buy pork like they do here in Guangdong,'' said Hua Hei Li, the general manager. 
''Up there, they buy half a pig at a time. 
In the winter, they can leave it outside, but they can't do that in the spring, or the meat goes bad, so they want a large freezer space.''
Wanbao also has a new three-section refrigerator, and so China Refrigeration, whose brand is Hualing, may be only keeping up with the competition.
The sluggish market last year also forced Hualing, which is about 10 times smaller than Wanbao, to slash refrigerator prices from the equivalent of $595 early in 1989 to $470 early this year. 
Wanbao also cut prices.
Last year's hardships embarrassed the company, especially as it was trying to lure the General Electric Company into a joint arrangement to export refrigerators to the United States. 
The factory's party secretary took over in November after Deng Shaoshen, its general manager, slipped into Canada while on a business trip in the United States.
It is not clear how much the company has learned from its experiences, but Wanbao is betting on a boom year again, hoping that refrigerator sales will top one million this year.

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_Developers in China Hit Hard Times.txt
text:
ï»¿
After a five-year development binge that has dotted Beijing's perpetually hazy skyline with dozens of new office and hotel towers, the Chinese are suddenly learning that the flip side of a boom is a bust.
With the chill in business and political ties between China and the West during the last year, offices designed especially for foreigners are lying vacant, rental rates are tumbling, loans for many building projects have had to be renegotiated and foreign residents are facing something they never imagined possible during the heady days of expansion - competition for their business.
As more buildings open in the coming months, the situation, many people here say, will get worse.
The excesses are in some ways a metaphor for the West's difficult business relationship with China during the past decade. 
The West's enthusiasm has tended to swing to extremes, and many foreign and Chinese developers are paying a price for the spurt of over-optimism.
Harsh Austerity Campaign
When the Chinese Government ended several years of fast growth, openness and economic reform in mid-1988 with a harsh austerity campaign to quell inflation, it was too late for many developers to turn back. 
Office buildings they had started earlier were already coming on the market.
The Government's bloody suppression of the pro-democracy movement last year only intensified the existing trend and frightened off some foreign corporations, the prospective tenants for the new office space.
Probably the best illustration of how bad things were before the building boom, and how things have changed, is the story of Shell China Ltd., a subsidiary of the Royal Dutch/ Shell Group, the world's second-largest oil company. 
Seven years ago, when Shell was shopping for office space, the best it could find was half of the sixth floor of the Hepingmen Roast Duck Restaurant building, about a mile south of Tiananmen Square in the center of the capital.
Â 
'It Always Smelled of Duck'
''All in all, it was quite adequate compared to the other choices, mostly hotels,'' said Christopher Evans, head of administration for Shell's 26-person staff here. 
''The real problem was that it always smelled of duck; it was not inferior duck or anything like that, but it's the largest Peking duckery in the world, and so they were cooking them all the time.''
Shell moved several months ago to the new China World Trade Center, the largest office complex in the country, which includes two hotels, a convention center, apartments, a shopping complex and much better ventilation.
''We like it because the telecommunications are a bit better than at the duck, and it's a better location,'' Mr. Evans said. 
An additional benefit, he said, is he can again enjoy ordering Peking duck at restaurants, something he could not bear while ensconced in the old quarters.
As one of the premier new buildings in the capital, the China World Trade Center, with 550,000 square feet of space, was expected to be filled by now. 
But its managers are generally happy to have commitments for about 70 percent of the space, all taken by foreign companies.
Â 
Rental Prices Fall
The maximum rents being charged are about $3.25 a square foot - less than the top rate of $4.15 a square foot they had expected before China's military crushed the pro-democracy movement last summer.
Yoshiaki Hashimoto, an administrative officer here for the Mitsubishi Corporation, said that after the turmoil in Tiananmen Square his negotiations with the World Trade Center's management took a decided turn for the better. 
The rent sought for the 26,000 square feet fell sharply.
Although he would not give the exact figure, Mr. Hashimoto said Mitsubishi ended up paying about half what it was being charged at its previous site, the Capital Hotel, whose facilities he said were poor. 
Like many other foreign companies here, Mistubishi had moved into a hotel in the mid-1980's because it was the only space available.
The granddaddy of hotel-office complexes here is the Jianguo Hotel - an exact replica of the Holiday Inn in Palo Alto, Calif. 
(The American investor in the joint venture to build the Jianguo Hotel was also an investor in the Holiday Inn and brought with him a set of plans.) It opened in 1982 and enjoyed close to 100 percent occupancy for years, drawing on tourists and companies taking rooms on long-term leases.
Now it is feeling the squeeze, too. 
Over the last year the Jianguo has lost about half its long-term corporate tenants and the overall occupancy rate is barely 50 percent, said Peter J. Hierzi, deputy general manager. 
$2 a Square Foot Some offices in other new buildings built for foreign occupants are being let for $2 a square foot, down from a minimum of about $2.75 just 18 months ago, according to Richard Ellis Ltd., a real estate brokerage firm. 
That is still high for what many companies regard as a hardship post, but nearly 25 percent below the peak.
Richard Ellis estimated that earlier this year there was 1.6 million square feet of office space suitable for foreign companies in Beijing, of which only 65 percent was occupied. 
The broker added that many new buildings have only let about 25 percent of their office space.
Apartments designed for foreigners - with central air-conditioning and Western-style toilets - have the same problems. 
A 1,600-square-foot three-bedroom apartment at the World Trade Center complex, a joint venture between a Hong Kong company and a Chinese Government entity, is going for about $4,000 a month -compared with $6,000 a month for the same size unit at the Holiday Inn Lido complex, on the airport road. 
Those apartments, among the few modern apartments for foreign business executives when they opened in 1985, had been fully rented before they were even completed.
Â 
Apartments Go Begging
Even with the price drop, most new apartments have gone begging for tenants. 
According to Richard Ellis, which recently closed its Beijing office because of the slow market, only 75 percent of the 2,400 apartments built for foreigners in the last five years are leased.
Another 1,270 apartments are scheduled to come on the market this year, with another 150 expected next year. 
Rents for a 1,600-square-foot apartment could tumble to $3,000 a month.
Caught in the squeeze are a number of foreign property developers. 
But the blow has fallen hardest on Japanese companies, which were partners in 12 projects under construction as of early 1988, amounting to several hundred million dollars, according to a study done by the National Council for United States-China Trade.
The lengthy list the council compiled gave evidence of how Chinese entities had leaped blindly into the development fray. 
Among the Chinese partners in these projects, many of which have been completed, were affiliates of the People's Liberation Army, the Ministry of Justice, the provincial government of Inner Mongolia, the State Farm Bureau and an aluminum factory.

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_Headaches in China for Investors.txt
text:
ï»¿
When officials of the Shanghai Center told the Chinese customs bureau that the complex planned to import 50 to 60 cars, they received a strange notice: for each model of a Japanese car it imported, it would have to bring in two extra samples. 
These would be turned over to authorities for ''test driving.''
''It doesn't matter that the model you bring in is already on the streets of Shanghai,'' said Patsy Whitcomb, an American executive who is helping to prepare for the opening of the $195.5 million Shanghai Center, which is being financed by American and Japanese investors.
The request for extra cars is just the latest snag in what has been a long, twisted process of constructing Shanghai Center, which will be the city's largest hotel, office and residential complex when it opens in March.
Â 
Little Flexibility
The center's owner, Seacliff Ltd., hopes that the new rule, which comes on top of a 280 percent duty on the imported cars, will be negotiable, although customs officials have shown little flexibility so far. 
They have already prohibited the company from importing a Mercedes-Benz, a car that they say would not suit China's new style of ''plain living.''
The experience of Shanghai Center suggests that China remains as much of a headache as ever to many foreign investors, despite the eagerness of the Government to attract investment since its bloody crackdown last June.
Yet for the Shanghai Center, there is profound injury as well as insult: it is opening just as foreign business clients are staying away from China in droves. 
And for all its commitment to China, the center finds itself running up against the same problems that keep its clients away.
With its retail shops and 1,000-seat theater, the center is a showcase project intended to add a cosmopolitan air to China's biggest city. 
Thus, it would have seemed a likely candidate to get help from the Chinese Government as Shanghai tries desperately to regain its role as a financial and commercial center for Asia.
Â 
No Change Since Crackdown
So far, however, the Shanghai Center has not found business any easier since the crackdown, according to Seacliff, a partnership among the Portman Companies and the American International Group, both of the United States, and a Japanese concern, the Kajima Corporation. 
The Shanghai Center was designed by John Portman & Associates, the American architectural firm.
Investors had hoped the Chinese would offer better terms, both to overcome international outrage after the bloodshed in June and to dispel the gradual disillusionment of many Western investors in recent years, particularly after an economic austerity drive that began in late 1988 reduced prospects for economic growth.
Many business analysts in Shanghai say that the center would have been highly successful before the austerity drive began, but that the business climate is now much more sluggish. 
Uncertainty has also scared away many new investors and potential clients, although some who have been negotiating plans for years still plan to come.
''The real challenge is that there are no new people coming in,'' said Michael C. Kalyk, the general manager of the center. 
''New business has to start up again before there's real business for us.''
Â 
Foreign Investment Dwindles
Like the rest of China, Shanghai has seen foreign investment dwindle since the crackdown. 
From January to June last year, there were 133 new projects worth $260 million by American investors, a Western diplomat estimated. 
The diplomat said that from July to December, only 66 projects worth $150 million were started, and most of these were begun before the crackdown.
The first half of this year will be more telling, since those who have invested less time in start-up negotiations may not feel burdened to continue their projects. 
Some companies who tried to pull out of their contracts apparently were not allowed to do so by the Chinese, diplomats say.
After the crackdown, many foreign companies facing dimmer commercial prospects hoped that Chinese bureaucrats would be more conciliatory at the negotiating table to restore the confidence of overseas investors. 
Some were offered interviews with senior officials, ministry-level bureaucrats, and at times, an audience with the Communist Party General Secretary himself, Jiang Zemin.
Foreign companies that demonstrated their commitment to China were thanked effusively and given encouragement. 
Some hope still lies in the prospect this spring that China will change the joint-venture law, extending the allowable term of a venture and authorizing the appointment of foreigners as a venture's chairman.
Â 
No Widespread Concession
Yet so far the high visibility has not led to widespread concessions, diplomats and business executives say. 
Only a small number of companies have obtained better terms, notably a foreign real estate developer in Tianjin. 
In fact, executives say some authorities, in an attempt to prove they are not to be cowed by foreigners, have actually become less cooperative with foreign companies.
''Despite the public relations, the environment for getting concessions is not easier, but harder,'' a Western diplomat here said. 
''There are regulations that may have been in place already, but now there is a trend to enforcing the regulations that people overlooked before.''
Seacliff is negotiating with Shanghai's local government for greater concessions, primarily on property taxes and an extension on its current 18-year land lease. 
But the Shanghai government, which has auctioned off expensive land-use rights for 50 years to a foreign company, might not want to offer a 50-year or even 40-year lease to the Shanghai Center at a bargain price for fear of offending its other client.
A Chinese business official familiar with the negotiations indicated that Seacliff would probably get an extension, although it was not clear for how long.
Â 
Commercial Reputation
Shanghai has enjoyed a reputation as one of China's most attractive commercial centers for foreign investment and business representation. 
When the Portman Companies first conceived of building a mixed-use complex in 1979 and then when construction began in 1986, there was a severe shortage of first-rate commercial complexes in Shanghai.
The company had estimated that in 1986 there were about 4,000 hotel rooms for foreigners. 
But since then, officials all over Shanghai, and throughout China, moved as quickly as possible to sponsor hotel projects.
There apparently was no central plan governing construction projects in Shanghai, and for competitive reasons owners and builders tried to keep their development plans secret. 
As a result, the Portman Shanghai hotel will add 700 rooms, in March or soon thereafter, to a city that will have a total of 18,000 hotel rooms, Seacliff estimates. 
When the hotel opens, Seacliff expects occupancy to be around 40 percent.
So far, the company has pre-leased about 25 percent of its apartments, 20 percent of its shopping complex and 30 percent of its office space. 
The complex will not be fully open until July, when the theater is finished.
Â 
Complex Behind Schedule
In mid-1985, executives of the Portman Companies indicated that the project would be finished in the spring of 1988. 
Revised plans set the opening date for December 1989, which then was delayed three months when work halted for 30 days after the June crackdown. 
Crews were sent to their homes overseas or to other provinces in China, and it took about two months to be ready again.
In late summer, Seacliff injected an additional $20.5 million in capital to cover cost overruns and help start the construction process again, bringing the total project cost to $195.5 million. 
On Jan. 
24, the company and its bankers, including the First National Bank of Chicago, signed an agreement, apparently initiated before the crackdown, to restructure the project's $145 million in loans.
Mr. Kalyk of Seacliff said the Shanghai Center would be able to cover operating expenses as soon as it opened, and he said he was confident the center would be able to meet its loan repayments. 
About a fourth of all operating expenses, he said, go to pay salaries for expatriate employees. 
This sum should drop once the center is running smoothly.

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_Pessimism on Chinese Trade.txt
text:
ï»¿
Ever since they sailed their clipper ships to China two centuries ago with cargoes of opium, foreign traders have brimmed with optimism about the potential of the vast China market. 
These days, however, on the first anniversary of the bloody suppression of the democracy movement, the flush of optimism is gone, along with much of the business.
While only a handful of American corporations have closed their doors and left China since the crackdown last June 4, and a few newcomers have set up shop, many companies say business is more difficult than ever, and in some cases slower than they had expected it would be.
For most traders with sales offices in China, business is in a deep slump.
''We feel that things just have to get better,'' said a foreign business executive in Beijing. 
''But I can't say we're past the bottom of the cycle.''
Â 
Curbs on Imports and Credit
Executives say these hard times stem from the austerity program China began in the fall of 1988 and intensified last summer, with the Government clamping down on imports and on credit to local companies.
But beyond that, they say the violent crackdown last year and the mixed signals about economic liberalization since then have made it nearly impossible to assess China's political risk with any confidence.
Doing business in China has always been difficult, particularly because China's bureaucracy often requires myriad steps and approvals before any agreement can be signed. 
Collecting and confirming seemingly simple information, like the amount of a new tariff, can often lead a company through a maze of bureacratic red tape without a definitive answer.
Â 
Sales Have Decreased
Now China has tightened credit, cutting off funds to many Government entities and industrial enterprises that would otherwise purchase from American companies, and so sales of American products are down.
For many foreign companies, this year has been marked by other obstacles, further tainting the business climate. 
Some obstacles, like martial law, are being removed. 
But in the meantime China has recentralized its decision-making process, so that the central Government and not just the local authority must agree to certain investment and trade proposals. 
This has created a more difficult and confusing investment environment.
It is also unclear how long China's leaders will stall decisions on economic changes, especially in such areas as freeing prices and expanding stock ownership. 
Many foreign companies had pinned their hopes on a more market-oriented business environment in China. 
Now, greater uncertainty about the direction of economic policy and about political stabilityII has led many companies to cancel or postpone plans for expansion in China.
Â 
Expansion Ruled Out
''We didn't set up any expansion plans before June 4,'' one executive said. 
''But of course after June 4, we wouldn't even consider it.''
The freeze on lending by the World Bank has also meant that loans from foreign institutions are few and far between, and business for bankers has slowed so much that two of the four American bank representatives in Beijing have been reassigned outside China. 
For many foreign bankers who remain here, much of their time is absorbed with loan problems, primarily hotel loans that need to be renegotiated because the debtors have not been able to meet their obligations.
''I guess I was wrong because I thought things would have picked up,'' one foreign banker said. 
''I've been disappointed too many times this year.''
Â 
Optimistic, but Restrained, Talk
Traders and corporate executives prospecting for lucrative investment possibilities have returned to China, and they fill the hotel coffee shops with optimistic, if restrained, talk of business. 
But the current economic recession in China has made prospects grim for new business and investment in the future.
''We're not seeing any new ideas in the pipeline,'' said John T. Frisbie, director of the United States-China Business Council in Beijing. 
''For traders, it'll be lean business years unless there is a significant change in trade policy.''
In the first quarter of this year, American companies signed 65 investment contracts worth $48 million, according to statistics from China's Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade. 
The ministry has not publicized comparable quarterly figures for previous years, but other statistics show that the latest figure is far below the level in the past.
In the first six months of last year, for example, American corporations signed contracts worth $382 million. 
That was nearly three times the new investment for the same period in 1988. 
At the end of 1989, the total amount of American contracts for investment projects was about $4 billion, an increase of about 20 percent over the amount at the end of 1988.
Â 
Investing Smaller Amounts
Industry executives say there are isolated cases of American and Japanese companies that are considering large investment projects of about $100 million. 
But in general, companies are investing smaller amounts -an average of $700,000 in the first quarter - and negotiations on contracts sometimes have become more cumbersome and protracted during the last year.
''The Chinese are generally strapped for money, so negotiating is as hard as it ever was before, and they are trying to extract as many concessions as they can,'' said Timothy A. Steinert, an American lawyer in Beijing who helps negotiate some deals.
Mr. Steinert added that there seemed to be a rising number of commercial disputes, as American companies become more willing to go to arbitration instead of turning a blind eye to what they believe are contract violations. 
''Problems that were swept under the rug before are now becoming conflicts,'' he said.
Â 
American Exports Down
United States trade statistics show that American exports to China had been on the rise, jumping 16 percent, to $5.7 billion, in 1989. 
The exports fell a percentage point during the first two months of 1990, to $876 million, compared with the same period a year ago.
Some companies say they expect the rest of the year to bring more business, and most companies in industries that China is strategically encouraging, including energy, telecommunications and transportation, say they are still closing sales. 
But most trade representatives say the last year has been a struggle, and they are cutting costs where they can to offset reductions in revenues.
The IBM China Corporation, for example, one of the most visible foreign companies in China, now has 100 employees in its office, compared with 127 a year ago. 
Many other companies have reduced their sales staffs and representatives. 
And most joint-venture hotels have cut down their expatriate staffing and electricity costs.
''The double whammy of economic retrenchment and political shock took the romance out of China,'' a Western diplomat said. 
''It takes a lot of vision and staying power to remain here.''

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_State_s Share Of Businesses Falls in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
It used to be that in Communist countries the factories were owned by the state and made things that local people could use and understand, like steel or boots or buckets.
Such outmoded visions of Communism elicit patronizing smiles in the fastest-growing areas of China, like this village in eastern Jiangsu Province. 
Here in Chengbei, there are more than 100 factories, not one of them state-owned, and several export to the world market: surgical gloves to New York, glass slides to Britain and West Germany, and telephone cables to Hong Kong.
The factories in Chengbei, all of which were started in the last decade, reflect the rise of the non-state economic sector in China. 
In some areas, particularly here in the fertile expanse around Shanghai, collectively owned and private ventures have flourished to the point that now it is they - not state-owned companies -that dominate the economy.
Is this still socialism, with the state controlling a dwindling minority of production?
Everyone insists that it is, but economically it is a world apart from the Stalinist models of the past. 
The small-scale economic dynamism of the fast-growing Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Guangdong Provinces is still far from capitalism, but it is just as far from China's Maoist past. 
Already the changing patterns of production are reshaping social and political attitudes.
Â 
'True Businessmen'
When a visitor asked the mayor of a town in Guangdong Province why it had attracted so much foreign investment, the mayor had a quick answer.
''Foreign investors like dealing with us because they know they're dealing with true businessmen, not Communist officials,'' he explained. 
That is not quite true, but clearly the local governments are becoming more business- and market-oriented.
In Jiangsu Province, state-owned companies last year accounted for 43 percent of industrial production, compared with 52 percent for the collective sector and about 5 percent for private enterprise. 
The non-state sectors are not only the biggest part of the local economies in some areas but by far the most dynamic.
When the Industrial Revolution began in England two centuries ago, it emerged not in what were then the biggest cities - London, Norwich and York - but in the backwaters of Manchester, Liverpool and Birmingham. 
Similarly, China's economic revolution is concentrated not in big cities like Beijing and Shanghai but in the smaller towns of Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Guangdong Provinces.
Â 
Remarkable Growth Rates
Each of these three provinces has seen industrial production grow by 15 percent to 20 percent a year, making their economies among the fastest-growing in the world. 
Indeed, some of this growth has been wasted - the result of zealous expansion even when it was not efficient - and the Government is trying desperately to rein in the overheated economies.
''It's a little sad,'' said Gu Songnian, the director of Jiangsu's Economic Research Institute. 
''It's not sustainable. 
We have to lower our growth rates.''
Already, some collective enterprises are feeling the pinch of the national retrenchment, as the Government cuts off credit and supplies of raw materials. 
In Wuxi County, where collectives have flourished in the last decade as almost nowhere else in China, one-third of the 12,000 township enterprises will have to close or merge, official news organizations have reported.
Despite some hard times, Jiangsu is expected to continue to prosper and its collectives to gain ground relative to the state sector.
As the state sector diminishes, Jiangsu Province and the other advanced areas fall into an uncertain economic zone that defies easy definition. 
They are like no other socialist economy, for the state is responsible for only a minority of production. 
And yet they are by no means capitalist or market economies, for various layers of the Government still control the prices and allocation of important ingredients, from labor and capital to electricity and steel.
In this, Jiangsu is only a more developed and extreme form of the national economy. 
Nationally, the share of industrial production from state-owned companies has fallen to less than 59 percent, from 81 percent a decade ago, while the share of collectives has risen to more than 36 percent, from 19 percent in 1978. 
Private businesses rose to 5 percent of industrial output from almost nothing.
Â 
'Collective' Means Many Things
But even if the share of collective enterprises rises further, it does not quite mean that private enterprise has taken over. 
Collective enterprise is a term that includes a variety of kinds of companies, from family enterprises to worker-owned factories to companies that are effectively owned by local governments.
''Our concept of individual and collective enterprises is different from yours,'' Jiangsu Province's governor, Gu Xiulian, said in an interview. 
Many of the collectives, for example, are operated by former workers' communes, with the profits shared by everyone in the township.
Even if collectives are not quite free-market enterprises, it is clear that they follow the market more closely than state-owned companies. 
A collective company that loses money, for example, is driven out of business, while a state-owned company simply picks up a subsidy from the Government. 
Collectives also have greater flexibility to pay employees according to their work, and to react to market conditions.
''China now has a problem,'' said Xiao Bin, director of the Dongfeng Auto Industry Corporation in Jiangsu's capital, Nanjing. 
''If workers work harder, they usually don't get much more than those who are lazy. 
More and more collectives will appear, because at collectives those who work harder will get a bigger bonus.''
Â 
The Freedom to Reward
Mr. Xiao's own company is an example of the flexibility that collectives enjoy. 
One of the biggest collectives in Jiangsu, with 1,020 employees, Dongfeng has to buy most of its raw materials on the free market instead of from the state at fixed low prices. 
But it also has the right to sell its trucks and vehicle parts at market prices, and to use the money to reward employees.
Yet in Jiangsu, as collective enterprises multiply, state-owned companies are feeling pressure to become more flexible than state-owned companies elsewhere.

file: INTERNATIONAL REPORT_Stock Markets_ Role Grows in Chinese Economy.txt
text:
ï»¿
Still coping with a trading system that is puzzling to foreigners and Chinese alike, China's stock markets are likely to gain new importance as the Government proceeds with plans to bolster the economy by turning state-owned businesses into shareholder-owned companies.
The latest sign of high-level, if cautious, support comes from Zhang Yanning, vice minister of the state commission for restructuring the economy. 
Mr. Zhang said on Saturday that the establishment of stock markets would be a main area of economic experimentation this year.
Prime Minister Li Peng has also made several statements in the last month that hint at changes in China's system of public ownership. 
Many Chinese experts assume such changes would mean a move toward a shareholding system, because its supporters have seized the linguistic high ground by asserting that ''publicly held'' companies are simply another form of the ''public ownership'' that has long been a fundamental tenet of socialism.
In any case, a new research institution was established last month to draft securities laws and make plans for a major national stock exchange.
''So far, the markets are all local ones,'' said Wong Poming, an adviser to a team of financial institutions that are trying to create the national exchange. 
''Only a national stock market can serve the role of a real financial center and larger capital market to allow companies to raise the kind of funds they need.''
Until national standards can be set for shares, the Government has ordered companies to proceed very slowly in issuing stock.
Trading on China's stock markets at present bears little resemblance to activity at the stock exchanges in the United States, Japan and other nations. 
For one thing, stock prices, which are mostly $5 to $30 a share, are usually determined more by the Communist Government than by supply and demand. 
As a result, prices rarely fall.
Â 
'They Only Go Up'
''People come from abroad and say, 'What is your morning price or your afternoon price?'
'' said Luo Zhenzhong, a manager of the stock market in the northeastern city of Shenyang. 
''But our prices don't change for a month at a time, and when they change they only go up.''
For another, the ''stocks,'' unlike General Motors or I.B.M. common stock, do not in most cases represent ownership in the company but simply the promise of a dividend and perhaps a chance to win a prize.
A third characteristic of China's markets is that few shares are freely traded. 
In the last five years, more than 10,000 Chinese companies have issued shares, but nearly all went to the employees of the issuing company. 
On the Shanghai market, for example, only six stocks are listed, along with six bonds, and on the Shenyang market only one recently listed stock is traded.
Â 
'Nobody Has Come to Sell a Share'
The Shenyang market is actually a bank branch that also trades in 40 bonds. 
It is a seat-of-the-pants operation where officials make decisions as they go along.
Asked whether investors could sell back shares at their original purchase price, Mr. Luo said, ''Nobody has come to sell a share, so we don't know what price to pay.''
The one stock traded on the Shenyang market, the Gold Cup Automotive Factory, is regarded by Western diplomats and economists in Beijing as the closest thing China has to a Western-style stock because, for example, shareholders can vote for the company's management.
The Shenyang market was the first stock market in Communist China, opening in the fall of 1986. 
But the stock market in Shanghai best reflects the metamorphosis of the Chinese securities markets.
Â 
Deathly Silence Ends
Two years ago, the Shanghai market, in the lobby of a state-owned bank, was deathly silent. 
The bank rarely adjusted prices, and so a lucky investor who was able to buy a share was never willing to sell. 
Weeks went by without a trade.
Now, 1,500 shares a week are traded. 
And Shanghai, far more than China's other stock markets, allows supply and demand to determine prices. 
Almost all transactions are conducted at the true market price, and the bank lobby is full of eager investors watching the show and looking for deals.
Not only do investors make money, but, perhaps more important for the development of the market, they sometimes lose money.
''There are no restrictions on price movements,'' said Huang Guixian, manager of the Shanghai stock market, who has the sensitive task of creating a capitalist-style stock market in Communist China. 
''And people can buy as many shares as they want,'' he added.
Â 
No Legal Underpinning
The greatest problem is that there is no legal underpinning for the shareholding system, Mr. Huang said. 
China has scarcely any securities law or company law, which accounts for why no one knows whether the shareholders really own the companies or what would happen if the shareholders tried to oust the management.
Because of the lack of a legal framework, as well as the proliferation of different pieces of paper that are all called stocks by the issuers, the Chinese Government announced in February that it would sharply restrict new stock issues over the next two years.
One Chinese official expects a new securities law to be implemented later this year, which he thinks will spur an increase in stock activity. 
Meanwhile, shares are being issued, but cautiously.
In Shanghai, a $6 million stock issue went on sale last week from the Shanghai Vacuum Electronic Component and Cell Company. 
That issue will bring a 60 percent increase in the total valuation of the stocks traded on the Shanghai market.
Â 
Lack of Understanding
In addition to the lack of a legal foundation, very few people really understand how a stock market works.
''People under the age of 50 don't understand stocks,'' Mr. Huang said. 
''We heard all the news about Black Monday in America, when stock prices plunged, and about an investor who was so upset that he shot his broker. 
But the good aspects of the stock system aren't reported. 
And so some people are suspicious.''
Until the Communist revolution in 1949, Shanghai's stock exchange was the biggest in Asia. 
But it was closed in 1950 and reappeared only three years ago.
Chinese officials still mostly endorse stock ''markets'' rather than stock ''exchanges,'' which they associate with capitalist speculation instead of socialist investment.
Â 
Very Simple Markets
''Today, the stock markets are very simple, and they're difficult to improve because people don't know much about securities,'' said Liu Guoguang, an economist who is an alternate member of the Communist Party Central Committee.
Mr. Liu pointed out that although Chinese stocks pay interest, they involve little or no risk. 
He said it was important to introduce risk in the markets, and he predicted that as the markets gained experience they would play a more important role in the economy.
Already, the Shanghai market has some of the paraphernalia of a Western or Asian stock exchange. 
There is an electronic ''big board'' listing the shares and their latest prices, and an electronic ticker tape that lists stock averages, not that they change very often.
The Shanghai market, primitive though it is, is far more advanced than those in cities like Beijing, Wuhan, Shenyang and Guangzhou.
Â 
Buy a Stock, Get a Prize
At Shenyang's market, for instance, there is no sign of the hustle and bustle found in Shanghai. 
In fact, one major reason that investors buy bonds on the Shenyang market is the chance of winning a prize. 
Companies have found that the way to make their bonds appealing is to attach lottery tickets, so that investors stand a chance at winning a television or a refrigerator.
Gambling is illegal in China, and so investing in bonds is the closest legal thing, even if the prices are almost guaranteed not to drop.
The Shenyang market's expansion plans included the offering of shares denominated in United States dollars to foreign investors, but so far the People's Bank of China in Beijing has not given the necessary approval. 
Mr. Luo, the exchange official, acknowledged that offering an issue to foreigners would be a bit more complicated.
''It's O.K. to issue locally, because people here don't really know what stocks are,'' he said. 
''But to sell abroad, with all those regulations and daily fluctuations, we'd have to make things perfect.''

file: Mass Migration of Chinese Floods a Prosperous Canton.txt
text:
ï»¿
A mass migration officially estimated at more than 2.5 million Chinese has flooded this city in the last few weeks, responding to the lure of southern China's prosperity.
''I'd heard that it was easy to make money here,'' Long Zaohong, a 30-year-old peasant from neighboring Hunan Province, said as he sat on a bundle of his possessions in front of Canton's railway station. 
Mr. Long arrived Wednesday with four friends, part of a human wave that reached a peak of 100,000 arrivals a day and has since receded to about 6,000 daily.
If the reports are not exaggerated, the flow of people exceeds the entire emigration from the Chinese mainland to Taiwan at the end of China's civil war in 1949. 
[Citing a threat to law and order, the Government in Beijing has ordered local authorities to halt mass migrations of peasants into Canton and other major cities, Reuters reported on Monday.] The authorities acknowledge that the existing figure on Canton's population, officially said to be 3.2 million in 1985, is a considerable underestimate. 
But by any reckoning, the latest influx, if most of the newcomers manage to stay, would place an extraordinary burden on the city.
The mass migration reflects the extent to which the economic revolution of the last decade has divided China into regions of markedly unequal wealth and prospects. 
The green rice paddies of Guangdong Province, in the south, used to be famous as the part of China that people left, on their way to America or Southeast Asia. 
Now, Guangdong is famous throughout China as the promised land to which people dream of moving.
A decade in which Guangdong has pursued wealth more than Communism, in which it has served as an experimental zone for all of China, has made it the richest and most envied spot in the nation. 
The migrants in front of the railway station bear the same dreams that inspired some Chinese a century ago to seek a fortune in Old Gold Mountain, as San Francisco is known in Chinese.
Rumors of the fortunes that could be made in Guangdong apparently spread during the Chinese New Year festival in the first half of February, for that is when the migrants began to arrive. 
At the peak, 100,000 arrived each day from all over the country. 
Guangdong officials frantically alerted their counterparts about the crisis, and spread the word that no jobs were available.
Perhaps more effective was the decision by railroad officials to suspend some services to Canton and to institute three special trains a day to take people back from Canton to their hometowns. 
Many thousands are stranded at railway junctions throughout the country and hope to continue to Canton, but officials think the worst is over for this year.
Nonetheless, thousands of people remain camped with their luggage in front of the Canton train station or living in parks or open spaces in the city.
''It's like an explosion,'' Yang Zhanchu, a manager in Guangdong's labor department, said in an interview. 
''They don't know the facts. 
They just come blindly.''
That such a wave of migrants could occur at all suggests the increasing loss of order and control on the part of the authorities, particularly in southern China. 
It used to be that changing jobs or residence was nearly impossible, but now many people simply ignore the rules and go.
Many of them seem to have come quite casually, planning to have a look around and take a job if they can find it.
Most do not use the Cantonese dialect spoken in Canton, which is also known as Guangzhou, and that makes job searches more difficult.
''I learned some Cantonese on the train here,'' said Yao Shanlong, a 33-year-old craftsman from Zhejiang Province. 
''My wife said, 'You should go and sell some handicrafts.'
''
A similar influx occurred after the Chinese new year in 1988, but this year has been much larger. 
Apparently, the 1 million to 2 million migrant laborers already in Guangdong went home for the new year and spread tales - often exaggerated - of the money to be made in Guangdong.
Some migrants have found jobs, and others have returned home. 
Many others apparently have dispersed throughout the province to continue their search.
Guangdong appears to be giving no warmer a welcome than America gave Chinese immigrants in the last century.
Local people say that thieves and prostitutes are disproportionally from other provinces. 
A lawyer in the southern city of Shenzhen says that local prostitutes include many college graduates from all over China who are earning money to study in the United States.
Guangdong's Governor, Ye Xuanping, warned this week that the migrants may be forcibly repatriated, and as a stark warning, the authorities have set up a display case near the railway station reporting the recent execution of 17 criminals.
But most of the migrants are looking for honorable jobs, and many seem to be giving up hope.
''We had heard that there was lots of work,'' said 21-year-old Zhu Wai, a gawky, wide-eyed peasant from Henan Province who came with four friends. 
''But we've been looking for 10 days now and there is none. 
We're going home.''

file: Rural China Learns to Earn a Little Extra.txt
text:
ï»¿
The way for peasants to get rich, Wang Hongjun used to think, was to raise more livestock and plant more grain and potatoes.
Then Mr. Wang, who heads a rural county in Sichuan Province, was sent three years ago to the State Training Center for Cadres from Poor Areas.
In the six-week course in Bejing and other parts of eastern China, Mr. Wang learned that in some parts of the country peasants had tripled their incomes by beginning small businesses, and he concluded that the road to wealth laynot in more farming but in running sideline businesses.
Upon his return to his county, Mr. Wang persuaded peasants to set up a silk-making cooperative. 
Instead of selling silkworm cocoons to Shanghai factories, they would process the silk right there. 
The factory has prospered, and Mr. Wang and other Sichuan Province officials describe it as an enormous money-maker for the county.
The Training Center is proud of the factory, and of other innovations that have resulted from its seminars. 
The center is part of a broad anti-poverty campaign in China that has shown considerable success in eliminating theproblems that afflict large numbers of people in other parts of the third world: malnutrition, epidemic disease and abysmal health care.
These days almost all Chinese have food to eat and roofs over their heads, so increasingly the trend in anti-poverty work is in spreading education and information rather than arranging income transfers.
"The Government used to try to spend money primarily on relief efforts," said Liu Yitao, deputy director of the training center. 
"If there wasn't enough grain in an area, then the Government would send grain. 
But these days the effort is mainly to help peoplehelp themselves."
Such efforts at education and assistance are aimed at the 110 million people, nearly 10 percent of the population, who are classified as poor because they earn less than $62 a year. 
Such people will not starve to death, but their lives are bleak: they live in mud huts or caves, eat meat only on festivals, and have trouble paying the fees to keep their children in school.
While China has been quite successful in alleviating the most dire forms of poverty, it has had little success in stimulating local markets and equalizing the opportunities among various parts of the country. 
While all China benefited immensely during the last dozen years of the open-door policy, the richer coastal areas gained the most. 
The gap between rich and poor areas has grown considerably in that period.Funds are limited, as is the effect the Training Center alone can have on the lives of the vast numbers of poor people. 
But since the center's founding in 1987, some 17,000 local workers have taken part in its programs.
Typically they spend about 45 days, partly in seminars in Beijing and partly touring parts of coastal China that have turned to agribusiness to help their economies.
Many of the officials in poor areas are peasants, and the tour of more prosperous regions comes as a revelation to them.
In particular, the program aims to show them how their villages can start rural enterprises -- everything from making shoes and buckets to processing tofu and sausage -- as a way to supplement the income from traditional agricultural products.

file: Shaky Numbers Behind China_s Rosy Economic Picture.txt
text:
