CHINA appears to be easing out of its worst economic slump in a dozen years, but Chinese and foreign economists say the recovery will be slow and painful and that there is no sign of any significant move toward a market economy.
Just a few months ago, there were some tentative hints that China might lift price controls and adopt other market-oriented changes.
But these days the central planners are again dominant, and drafts of the country's five-year plan that will take effect in January reportedly contain little in the way of a commitment to change.
"They talk about reform, but there are no specifics," said a Chinese economist. 
"It's a blank when it comes to reform."
Still, Chinese officials, in public at least, are emphasizing the good news: industrial production is rising again. 
At the beginning of this year, some diplomats and Chinese thought that the economy might continue to deteriorate and lead to large numbers of factory closures and new protests, but that risk seems to have receded.
"The economy is now taking a turn for the better, thereby promoting political and economic stabilityI," Zhang Zhongji, spokesman for the State Statistical Bureau, said at a news conference last week.
He noted that industrial output in September climbed 7.5 percent from the same period a year earlier -- the best performance since July 1989, a month after the army crackdown helped push the economy into a slump.
Mr. Zhang also noted other good economic news:
* A bumper harvest, including a record 420 million tons of grain, is expected this year.
* Inflation has been subdued, and the index of retail prices stood last month only 1 percent higher than a year earlier.
* China's foreign exchange reserves are rising because of a strong trade surplus, which totaled $4.9 billion in the first nine months of this year.
Yet some official reports acknowledge that the situation is still grim, and most ordinary Chinese apparently feel the same way.
Beijing workers say that in recent days they have been summoned to meetings in which officials have read to them a document announcing hefty price increases in coal, cooking gas, natural gas, electricity and other necessities.
The price of the ubiquitous cakes of coal that are used as fuel in Chinese homes all winter also soared, by 50 percent, the document discloses.
"Of course, we're unhappy," said a worker in his 20's. 
"But what are we to do?
The Government spent so much money on the Asian Games that they have to get it back somehow."
The price increases have invited some sarcastic comments at these worker meetings, but no strikes or other significant indications of rebelliousness have been reported.
THE Asian Games, a mini-Olympics, concluded successfully in Beijing early this month, and the authorities apparently felt that security was tight enough and the atmosphere calm enough that they could introduce the price increases -- which have not been disclosed in the news media -- without provoking unrest.
But diplomats here and Chinese economists say there is much more to the story. 
For most of this year, the increases in industrial output simply went into ever-higher mountains of inventories. 
The inventories continued to increase even last month, the diplomats and economists note, and they will impede the recovery that may now be under way.
Moreover, part of the reason for the industrial growth is a statistical fluke: China calculates each month's growth as a comparison of the same period one year earlier. 
Since the latter half of last year was severely affected by the slump, it is therefore easier to show growth now in comparison with that period.
Seasonally adjusted production figures, developed by Rock Creek Research Inc., an American consulting firm, also show China's industry generally improving since March of this year. 
But Rock Creek's figures underscore the problems that remain: its models suggest that industrial growth slipped badly in July and August of this year.
Likewise, inflation is subdued now, but the Government has sharply eased credit this year -- $20.4 billion in additional loans in the first eight months of 1990 -- to stimulate the economy. 
Government payments to farmers for the grain harvest in coming months will also expand the money supply and perhaps lead to inflationary pressures, after a lag of six months or more.
"There'll just be more inflation down the road, and we'll be back to the cycle of boom and bust," said a Chinese economist.
One of the main reasons for the economic slowdown was that consumers simply stopped buying goods, apparently in part because of the turmoil in the capital and uncertainties about the future.
Refrigerators, televisions and electric fans piled up at stores around the nation, and some store managers resorted to desperate measures to clear their stocks: they promised to refund the sale price in full, after five years. 
That brought in some cash, but no one knows the extent of this liability or how it will be paid off.
NOW retail sales are gradually picking up again, but companies that make household appliances are still in desperate shape.
In the first three quarters of 1990, production of washing machines was only 69 percent of the level in the same period of 1989, and output of refrigerators was at 64 percent of the level of 1989.
What pains many economists -- Chinese as well as foreigners -- is that the Government has not made use of the slowdown to remove price controls and introduce a restructuring. 
Freeing prices might have been accomplished relatively easily earlier this year, when inflation was subdued, but will be much more difficult as the economy picks up.
Moreover, the economic purpose of a recession, to weed out inefficient companies, is neglected in China because the state always protects companies from bankruptcy.
"There hasn't been any fundamental structural change accompanying this recession," said a Western economist in Beijing. 
"The fundamental problems are still here. 
I don't believe state enterprises are one iota more efficient now than they were two years ago."
Indeed, they may well be less efficient. 
The state-owned sector of the economy is a disaster area: one-third of state-owned companies are losing money, and the total losses in the first three quarters of this year were double the total losses in the same period last year.
WITH state enterprises on the ropes, the recovery is coming from the sectors that have been most pummeled by the central planners over the last year, but that have still managed to maintain a measure of vitality.
Of the 7.5 percent industrial growth in September, for example, the state sector saw growth of only 3 percent, while rural collective enterprises grew at a rate of 9.4 percent, and the tiny sector that includes private businesses and joint ventures soared 57.7 percent.
"There are all these conflicting strains in the economy, in terms of regions and in terms of types of ownership," said a Western diplomat. 
The diplomat noted that growth was strongest in the coastal areas of China that already are richer than the interior.
Many economists would be more optimistic if they saw signs that the Government was embracing proposals for structural change. 
But instead the Government apparently intends to postpone any major changes for at least a year or two.
The only changes that apparently have been agreed upon involve modifications in the contract system that governs most Chinese enterprises.
Chinese and foreign economists say the leadership has agreed that new contracts will include a more systematic method of taxation in which enterprises' taxes will be paid as a proportion of revenues. 
The taxes will also be the companies' first obligation.
A second change is that payments of principal on certain loans will no longer be deductible from the companies' taxes.
These are minor adjustments compared with the sweeping economic changes that many foreign economists recommend and that some Chinese officials have been lobbying for in recent months.
Â 
Â 
THE UNEMPLOYMENT RISK
ONE of the principal political risks for the Chinese Government is rising unemployment, in part because it is the employer that has prime responsibility for monitoring and controlling workers. 
Unemployment not only distresses workers, but it also makes it easier for them to act with impunity.
"The unemployment situation is very grave," Economic Reference News, an official newspaper, reported last month. 
It said the unemployment rate has risen to 4.4 percent, from 2.5 percent, "greatly surpassing the warning level of 3 percent."
In China, however, statistics are often at odds. 
Zhang Zhongji, spokesman for the State Statistical Bureau, said the unemployment rate was unchanged, at 2.6 percent.
In any case, these figures do not include large numbers of young people who are officially "awaiting assignment."
In the next five years some 92 million people are expected to enter the ranks of the labor force, and the Government will be hard put to provide jobs.
Perhaps as a result, the leadership has already stopped criticizing private and collective enterprises and is now hailing them and the "free markets" where private traders sell their goods.
"The leaders know that they can't solve the employment problem through the state sector or the agricultural sector," said a Western economist in Beijing.

file: Shenyang Journal_A City That Undoes Mao Under His Steady Gaze.txt
text:
ï»¿
This drab, Dickensian city, where a statue of Mao presides over the snow-covered central square, is best known for its soot and industry.
Now, relying on an imagination that rivals Dickens's own, it has found a new product to earn it recognition: ideas about how to make China work.
No one knows quite why Shenyang has become a prime battlefront in the struggle to revitalize China's economy, but there is little doubt that this wintry city 400 miles northeast of Beijing has become a testing ground for the entire country.
''We are proud that we can contribute to our country's reform process,'' said Han Yaoxian, a city official who wrote the nation's first bankruptcy law - and then applied it to several companies that until then had cheerfully been losing money for years.
Shenyang was the first city in China to open a securities market, the first to float shares in a large state-owned company, the first to allow a company to go bankrupt, the first to propose selling stock to foreigners, the first to institute wide-scale job transfers and layoffs, and the only one to open an office in South Korea. 
#5.3 Million People In effect, this city of 5.3 million is pioneering the next big task for China's economic development: revitalizing the state-owned companies that produce more than two-thirds of the nation's output.
Guangdong Province in the south pioneered the system of special economic zones and joint ventures with foreign partners. 
Jiangsu Province pioneered the development of rural enterprises that have flourished in the last decade. 
And now the greatest challenge - to foster incentives in the country's heavy industrial base and inject dynamism in state-owned companies that dominate the economy -is being confronted in Shenyang.
''Shenyang is on the leading edge of reform in many different areas, in housing, foreign trade, stocks, management and development of the private sector,'' said Carl Eugene Dorris, the United States Consul General in Shenyang.
Part of the reason, Mr. Dorris said, is that Shenyang has some leaders who are unusually capable, and some factory managers who are unusually upset with the status quo. 
''These people have become real radicals,'' Mr. Dorris said about the factory managers. 
''They're tired of the dead hand of the state on their businesses.''
Some of Shenyang's experiments, such as the securities exchange and a proposal to sell stocks to foreigners, already have been copied in other cities. 
Others, such as large-scale sales of housing to private individuals, are scheduled to be carried out around the country before long. 
But it still is too early to know how successful the city will be in its most important experiments, those seeking to improve the efficiency of state-owned industries.
Â 
Opening Ties With Seoul
In the last few months, Shenyang's pioneering spirit has been most evident in its relations with South Korea. 
Officially, China recognizes only North Korea, not South Korea, and while Beijing sees immense opportunities for business with Seoul, officials are cautious about proceeding too openly for fear of offending North Korea.
Yet in August, the city of Shenyang opened an office in Seoul and sent a senior Deputy Mayor, Zhang Rongmao, to the ribbon cutting. 
This is the first Chinese office in South Korea, and it is not clear if Beijing was consulted. 
The central Government had designated a different area, Shandong Province in the east, to open the first office in Seoul and to lead the way in forging ties with South Korea, but those negotiations have dragged on and Shandong still has not exchanged offices with Seoul.
In a sign of the sensitivity of the issue, Shenyang's Foreign Affairs Office disclaims any knowledge of the Seoul office. 
While the city set up the office so that it formally does not represent the city of Shenyang but simply the ethnic Koreans who live in the area, it was a daring move - particularly since North Korea's only diplomatic mission in China outside Beijing is in Shenyang.
Liaoning Province, which encompasses Shenyang, has even set up a concern called the Bohai Company to specialize in trade with South Korea.
One man often credited for Shenyang's dynamism is Li Changchun, the 44-year-old Governor of Liaoning Province and former Mayor of Shenyang. 
Mr. Li, an electrical engineer and former factory manager who is the nation's youngest Governor, has a reputation for being unusually open to new ideas.
Perhaps Shenyang's most risky undertaking is its plan to shuffle 300,000 workers, 15 percent of the city's work force, out of their jobs. 
The plan is a direct attack on the ''iron rice bowl,'' the system in China of lifetime employment, where it is common for companies to have more workers than they know what to do with. 
Streamlining the work force will make industry more efficient, but it could spark unrest among workers who fear being laid off.
Â 
'Way of Increasing Production'
''Removing surplus workers is a way of increasing production,'' said Guan Weiguo, the executive director of the Economic Restructuring Commission in Shenyang.
While the experiments in Shenyang amount to undoing Mao's work, one of the few changes apparently not being contemplated is tearing down the statue of Mao in the center of the city.
''Mao was a great person, respected by people all over the world, so we couldn't tear down the statue,'' Mr. Guan said, carefully adding: ''Mao had many, many ideas. 
Some of them we can draw upon for reforms, and some of them we can ignore.''

file: The World_At the Businesses Owned by Beijing, The Ink Is Red.txt
text:
ï»¿
A UNIVERSAL joke in socialist countries is that employment in state-owned companies is a matter of make-believe: "We pretend to work, and they pretend to pay us."
In China, this game is carried to extremes. 
Employees in state-owned companies receive only about $30 a month, and some quip that they don't even deserve that much, what with late arrivals, tea breaks, lunch breaks and early departures.
But these days the situation is becoming less humorous: The state sector is losing ever-increasing amounts of money, to the consternation of the hard-liners who run the country.
One-third of state-owned companies are losing money, another third earn negligible profits, and only a third earn any money for the state. 
The total losses in the state sector doubled in the first nine months of this year, compared with the same period of last year.
This is helping to provoke a fiscal crisis, both because there are fewer profitable enterprises to hand over earnings to the state and because there are more failing enterprises to subsidize. 
In China, inefficient companies are subsidized because of the fear that if they closed, disgruntled workers would foment unrest.
"We should waste no time or effort in boosting the economy," Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader, said early this month. 
"Without economic growth it would be difficult to maintain political stabilityI."
The crisis in the state sector is, paradoxically, perhaps one of the most important forces left for reform here. 
The hard-liners, fearful that they will be blamed for the economic slump, already have eased up on their initially tough economic policy. 
The leadership has relaxed its retrenchment policy and ended attacks on collective and private businesses.
"They are terrified of a recession," said a Chinese businessman. 
"They are becoming a lot more flexible than they used to be, because they want practical measures to get the economy going. 
They know that's the only way they'll get popular support and survive in office."
Provincial leaders, showing unusual gumption, are said to be rebelling against the central government's plans to make them hand over more money. 
And the shortage of money has driven the leadership to a course of action it had long shied away from: raising prices for necessities such as coal, sugar and even bus fares.
Ordinary people are muttering, but so far there have been no major protests.
"Everybody's angry about the price increases," said a middle-age woman as she returned from the market. 
"But there's nothing we can do but complain to each other."
Some Chinese intellectuals chuckle that such price rises are terrific. 
On the one hand, they make the economy a bit more rational by bringing price levels closer to the market. 
On the other hand, they cause widespread indignation at the central planners who now dominate the Government. 
When change comes, these Chinese say, it will be all the faster because central planning is being so thoroughly discredited.
Over all, the economy is showing signs of recovery. 
Industrial production in October was 12.7 percent higher than it was in October 1989 -- the best performance in more than 18 months.
But most of this resurgence is coming not from the state sector but from other parts of the economy. 
In September, the last full month for which figures are available, the state sector enjoyed a growth rate of only 3 percent, while collectives (mostly in rural areas) grew at 9.4 percent and private companies and joint ventures soared at a 57.7 percent growth rate.
"The most interesting thing about the economy is that for all the favoritism shown to the state sector, it's been greatly outperformed by rural enterprises," said a Western economist in Beijing.
That leads to what may be the lesson of the Chinese experiment that is most relevant to other socialist countries. 
China's economic restructuring has lasted much longer and in most cases gone further than the economic changes in Eastern Europe, and it has achieved breathtaking results -- per capita incomes have approximately doubled since the process began at the end of 1978.
But the most glittering parts of this massive accomplishment were supplied by the non-state sector: in private agriculture, private business, and especially in rural collective enterprises. 
All the experiments and changes have not enabled state companies to become more profitable.
"China has made virtually no progress toward systematically putting the state sector on some kind of legal, independent basis, as they had intended to," said Barry Naughton, a specialist in the Chinese economy at the University of California at San Diego. 
But he added that he was not as critical of China's state sector as many Chinese economists are, and that part of their difficulties are simply the natural result of a cyclical downturn.
The Government is hoping to save its state sector through what it bills as a "reform" program. 
Among the elements are the merger of failing companies into healthy ones to create enormous conglomerates, and a more rigorous tax system, so that tax obligations would be a matter of law and not of negotiation.
The southern city of Shenzhen is pioneering the auction of Government enterprises to anyone with the cash and inclination to take them over. 
And both Shenzhen and Shanghai are competing to be the first to open a modernized stock exchange, in the hope that stock in state enterprises can be sold to shareholders.
A couple of years ago, some Chinese officials hoped to get rid of most of the state sector. 
They never used the term privatization, but rather a variety of euphemisms that amounted to much the same thing. 
These days, however, "ownership reform" is ideologically impossible on any large scale, and even share ownership is now intended to supplement rather than supplant state ownership.
That is the nub of the problem, many Chinese officials complain. 
They say that tinkering with state ownership will not succeed, so the Government should scrap the system altogether. 
Their advice to Eastern European countries now considering what to do with inefficient state sectors is not to copy Chinese experiments, but to try to dump the companies on anyone who will take them.
"Most people know that state ownership is the root of the problem," said a Chinese economist, "but for now, it's ideologically impossible to do anything about it."

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_Hard-liners Seem to Control Politics, But the Economy Is Another Matter.txt
text:
ï»¿
While China's leaders tighten their grip over the political situation, they now face the even more complicated task of controlling the economy after their military crackdown shook the confidence of Chinese and foreigners alike.
For the Government to consolidate its control and win popular support, it needs to demonstrate that the economy is stable and that everyone will enjoy economic gains. 
But diplomats and others say the crackdown has already eroded confidence that had been carefully nurtured over a decade, and it will be an immensely difficult challenge to restore this confidence and achieve broad economic satisfaction.
Even before the pro-democracy demonstrations began two months ago, there were signs that the country's economy was facing difficulties, and some say that these contributed to the public dissatisfaction with the leadership.
''The economy is in very serious trouble, which is partly why people took to the streets to begin with,'' said Christine Wong, a specialist in the Chinese economy at the University of California at Santa Cruz. 
''There are many structural problems.''
#3 Areas of Difficulty Diplomats and economists suggest at least three areas in which the economy faces severe new difficulties as a result of the crackdown:
* Foreign investors and lenders will be wary of providing the capital and expertise for China to sustain its export-oriented development strategy in coastal areas.
* Tourists, who have been a growing source of hard currency, will be frightened away for some time, and in the meantime the many tourist hotels around the nation are likely to lose money. 
This may also shake the confidence of investors.
* The Government will be tempted to buy support from workers by increasing wages and bonuses, making it tougher to enforce the austerity plan to which it is committed. 
Without austerity, inflation is likely to rise and create new political problems.
These challenges could create major political difficulties for the leadership, which some diplomats say could prevent Prime Minister Li Peng and others in power from holding on to their positions for very long.
The June 4 crackdown, in which the army opened fire on civilians, led almost all foreign business executives to leave the country. 
Many of the executives have no specific date for their return, and many tour agencies have canceled trips to China until mid-summer.
International organizations like the World Bank, as well as foreign governments and private lenders, have postponed approvals for loans and are reviewing their credit assessments of China in light of what has happened. 
Eroding Confidence In Chinese Intentions Growing tensions with the United States will also make American companies think twice about how the business climate will be affected, especially if the tensions lead to anti-American sentiment in China.
Most fundamentally, the confidence around the world that China was really entirely committed to economic restructuring has been eroded. 
Some of the elderly leaders who seem to have reasserted control during the crackdown may be less enthusiastic about change than those who had been in power, and this could significantly reshape the landscape for foreign businesses.
''People had convinced themselves that China was heading for capitalism,'' said William H. Overholdt, director of research at the brokerage arm of Bankers Trust Company in Hong Kong.
''There's been a great disillusionment. 
If they had listened to what the leaders were saying, they would have understood that there was a very important market-oriented reform, but a very limited one and democracy is not what they had in mind.''
In a sign of concern at the economic consequences of the crackdown, senior officials have begun to reaffirm the open-door policy and stress that they will protect foreign investments. 
For example, Mayor Li Ruihuan of Tianjin said today that China would not only maintain its reform and open-door policies, but even carry them further.
Â 
'Could Mislead Investors'
Localities have also announced that their policies toward foreign investment will be unchanged and that their regions are safe for foreign tourists.
For businesses that already have operations in China, there is little talk of leaving, especially if they have been profitable up until now. 
The problem the Chinese will have to grapple with is persuading companies to make new investments in China.
''Some foreign businesses are likely to come to the conclusion that a Government that tells its people and the world that there were no students fired on in the square could also mislead potential foreign investors,'' said Stanley B. Lubman, a lawyer who specializes in China at Thelen, Marrin, Johnson & Bridges in San Francisco.
It is not clear exactly what it will take to reassure investors. 
Some say it will take a clear indication that the policies of liberalization, like enterprise restructuring, experiments with joint-stock companies and price liberalization, will continue. 
Some say it will take a long period of calm to reassure investors.
China's Business Begins to Suffer ''There will be some risk-takers,'' an investment analyst in New York said. 
''But for now, 90 percent of them will be scared away.''
Others are more optimistic, and they have begun to compare the crackdown in Beijing with incidents like the suppression of a rebellion in the South Korean city of Kwangju in 1980. 
At least 191 people died then, but business bounced back and is now stronger than ever.
Business in China, however, was beginning to suffer even before the pro-democracy demonstrations began. 
Foreign businesses were feeling the pinch from China's retrenchment policies that began last fall, and Prime Minister Li has said the next few years are to be those of austerity. 
The tightening of credit had local companies short of liquidity, and this had affected some joint ventures whose payments were delayed.
Â 
Regional Variations
But a great deal also depends on where the investment is. 
Guangdong and the coastal areas, for instance, seem to be affected less by the demonstrations, although there were some in major cities. 
As long as those areas are allowed to exercise the economic freedoms they have been given, then investors will probably continue to move in, diplomats and economists say.
''Western companies are faced with a moral dilemma,'' a Western resident in Guangdong said. 
''Headquarters may have instructed them not to continue with talks and ordered them to leave because they felt it was not appropriate to be in China when the Government massacres its people.''
''But like the Cantonese themselves, the joint ventures have a real stake in the economy,'' he added. 
''They are here to make money and to expand their share. 
It is hard for them to walk away.''
11,535 Tourists Who Won't Show Up So far, China's travel industry has been hit the hardest. 
Pacific Delight Tours Inc., based in New York, says it canceled tours through mid-July, a move that affected ''several hundred'' travelers.
The authorities here reported that 11,535 potential tourists had their trips to the capital canceled, and that for the month of May, the tourism bureau lost about $4 million, or 10 percent of its annual projected earnings, the English-language China Daily said today.
China's economic landscape is complicated by the task of restructuring the national economy and shedding rigidities and inefficient institutions. 
Many economists say China needs to focus on building institutions - like its banking system, tax system, legal system and physical infrastructure - but there are doubts about whether the leadership can concentrate on these tasks when it is preoccupied by political turmoil. 
10% Growth a Year in Economy ''This is a very complicated process that they were right in the middle of,'' said Albert Keidel, who runs Rock Creek Research, Inc., an economic consulting firm in Washington, D.C. 
''It involves some masterful combinations.''
There is no question that China's economy has been growing at a remarkable pace - about 10 percent per year over the last decade - so that even if it suddenly were cut in half, the economy's growth still would be respectable. 
Indeed, China's difficulties arise from growth that is too fast, rather than too slow.
But some of the measures for controlling an overheated economy -tightening credit and investment spending, holding down wages, at the same time finding new sources of raw materials and energy - are unpopular, and this can be politically risky when people have already demonstrated discontent with the Government. 
Trying to Beat Galloping Inflation Already the rate of inflation in the first quarter of this year reached 27.5 percent on an annual basis, among the highest rates the country has seen since 1949, and some unofficial estimates put the number much higher. 
While this number is small compared with some other developing countries, the Chinese are sensitive to inflation not only because they have never experienced such high inflation in the recent past, but also because one of the platforms of the Communist Party is stable prices.
In many ways, inflation is a necessary product of economic restructuring, especially price liberalization, so that the problem facing the leadership is largely one of managing the perception of inflation.
One ineffective but tempting way to manage this perception is to ''buy off'' workers by giving them higher wages and bonuses, Western economists say. 
Even before the crackdown, factories were paying their workers to keep them indoors and off the streets when pro-democracy demonstrations were taking place. 
And the television news this week has shown scenes of soldiers distributing grain to citizens when there were shortages last week.
Â 
'More of a Squeeze Later'
The intention has apparently been to appease workers by giving them material benefits. 
But paying more money to workers means expanding the state budget, and this could lead to new inflationary pressures if the Government needs to borrow or print more money.
''Anytime you get political turmoil, you get a kick to inflation,'' said Mr. Overholdt of Bankers Trust. 
''And obviously it is a kick to inflation that was already very bad, and that means more of a squeeze later. 
The question is whether it is an ongoing process or a one-time kick.''
Buying people's loyalty is a major challenge for another reason: the central Government is desperately short of cash, and this could lead to unrest in both rural and urban areas. 
Some one-third of state enterprises are in financial difficulties, according to official estimates, and the lack of funds has also begun to affect the peasants who make up about two-thirds of China's population. 
A Harvest at Hand, But So Little Cash The shortage of cash is an urgent problem because the harvest season is near. 
The Government already says it lacks nearly $3 billion needed to pay for about half of the grain, oil, tea and raw silk that will be harvested this summer.
Moreover, the price at which the farmers are forced to sell their grain to the state is about one-third the market price, so that farmers are reluctant to turn over a portion of their grain to the state, when they can fetch much higher prices on the market.
Local governments in many parts of the nation have been forced this year to give ''white slips,'' or I.O.U.'s, to farmers instead of cash to pay for pigs and tea and other commodities sold to the Government. 
These slips of paper are likely to be prevalent this year, official press articles have said.
A recent article in Peasant's Daily described how much the farmers dreaded the visits by local government officials who came to collect the grain. 
In some villages last year, the article said, children were given large bells and told to hide in tree tops, and when they saw the grain officials approaching, they would ring the bells as a signal for the farmers to run home and lock their doors. 
What of Rural Areas?
Thus, for the Government, paying low prices and then not giving farmers cash for their crops will create greater political risks at a time when urban populations have already shown their dissatisfaction, diplomats say.
The recent political turmoil, which occurred mainly in the cities, will probably not have a direct effect on peasants, who tend to be scattered across a vast amount of land, specialists say. 
But unless the Government cashes in the ''white slips,'' the farmers are unlikely to show much enthusiasm for the Government.
''The peasant dissatisfaction is certainly real,'' a Western diplomat in Beijing said. 
''But it is unlikely that peasant discontent could turn into resistance. 
They are spread out, so it is hard to organize resistance.''

file: UPHEAVAL IN CHINA_Reluctant Rebel Joins Students_ Cause.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Gao Xiqing, a former Wall Street lawyer, spent the night on Tiananmen Square in solidarity with students of his who were demonstrating for democracy, he was shaken awake at 2 A.M. by a friend who told him that armed troops were trying to move in on them.
The night passed without incident, but this was not the kind of risk that Mr. Gao had contemplated when he left his New York job last year on a personal mission to help modernize China.
The 36-year-old Mr. Gao had returned to his homeland last year because he believed that there was great hope for China and that the country needed American-educated minds like his to negotiate its way through this stage of dramatic change.
Mr. Gao took a job teaching law at his old university in Beijing, and he began working on a project to establish a national stock exchange in China. 
Above all, he was going to work within the system, to build the institutions that could push the country forward.
''Building the economy is the best way to change China,'' Mr. Gao said two months ago, before the student movement began. 
''In the long run, what we're doing with the stock exchange is more effective than sending off petitions. 
It's the most effective way to create a more democratic nation.''
Â 
The Making of a Rebel
But now, after seeing his own law students put their careers and even lives on the line for the democratic movement, Mr. Gao is changing his mind. 
With his dreams beginning to shatter, Mr. Gao is turning into a rebel.
He has already been told by the school authorities that he has been singled out as a troublemaker, and stands to lose his job if there are widespread purges of intellectuals involved in the democratic movement.
Mr. Gao's story is especially poignant because it is about the disillusionment of a bright young Communist Party member, fiercely dedicated to concepts of democracy, personal rights and egalitarianism that he has believed in ever since he first read Karl Marx.
A thin, strong and energetic law teacher who has recently taken to wearing brightly colored T-shirts and sunglasses to help him bear the hot sun on Tiananmen Square, Mr. Gao had been throwing all his energies until recently into his teaching and into the stock exchange. 
Often sleeping for only four hours a night, Mr. Gao worked furiously to draft China's first securities law.
But all that seemed to vanish one day after he asked the whereabouts of one of his liveliest students. 
He was told that she had been on a hunger strike in Tiananmen Square for several days already.
Â 
'Obliged to Support Them'
''I was shocked that a person would do this,'' Mr. Gao recalled. 
''I had told my students that democracy is a long process, that you can't put a timetable on it. 
But when they started the hunger strike, I felt obliged to support them.''
His students at the University of International Business and Economics, one of the nation's most prestigious schools, were the last to join in the demonstrations. 
Of all the students in Beijing, they tend to have the greatest vested interest in the current system; they get the best jobs with the highest pay in foreign corporations.
Mr. Gao had graduated from the same university and then lived in the United States for six years until his return last summer. 
He attended Duke University Law School, and then became the first citizen of the People's Republic of China to pass the New York State bar exam. 
Later he worked at Mudge, Rose, Guthrie, Alexander & Ferdon and became an adjunct associate professor at Duke University Law School.
The trappings of life in the United States - the material satisfactions of Wall Street, including ski trips whenever there was time - were a far cry from the deprivation he had experienced as a child and teen-ager in the central Chinese city of Xian. 
He nearly starved during the Cultural Revolution launched by Mao Zedong in 1966. 
His father was jailed for five years and his mother was sent away to the countryside.
Â 
Hunting for Food
For nearly two years, Mr. Gao, a homeless teen-ager, roamed the streets, hunting for food when his small monthly stipend ran out. 
Once he walked almost 20 miles to the home of relatives, only to be told that they had no food to give him.
''We'd go out and steal from shops and military camps,'' Mr. Gao acknowledged, looking embarrassed.
But during that time, Mr. Gao read all of Mao's works, and he read Marx, Engels and Lenin.
Now, as rumors of arrests of intellectuals circulate throughout the capital, Mr. Gao worries about being banished once again to that kind of life, or of being confined to a jail cell with no books or writing paper. 
Mr. Gao already believes he will not be allowed to leave the country to return to Duke University to teach.
Yet as he insists on sticking with the democracy movement, he gives practical advice to his students.
''This may be a dangerous time, and you shouldn't all feel you have to be heroes,'' he told his students as they gathered around him in Tiananmen Square on the night when martial law was first imposed May 20. 
''Those of you who are women, or are single children, should leave right now. 
There is no shame in leaving.''
When one student stood up to say that all the students would remain, Mr. Gao reproached him.
''You've got to learn about democracy,'' Mr. Gao said. 
''Democracy means not only that the majority rules, but that the minority also has rights. 
If someone wants to leave, then that is absolutely their right.''

file: WASHINGTON TALK_Crisis Management For Business in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
From a sunny second-floor suite of five offices, a copying machine and telephones that ring almost constantly, word has just gone out that the Bank of China is honoring its letters of credit and that most of China's ports, with the exception of Shanghai, are operating normally.
Since the bloody crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square on June 4, the Commerce Department's equivalent of a China desk, has served as a crisis management center for the more than 350 American companies that in the past 10 years invested $3.5 billion in China - more than a third of the total foreign investment there.
Among the investors are General Foods, which makes coffee products in Guangzhou; Gillette, razor blades in Shenyang; Ingersoll Rand, air compressors in Shanghai and Nabisco, bakery products in Beijing.
''Basically, we're telling them to sit tight, and if they were contemplating an investment to hold off for a while and see how things shake out,'' said Christine L. Lucyk, who is Commerce's top China hand.
Daily Contact With China
Other Cabinet departments - State and Treasury, and the Central Intelligence Agency - have their own experts, who concentrate on their department's areas of expertise. 
Mrs. Lucyk's team of seven keeps up on developments affecting American-Chinese commercial relations through daily telephone calls to commercial officers at the Beijing Embassy, principally Lyn Edinger, commercial counselor, and Tim Stratford, commercial attache, and through contacts with scores of executive suites.
This is not to suggest that Washington's clusters of China-watchers work in isolation. 
Over the last two weeks, at the urging of State's desk, Commerce's has been telling companies to get their American personnel out of China. 
There are 1,000 there now, as against 9,000 before June 4 .
''They were very reluctant to leave,'' said one of Ms. Lucyk's aides, David K. Schneider. ''They were concerned about the fate of their Chinese employees, and about what would happen to their business.''
''In some cases,'' he said, ''their Chinese partners were telling them they shouldn't go because there was nothing wrong. 
Now we're trying to help some companies develop approaches to their partners to explain to them why they had to leave.''
Â 
Advice to Companies
The Commerce desk has also been offering advice to companies on how to deal with shipments of machinery and other goods needed to keep plants operating in China or fulfill contracts under the more 600 joint ventures American companies operate with Chinese partners.
The desk has also focused on such day-to-day matters as the state of mail service (the main Beijing post office is open but many branches are closed) and transportation (Japan Airlines has just resumed service to Beijing but with reduced frequency).
Although corporate aides often have not been pleased with what they hear, they are not reluctant to praise the messenger. 
''They're doing an awfully good job for the task at hand,'' said Richard E. Gillespie, vice president of the U.S.-China Business Council, representing 300 American multinationals with China operations.
Before martial law was imposed late in May, Commerce had a number of diplomatic and other activities planned for China. 
On the commercial side, Roger Severance, the Deputy Assistant Secretary for East Asia and the Pacific, was about to lead a delegation to China to take up a growing list of individual corporate problems with national and provincial leaders. 
These chiefly related to bureacratic interference in joint ventures and the inability of Chinese customers to obtain needed foreign exchange for payments.
Â 
Interrupted Operations
Also in July, the U.S.-China Joint Commission for Commerce and Trade, a high-level organization of the two governments created in the 1970's thaw, had been expected to meet to give new impetus to the commercial relationship.
This would have brought the Commerce Secretary, Robert A. Mosbacher, together for the first time with his counterpart, the Chinese Minister of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade, Zheng Tuobin.
When China reopened to the West 10 years ago, many business leaders had romantic notions about the huge market, with visions of 1 billion Chinese buying tube socks or other American miracle products.
But with many projects canceled in 1982 and with economic retrenchment last September, Americans now have a ''much more realistic view of doing business in China,'' Ms. Lucyk said.
''In China,'' she observed, ''we long ago lost our innocence.''

file: WORLD BANK LENDS CHINA $114 MILLION.txt
text:
ï»¿
The World Bank today approved the first loan to China since the student uprising last year that goes beyond the confines of meeting basic human needs.
The approval of the $114.3 million loan marked the first time in more than a year that the Bush Administration did not object to other than humanitarian assistance to China.
The World Bank's approval of the loan for technological improvements in rural industry had been expected for weeks, but it was uncertain whether the United States would vote against it. 
Such a move would have been largely symbolic, because both the European Community and Japan have resumed normal economic relations with China and both supported the loan.
Â 
Bush Met With Beijing Aide
The decision comes less than a week after President Bush met last Friday for the first time since the crackdown with the Chinese Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen. 
The meeting occurred a day after China abstained, rather than opposed, a vote by the United Nations Security Council authorizing the use of force to expel Iraq from Kuwait.
While the World Bank is owned by 155 member Governments, an American has headed it since it was founded in 1945 and the United States has a 20 percent vote on all major issues. 
The bank makes loans and helps countries in other ways to strengthen broad economic sectors by building such projects as dams, fertilizer plants, irrigation works, ports and highways.
Before the military crackdown on the democracy movement in June 1989, China had been receiving World Bank loans of more than $2 billion annually. 
Largely at the insistence of the United States all loans were initially blocked to China as part of a sanctions package.
Â 
Hostility on Capitol Hill
Since then, World Bank loans to China had shrunk to $650 million, primarily in the form of rural credits and assistance to small cooperative business enterprises in towns and villages.
The American position against non-humanitarian aid reflected opposition from Capitol Hill, where many lawmakers had been hostile to Beijing. 
But that opposition has been steadily softening since Iraq took over Kuwait in August and the Bush Administration began reaching out to a wide range of allies and other nations for support in challenging the invasion.
The package approved today consists of a $50 million loan and $64.3 million in credit.
Attila Karaosmaonoglu, the World Bank's vice president for Asian Affairs, said that other loans by the bank toChina were being prepared.

file: World Bank Seen Shifting China Stance.txt
text:
ï»¿
As the Bush Administration gingerly moves to repair economic ties with China, the World Bank seems likely to soon resume lending programs suspended after the crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in June, say officials of the bank, the United States and foreign governments.
To resume its lending, the bank needs formal approval from its 152 stockholders, including the United States, which holds 20 percent of the shares. 
The bank and Administration sources say the loans could be made as early as next month.
Â 
A Step Toward Approval
The Administration officially insists that its policy against World Bank lending to China remains unchanged. 
But the lifting of some American sanctions against China on Dec. 
19 was seen as a step toward Administration approval of such lending in the near future.
''That's the kind of talk we're hearing around the bank,'' said a senior World Bank official. 
A World Bank mission has just returned from two weeks in China.
Criticism of any new China loans is likely in Congress, where some members are seeking tougher sanctions against Beijing because of what they consider continued represssion of human rights.
But Administration officials plan to argue that new lending should encourage liberal forces within the Chinese leadership pressing both for a greater opening to the outside world and more respect for human rights, an Administration economic official said.
The China director for the World Bank, Shahid Javed Burki, a Pakistani, has just returned from his second mission to China since June. 
In an interview, he said that projects are ready to begin in areas like agricultural development, rural road building and thermal power generation.
Asked when the programs might start, he referred to a statement made Dec. 
14 by the bank's president, Barber B. Conable Jr.: ''It is our hope that in the not too distant future we can resume lending to China, but we do not have a specific date.''
Mr. Conable had also said the bank would be guided by China's economic performance, not political considerations.
Â 
Others Would Also Make Loans
Because of the World Bank's prestige as the biggest lender to the third world, approval would encourage lending by others, like the Manila-based Asian Development Bank and Japanese commercial banks, which also stopped loans after the June crackdown on dissent.
The World Bank, which is based in Washington, has provided $8 billion to China since 1981. 
It suspended $750 million of loans last June.
Since fall 1988, Beijing has moved toward central planning and away from the market-oriented policies that over the decade had attracted $14 billion of investment from industrial countries, of which $3.5 billion came from the United States.
An Administration official said Washington is trying to use a promise of World Bank lending to get the Chinese back to market-oriented policies.
Last Tuesday, the Adminstration announced that it had decided to approve the export of three American-built civilian communication satellites to China, all built by the Hughes Aircraft Company, and to lift bans on lending to China by the Export-Import Bank, an agency that provides financing for American exports.
Within 48 hours of the American action, Beijing announced plans to lift some restrictions on foreign investors. 
It said it would provide guarantees against confiscation, give investors the right to choose the chairman of a joint enterprise and end rules on the length of time a foreign project may operate in China. 
Previously, all joint ventures were for fixed periods, often 20 or 30 years.
Administration officials said the reaction indicated China's keen interest in maintaining economic links.
In defending his actions both in easing the sanctions and dispatching high-level missions to China after the crackdown, President Bush, a former ambassador to China, told a press conference Thursday, ''I know how China works.''
He added that the Administration wanted to ''see what we can do, make a representation on how strongly we feel against the human-rights abuse, but see what it's going to take to go forward.''
Â 
Cloudy Prospects
Business representatives said that despite the recent moves by both sides to improve the climate, the prospects for business remained cloudy.
''Nobody wants to pull out,'' said Roger W. Sullivan, president of the United States-China Business Council, ''but companies are operating at a lower level than before.''
The council represents 300 American multinational companies that do business in China.
Mr. Sullivan, a former State Department China specialist, said that American business was now most concerned about China's ''backtracking on enterprise reform.''
He said that the Chinese had previously wanted enterprises to respond to market forces, but they now have upgraded political and ideological control, giving party functionaries greater authority in factories.
''Faith in the inexorable progress of China has been badly shaken,'' he said. 
''Companies can't deal predictably anymore.''
Although the Export-Import Bank had been barred from making loans to China until the Administration's action earlier this week, the bank, which makes loans to finance American exports, continued to study China projects.
Since June it has made preliminary offers on four projects totaling $108 million of exports. 
Loans totaling $39 million are in the final stages of approval.

file: World Markets_The Cable and Wireless Conundrum.txt
text:
ï»¿
Cable and Wireless P.L.C., the British-based telecommunications company with a presence in 50 countries, pleased investors earlier this month when it reported pretax profits up 15.5 percent for the fiscal year ended March 31. 
And this in a recession year.
Moreover, more than 60 percent of the company's revenues are dollar based, so the strong rally of the dollar in the last five months sent analysts back to their calculators to raise their earnings forecasts for the current fiscal year. 
Although its headquarters are in London, the company's heart is Hong Kong where the currency is tied to the dollar. 
Cable and Wireless has a 58.4 percent controlling stake in Hong Kong Telecommunications, which provided 43 percent of the company's revenue and 59 percent of its profit last year.
Company officials, including its group managing director, Gordon M. W. Owen, and finance director, Rodney J. Olsen, crowed about these numbers on a recent visit to New York City. 
They waxed enthusiastic about the company's global digital "highway," including an American link with US Sprint. 
The highway is a fiber-optic cable system linking major financial centers and offering business customers such things as high-definition television and video-conferencing, high-speed data transmission and faxes. 
Cable and Wireless also owns Mercury Communications, the first and only competitor to British Telecommunications, the Government-owned phone company.
Despite its good looks last year and prospects in the current year, there are questions about Cable and Wireless which, at current prices, make the stock less attractive.
The stock's volatility reflects some of this uncertainty. 
In June alone, its price fell to 490 pence ($9.08 at Friday's exchange rate) and then rallied to 560. 
It closed Friday at 529. 
The company's American Depository Receipt which trades in New York has moved from a low of 24.875 to 26.875. 
It closed Friday at 25.50.
The stock already trades at a 13-to-20 percent premium to the British market as a whole, based on earnings projections.
Then there are the questions about the quality of Cable and Wireless' earnings. 
The company has had a good stream of average earnings over the last decade, but the yearly numbers are subject to big hits from exchange rate moves. 
Last year, for example, the company estimated that pretax profits would have doubled to 31 percent if the dollar had not been so weak. 
Now the high hopes for the current fiscal year are based on the current strong dollar retaining its strength.
Some of the pretax profit last year was based on special factors that should vanish this year. 
One was the sale of a managing director's house in Hong Kong that added 9.2 million pounds ($16 million) to the books.
In addition, the sale of 20 percent of Cable and Wireless' stake in Hong Kong Telecommunicatons to the Chinese Government reduced the company's borrowing needs in 1991, dropping the bank loan level from 59.9 million pounds ($104.2 million at the end-of-March exchange rate) in 1990 to 16.3 million pounds in fiscal 1991. 
Company executives acknowledge that borrowing will pick up again this year.
Such things accounted for a swing in the company's net-interest and other-income line from a 46.9 million pound deficit in 1990 to a 31.2 million pound surplus the following year. 
The 78.1 million pound shift accounts for all but 3.7 million pounds of the increase in profits before taxes.
All of these considerations must be weighed against larger questions about the future of Hong Kong, which reverts to the control of China in 1997. 
Hong Kong Telecommunications is not only Cable and Wireless' main business but also a source of money needed to expand Mercury back home in the United Kingdom, enhance the global digital highway and eventually make the company much less dependent on Hong Kong.
Cable and Wireless, as well as analysts like Robert B. Morris 3d of Goldman Sachs in San Francisco, are not worried about the takeover by China. 
Mr. Morris is more concerned, at least in the near term, about how a tax increase in Hong Kong will eat into Hong Kong Telecom's earnings this year.
"The investment program we have in Hong Kong would not be going on there unless we had confidence," said Mr. Owen, the group managing director for Cable and Wireless. 
But Hong Kong's future will still hang over the company and the stock for some time.
Finally, there is the fallout from recent government decisions about how the British telecommunications industry should be regulated. 
Analysts have generally concluded that the new regulatory approach gives breaks to both Cable and Wireless and British Telecommunications. 
But how they sort out to the bottom line in the next few years is still being debated.
Negative interpretations, like that of Partick Wellington of County Natwest Securities in London, emphasize that new costs Cable and Wireless could incur for access to the B.T. network and the price restructuring that will enable B.T. to lower prices to business customers could hurt the company. 
Postive views, like that of Michael Armitage of Morgan Stanley & Company in London, conclude that what is good for B.T. is good for Cable and Wireless.
